First of all, I uploaded some photos next to a soda can so you can visualize the size of the labelmaker.I love label makers.  My husband would say I am addicted to them.  Starting with the Dymo tape labels (remember those? You turned a little dial and squeezed the handle?) I have owned dozens.  This one is by far the fanciest.*Good:I set up the software for Windows.  First you need to download a program to update the software on the machine, then the software used to make labels.  You do have to get these from the Dymo site.The software is intuitive, although I was surprised that it could not tell which tape was loaded into the machine (my Brother can do that) automatically.A helpful window is provided on the underside for checking which tape you have loaded without having to open the machine.It can use lots of widths of tape.  It comes with a 1 inch sampler, which is actually pretty huge, but you can get all kinds.*Neutral:The touchscreen requires more force than the ones we are all used to now (Ipods and so on).*Bad:I do not like proprietary batteries, especially in devices like this where you will probably have to buy a brand name version when it dies.  This merits a star demerit when combined with the fact that it complains if you try to plug it in without the battery pack.Suggestions for purchase.This label maker is for those of us slightly insane about labels, or for commercial use. The reality is that it is much easier to make labels on the computer than on the machine (even this fancy one).  If you need portability or will not have it connected to a computer then this version will fit the bill.  If you use a label maker every day, again this machine would be worthwhile.  For your everyday person who just wants to slap a label on the tool chest, this is decidedly much more than you need.  In that case, look for a simpler model at a lower cost.

I thought I'd give these Avery Sticky Notes a try over the other brand, thinking "how different could a sticky note be?"Turns out, quite different. The first thing I noticed is that you can actually see the adhesive on the note. It's either residue on the next note left after you remove the top note, or the adhesive is just coming through the back of the note to the front. So the notes appear to have a two-tone color to them, where the top quarter of the note is a different color.They seem to require a lot more force to remove the top-most note from the pad. The adhesive seems to hold the pads together quite well.However, I suspect that some of the adhesive is left on the next note. Why? They don't stick well on many surfaces. I recently tried these out before going away, by leaving notes on certain doors and surfaces, since somebody who was stopping by to check on things. Within 30 minutes, several of the notes fell to the floor. I had to add a strip of tape to the notes to keep them in place. This defeats their intended purpose.If you remove a note from the pad, the corners at the adhesive turn-up dramatically. I think this keeps the notes from remaining attached to the intended surfaces. The paper will curl-away, and eventually the note will fall to the floor.I'll only use these for writing notes to myself or for attaching them to other papers, where they seem to adhere well. For other purposes, I wouldn't rely on them. If you leave a note for somebody, it will probably fall to the floor and end up missed.

This is a large printer with lots of features that work well.  I set this up on the wireless function to operate with my Mac. Yesterday, I needed to print out a color chart for our business products and I did a couple on the normal settings on my HP.  Then my ink got low so I switched over to the Brother to make a couple on there.  I decided to put it on the best quality settings because I wanted the colors to be very vibrant. We have a family of 5 with a small business and 3 kids in school; so, the stapler tends to get a lot of use.My first impression of this stapler was that it was light-weight and "cheapy" feeling; but, it actually works very well.The main difference between this unit and a traditional stapler is that it stores all the energy from the press until the last moment - at which time the spring releases and "shoots" the staple into whatever is being stapled.  That's kind of a cool idea to avoid the problem where the stapler hasn't been pressed hard enough.Because of that design, it actually is very easy to staple small stacks of documents or school papers/projects.  I'm not sure I'd use this in a busy office setting; but, it works great for standard home use.I will say, however, that it takes some getting used to.  Pretty much everyone who has used this stapler for the first time ends up with a wide-eyed expression when the staple suddenly shoots into whatever was being stapled.  The funny thing is that my kids just don't seem to be getting used to it - even though we've been using it for weeks now.  (For some reason it still seems to surprise them when it pops at the end.)Overall, I would recommend this little stapler.  It works different than you are probably used to, but it does the job very effectively.

When UPS delivered a box to me yesterday I wondered what it was because it was too light to be the printer I was expecting. Yes, it did turn out to be the Epson XP-400 All-in-One inkjet I had been waiting for. I didn't know if this relatively light box was a good thing or not, because it started me wondering what they had left off this all-in-one that my HP Officejet had on it that I really couldn't do without.It was extremely well packaged but took only a minute to get it completely plugged up and ready to install. I sat it in a very small space on my desk, since the printer only measures about 12 inches by 15 inches, even with the paper feed slot opened. What a difference between that and my Big and Heavy HP. It didn't take more than five minutes to put in the disc provided and update my firmware, and to connect the printer to my wireless network. Very easy. If you ever have a problem loading a printer, youtube is always there to help you out. But really, this was a snap.I ran a few test pages of black print and they were nice and dark. Then I ran a full-size photo on regular copy paper. It started printing....and printing....and printing. Since I work out of a home office, when it seemed to be taking forever to advance, I went to the basement and took some wash out of the dryer and put some more wash in the washer. When I came upstairs, it was still printing. So I took the wash upstairs to the linen closet and came back. It was just about finished. I should have timed it, but maybe that gives you an idea of how long color printing takes. A long time. But the color was good. I didn't gasp in amazed delight over it, thought it had a tad too much yellow compared to the screen image, but you know how that goes. The next picture I ran smaller on photo paper and it was good. Ran faster, of course, and the finished product was as good as any inkjet not specifically for photos that I have had.....and I've had quite a few.The cartridges seem to be holding up well. There is a function on the printer screen for checking ink levels whenever you like, not just when they are running low. Replacement cartridges are reasonably priced (that's usually where these low-priced printers get you, is in the after-sale of ink.)I can see this being a great printer for my small office. I do a lot of color printing and even if it takes a bit longer with this Epson, the overall result and cost will make it worth it. Think of all the wash I'll get done during working hours.Update:I have been running a lot of colored copies in the last few days and have never had a repeat of the very long running time that I experienced at first. I can only think the machine was working out the kinks or something. Much, much faster now - comparable to most of the other printers I've had. Only negative so far is some slight banding on standard copy paper that I don't see on the photo paper. But some of the prints have been rather outstanding, actually.Further update 10/04/12:Wish I didn't have to make this particular update, but if I were considering buying the XP-400 printer I would want to know. It may be just this single unit that is doing it, so read other reviews and see if it is a common problem before you decide not to buy. I haven't used the printer an excessive amount. Normally my printers get much more use than I have put on this one. But already I am getting blurry roller lines on my work. I don't know a cure for that other than having the rollers replaced, which of course isn't worth it in a printer in this price range. So the Epson XP will be replaced a lot sooner than I had planned.

I had a Canon BubbleJet BJC-4200 long ago, and after that printer I was very hesitant to even consider another Canon printer. When my most recent printer died, an HP DeskJet 970cse, I needed to find a good printer that could print duplex and produce quality output. After reading many, many reviews I decided to give Canon another chance. I am very glad that I did so.The Pixma iP4500 arrived in a huge box, and as it turns out it needed the space. This is a larger printer than I expected, and as a result I had to rearrange my desk to find room for it. That's a small oversight on my part. The printer itself is an unassuming-looking box of a machine, though it resembles more of a printer when the paper trays are populated.Setup was easy and straightforward, though I do recommend using the "getting started" insert before setting everything up. Though setting everything up is relatively self-explanatory, it is helpful to see the illustration of what to do in order before making the leap. Overall, setup took maybe 20-30 minutes once the parts were all out of the box and everything was set up.Once configured, installing the drivers is simple. Drop in the CD, follow the prompts, and turn on the printer at the right time. No fuss.Once set up and powered on, the printer is ready to go to work. I print a majority of my things in duplex mode so I tweaked the driver configuration to make it the default, after which the setting is more or less invisible. Everything in the driver configuration is very easy to find, straightforward, and simple.There are two ways to feed paper into the iP4500. There is a top-loader which is the default paper source and there is a front-loading paper tray ("cassette" according to Canon's documentation). Heavier papers such as card stock should be loaded from the top-loader.So, how does this printer perform? I'll break it down into two parts, speed and quality.Speed - this is a relatively fast printer! Feeding it a print job that conists of a two-sided black and white print this printer can churn out the pages, including the dry time for the front page, in about 20 seconds. Granted, this is my experience and your mileage may vary but it's a good starting point from which to base your evaluation of the speed. My previous printer would take at least a minute to print the very same documents, and it still couldn't keep up when in draft mode. For photo printing it churns out a full-page 8.5"x11" borderless photo in roughly 45 seconds.Quality - what good is speed without quality? This printer backs it up. The text and basic image quality is acceptable, though it could be a touch better. This is not noticeable in day-to-day print jobs. On photo printing, though, this printer is an absolute showstopper. The photos it prints, on photo paper, are better than most magazine prints and could easily be used for photo studio gallery shots.It would be nice if the printer actually had a USB cable in the box, but this is a small thing.Overall, this is a high-quiality, high-performance printer that is sure to please even the staunchest of critics. It is fast, creates beautiful output, and is very easy to set up.

I was surprised to see the Epson WorkForce WF-M1030 Wireless Monochrome Printer introduced. After all, doesn't everybody want a full color ink jet these days? But, after using it, I think Epson may be on to something with this idea.For about as long as there have been personal computers users have had to weigh the competing problems of initial cost, for the printer, plus cost per page, the cost of refills for ink or toner. Back in the Jurassic era, when a "printer" meant a dot matrix printer, the original Apple Laser Writer was a revolution in all ways that word can be used. It also cost over $3000.00 for a 4ppm all mono printer behemoth that weighed a ton and had no networking. That opened up the field to ink jets, which from the beginning have taken a razor and razor blades approach, cheap initial cost for the printer followed by expensive ink refills and a high per page cost.Over the past few years the cost of mono laser printers have been plummeting, until you can now buy a basic laser printer for under a hundred-dollars with performance and features that would have made an Apple owner weep twenty years ago. Ink jets have vastly improved in speed and quality over this same period, while the initial cost has only dropped modestly. The sticking point has still been the per page cost, driven by the industry wide practice, until recently, of pricing the refills at as high as the market would bear. This of course opened up the market for cheap, and sometimes not so good, refills. But that's another story.Enter the Epson WorkForce WF-M1030 Wireless Monochrome Printer. Epson has been wising up on refill costs recently. This printer features not only a high per page speed, and both wireless and ethernet networking, but also a small footprint and, most importantly, relatively high capacity ink refills for prices that make the per page cost competitive finally with lasers.After using this printer for a while, and outputting letters and labels and all the rest, I can say it's a great printer, easy to set up -- very much like my recent Epson color inkjet in that regard. If you need only mono then I would say that it's a fine alternative or replacement for a laser. If you want to keep a color printer for photos and so forth as well as a mono printer for low cost output needs then this looks like a winner.If automobiles had followed the same price trajectory as computers and printers for the past thirty years then a new Lexus or BMW would only cost about five-thousand dollars these days. Sadly, that's not the case for cars. But this is an amazing printer that, happily, is available at a low initial cost with reasonable per page costs on refills. RECOMMENDED.

First of all, XP-610 arrived with one out of five ink cartridges (magenta) missing.  Since I also have XP-810, which uses the same cartridge, I just replaced it to get this one working. I also don't have time these days to sweat the small stuff.  I've bought numerous printers in my life and this is the first time I've ever encounter a missing piece. I hope this is a unique and rare situation and it doesn't happen to anyone else.  So my review is on the quality and functionality of the printer itself.Design wise, XP-610 is very cute and much smaller than I had imagined because my previous multifunction printer was Canon MX870, which is much larger than this one.  However, you might want to buy this printer only if your purpose is to have great photo printouts, along with other minor daily printing needs.  If you don't need great photo outputs, you might want to consider other options because XP-610 has some seemingly flimsy parts due to the size.  It's not that these parts are fragile, but if you have a teenage boy at home, it might not stand the test.  If you are usually gentle with your products, this should not be a problem.The wireless setup is very easy.  My computer (with Windows 8.1) recognized it instantly. I downloaded the driver and utilities from Epson website to install the printer instead of using the CD that comes with it.  I didn't even consider the wired network because the wireless connection is very stable and convenient. I can move the printer anywhere I like to print, since it's also very light, without having to worry about the network wire.The paper tray is very thin and it holds only about 100 sheets of paper; not enough for frequent printing in an office, but more than enough for home use.It has a secondary tray that holds about 20 sheets of premium photo paper.  However, I get paper jammed frequently when I print from this tray.  It could be because my photo paper was too thick (I used Cannon premium glossy photo paper.  Epson photo paper are a little more expensive.).  It didn't damage the paper, just didn't pick it up properly.  So I had to remove the jam and restart printing.  So I remove one star for my paper jam experience.  Otherwise, the printouts have been outstanding and I am very satisfied with them.There is also a tray for printing CD and DVD.  That's what I love about my previous Epson printers also.  Even though I don't print CD/DVD so frequently, it comes very handy when I wanted to present a disc to someone with style.The main difference between this XP-610 and a more expensive XP-810 is the double-sided feature, otherwise they are almost identical.  The double-sided scanning, copying, faxing, and printing can save a lot of time if you need it often.  However, the more mechanism a product have the more likely it will break.  So if you don't need the double-side feature and would like to save some money, XP-610 should be enough.

The fabric picks up dirt, hair, skin, and body oils, and every single one I've owned eventually "blows out" and starts losing gel from the sides. It's not something that happens overnight, but over time they get to be pretty yucky. It serves its intended purpose perfectly, and functions better than expected.

Executive Summary - It's hard to find a use for these that other things don't do better.  And the product's flaws make it a questionable solution for things that you do use it for.These labels are fighting for space in the weakly adhesive note niche dominated by Post-It notes.  Avery's idea is to make a weakly adhesive note specialized for labels.Problem.  When you want to put a label on something, you want the label to stay there.  You can't rely on these labels to do that under normal conditions.  The part of the label on the opposite edge of the tear away tab curls up when you pull it off the pad.  Then, when you apply the label - that curled part will pull away by itself after a few minutes.  If you push it down, it pops right up again.  The adhesive is too weak to hold it down against the curl of the paper.  This happens on every surface (paper, cardboard, smooth plastic, rough plastic, painted wood) I tested except for clean glass.  This can be a problem if you have the label on a moveable item - like a file folder.  Put these labels on 10 file folders.  Lay those folders out on a desktop - move them around - let one slide over another.  Stuff you would actually do in the real world.  There's a good chance that curled up part will catch on another folder and peel right off.  Worse than useless!So you can only use these labels on things that don't move or come into contact with moving things - like sticking them on a wall or a chart.  But a Post-It note would work just as well in that situation.On the positive side, the labels are easy to write on.  When you pull them off there is no adhesive residue.  They look good.  Since they're not actually harmful, I can't give them a one star.

I generally have no use for all-in-one printers.  I don't fax, I rarely copy, and scanning is only an occasional task.  So my standalone scanner usually spends most of its time in the box, and I take it out when I need it.I've had an HP Scanjet 2200c for over 9 years, and it's been just fine.  But because of its age, it was not going to work with my new Windows 7 computer (HP stopped supporting it after XP).  I had my eye on the Canon LiDE 200 series for a while, particularly because they draw power through the USB cable, eliminating the extra power cord and bulky transformer.  When I saw at the Canon site that an updated model (210) was coming, I waited for its release and bought one.A couple of nice benefits:- very small/slim design, thanks to the use of LEDs instead of the traditional fluorescent tube- one-touch scanning to PDF- auto-sizing that works (no more manually designating the edges of a less-than-letter-size object)The software is a little bloated, but you can easily deselect what's not necessary during the installation.  The unit scans very quickly (thanks to the faster warm-up time of the LEDs) and both documents and photographs come out very clean and sharp.  I'm still getting used to some of the settings (after using the HP software for so long), and I don't expect to use the LiDE 210 all that often, but this is exactly what I needed.If you're just an occasional scanner like me and don't want the size/bulk of an all-in-one on your desk, this unit is right up your alley!

I selected the Smead Erasable SuperTab File Folders because the 'erasable' label area is a strong selling point.  Imagine my chagrin when I received the folders to learn in small print on the package: "Permanent marker and white eraser required (not included).  Not compatible with ballpoint pens, #2 or mechanical-style pencils or standard pencil erasers."Huh?Was my imagination at work once again (happens all the time when I try to fit my bod into a size too small, but that's another story).The PR description reads: * Erasable SuperTab allows you to revise or reuse folder* Handwrite directly on tab with a permanent marker, erase with a standard eraser* Oversized tab for larger or more lines of text* Eco-friendly solution'I suppose it's all in how one defines 'standard eraser.'  I've since learned that the eraser in question is made of hi-polymer and sells for a bit more than the pink ones.So don't order the folders expecting to use just any old standard eraser.I bought the white eraser and new sharp Sharpies and the folders do erase quite well.  The PR's right - it would be easy to erase and revise (if you can locate that white eraser).  The tab is truly large which is good since labels can't be typed and must be hand written with that marker.And with regard to 'eco-friendly' - there's a 'minimum 10% post consumer recycled content.'  And, of course, if you discount the eco factor in buying the new eraser, it's saving a folder label.The folders are sturdy and erasable; five stars to the folders.One star to the misleading advertising.

The best way to review this printer is to compare it to peers in its class I have also owned and have conducted A/B comparison tests with to see where each excels. I have included the R2000 as the first in the comparison.EPSON R2000 - MSRP $599-PIGMENT based printer+Excellent quality on Fine Art & Matte paper+Very good color, but not as much pop/dynamic range as dye+Excellent black & white-Very good quality on Gloss, Semi-Gloss, and Luster paper-Non-matte paper requires an extra overcoat of gloss, which is one of the replaceable ink tanks. If you print on gloss/semi-gloss/luster primarily, you will be changing the gloss optimizer cartridge more than any other one.-100+ year lifespan on all papers, with the exception that pigment is more likely to chip, scratch, or flake if not protected by glass since it sits on top of the paper unlike dye.-Water resistant-Good build quality, fit and finish. Oddly you need a spare parts box for this printer as things like the DVD tray and large paper tray do not slide into the printer as they do in the Canon printers. The roll adapter also must be stored seperately.-Fair quality paper feed path, has problems with some types of paper (for instance HP trifold matte paper gave it problems at times). Expect more paper jams with this one.-Can print roll paper for panoramic-Since it is pigment, less variation in finishes as ink sits on top of the paper.-Must be turned on and nozzle check pattern printed 1x/wk to prevent clogging. Has a reputation for clogging more than CANON, which may be due to smaller nozzle size.CANON PRO-10 - MSRP $699PIGMENT based printer+Excellent quality on Fine Art & Matte paper+Very good color, but not as much pop/dynamic range as dye+Excellent black & white+Very good quality on Gloss, Semi-Gloss, and Luster paper-Non-matte paper requires an extra overcoat of gloss, which is one of the replaceable ink tanks. If you print on gloss/semi-gloss/luster primarily, you will be changing the gloss optimizer cartridge more than any other one.+Over 100 year lifespan on all papers, with the exception that pigment is more likely to chip, scratch, or flake if not protected by glass since it sits on top of the paper.+Water resistant+Fantastic build quality, fit and finish. Built like a tank.+Fantastic quality paper feed path, will take nearly any paper easily-Cannot print roll paper-Since it is pigment, less variation in finishes as ink sits on top of the paper.-Must be turned on every other week to prevent clogging. Turning printer on will be enough to prevent clogging with this printer.CANON PRO-100 - MSRP $499DYE based printer+Excellent quality on Canon Platinum Pro Gloss, Semi-Gloss, and Luster paper+With above paper, photo will last 50 years framed or 300 years in photo album w/o fading+Very good quality on Matte and Fine Art paper, but...-No guarantee on fade resistance with fine art & matte paper since it is uncoated & porous+Excellent pop and dynamic range than pigment printers - great for posters!+Good Black & White, but it has a very slight brownish tint you would not notice unless you had a PRO-10/R2000 print to compare it to-Some papers are water resistant, but dye is much more prone to water damage than pigment+Fantastic build quality, fit and finish. Built like a tank.+Fantastic quality paper feed path, will take nearly any paper easily-Cannot print roll paper+Since it is dye, your prints will more closely take on the characteristics of the paper it is printed on as the ink is absorbed into the paper.+Can sit for over a year without printing or being turned on with no clogsOVERALL, I felt if you want the best printer for all situations, having both a PRO-10 for black & white and very important photos, and a PRO-100 for highly saturated prints like posters is the best combination. I was not impressed with the Epson R2000 as a package due to its build, fit/finish, and paper feed issues despite its quality prints (similar to PRO-10 in quality).If you can only pick one, look at the PROs and CONs and pick which is best! :)

I am a scientist in addition to being a private instructor in math and science. I typically use 0.9mm mechanical pencils when I am teaching/writing instructional material for my students because the thicker lead is bolder and easier to read, along with being erasable (absolutely essential when you teach math!)  I have long wished I could use pen because its much easier to read on paper and makes lasting, professional looking notes.  After trying the Sharpie erasable pencil and the Papermate erasable ball points, I was disenfranchised from the whole "erasable pen" idea and just trudged on with my fat pencils.  When I found some Frixion's locally on clearance, I decided to give them a whirl and they were an absolute HIT with my students.  Not only do they yield beautiful, dark and steady ink flow, they are actually and truly erasable leaving no sign of previous markings on the paper.  My students LOVE these pens and have all commented that they are much easier to read than pencil.  As an added plus, they are very easy to write with and among the best gel pens I have ever used (and I've used them all...)Now, why the 4 stars? Well there are a few MAJOR disadvantages, or trade-offs, for the erasability.  1) The ink is erasable due to friction, hence the name "Frixion."  This means whenever the ink is exposed to any rubbing or abraision, it disappears without a trace.  I learned this the hard way when I was doing some erasing on the back side of a double-sided page of notes I was composing.  When I erased on the back, the writing on the front was rubbed off too.  Then, later in the day, my notes were erased when my notebook was shuffling around in my backpack.  Not good.  2) The ink runs out fast and goes illegibly light when there is still visible amounts of ink in the barrel.  I can usually get about 20 pages front and back per pen before all the ink has been used.  Considering they run nearly $2 per pen, thats pretty pricey; particularly when you write 50+ pages a week like I do.Overall: these are bar-none the BEST erasable pens on the market.  They are WELL WORTH the purchase even for those curious to try a novelty writing instrument.  Excellent and very much recommended!  See my photos for samples of the ink!

When I teach lower level math or science classes, I often recommend to my students that they buy a Casio,  usually the fx-300 series because they are much more intuitive that the TI series, deal well with fractions (which are often difficult for students) and the natural display ( what you are entering LOOKS like what is in your text or your problem) is more intuitive for them.  Dealing with natural logs "e", and powers of ten are also more straightforward on a Casio.  Plus, they are cheap.This calculator would be a natural progression for use in the next level of classes, as it adds the functions needed for more advanced algebra and graphing.  I had no trouble figuring it out, but I have spent many hours messing with calculators (I think I know where the ln and log button are on at least 15 different kinds).  This Casio IS more intuitive than at TI.  If you are used to a TI you will figure this one out, if you have never used a graphing calculator, the Casio is simpler to manage.However, for more advanced classes , many professors/teachers are only familiar with the TI series and if you show up with a Casio, you are on your own as far as figuring out how to use it.  It is not that the TI is better, but it has a larger market share in upper level classes (college algebra, calculus, physics...) so teachers are used to it.The computer connection leaves something to be desired.  It ran ok on my 32 bit machine, but I ended up spending two hours trying to  download the 64 bit from Casio (it is available at edu.casio.com) and failing.  You have to create an account and then website is confusing and full of the sort of English that is almost right, but not quite with instructions that leave you wondering how a company that makes such great calculators can have such a clunky website.  The 32bit interface looks like something designed 15 years ago, with little updating.  The computer connection is really just not operating at the level it should be.This calculator still has the problem (also common with TIs) that it will happily graph a function such as (x-2)/((x-2)(x+2)) without in any way noting that there is a hole in the graph at x=2.  I am not sure what graphing calculators can do about this, as the screen resolution is not that great, but some sort of warning would be useful.  I am not taking any stars off for this, as I have not yet found one that is explicit about warning students about this issue.I like that it uses regular AAA batteries, rather than button cell.The buttons do have a cheaper feel than on the Tis, but I have been using some Casios for 15 years with no problems with the buttons.So, in a nutshell, this calculator will do everything you need it to do for class, but most teachers will be less familiar with it than the TI.  It is a very good value for the money and more intuitive to use than a TI.  If you are willing to puzzle it out yourself, this is a good deal.  If you are going to need your teacher to step you through how to use it, make sure he/she is familiar with Casio calculators.

We have three cordless phones in the house, but we've always kept one hard-wired phone to use when the electrical power goes out. (The power lines in our area are aboveground, but most telephone lines are underground. During storms, we often lose electrical power, but the phone lines are usually intact. The cordless phones, which require AC power, are useless at those times, but a hard-wired phone still works.) When our hard-wired phone recently died after about twenty-five years of service, we replaced it with the AT&T; 210 Corded Phone. It's a fine telephone, reminiscent in style of the old AT&T; Princess Phone of the 1960s, but modernized with memory-dial. Other than that, it's pretty much a basic, bare-bones telephone, which is what we need during power outages.The AT&T; 210 appears to be solidly built, and we expect to get many years of service from it. For the very low price, it meets our expectations perfectly.

At first glance the clear acrylic of this memo and paper clip holder might make you think its glass.  Obviously that's not the case, but it is far more substantial than "just plastic".I'm not one for littering my desk with well-intentioned storage googaws but this is just stylish enough that I decided to go for it.  It has the weight that you need to be able to snatch a page from a Post-it pad without sending the holder across the room, and it dresses things up quite nicely.

I'm very impressed with these boxes.  I don't use them to put file folders in.  Instead I use them to store teaching items and they can really take a beating.  Heavy, awkwardly shaped items and being tossed around isn't uncommon for them.  They stay together, firm and strong.  I like them better than moving boxes as you can lift the lid or peek through the handles to see what's inside.Well worth the money and better than other ones I've used.  They take a lickin' and keep on tickin'.  (Bad joke, I know!)

The actual glue is comparable to every other name-brand super glue/Krazy glue out there, which is to say it's pretty darn good. What sets this apart is the container, which is a precision applicator. The front and back labels rest on buttons that pop out slightly from the container, and squeezing them results in a mini-eyedropper effect. This cuts the mess to nil and prevents one wrong squeeze from wasting the whole tube.Just one tip of caution: store the container upright. I did not have this particular problem, but another reviewer had it leak when they laid it on its side.

As an Amazon Vine participant, I thought I'd use this as a back-up to my Epson 340. Well, the 340 will be moving to the back burner. Except for printing photos and CD/DVD labels, the 600 is a great little printer. (Well, actually, it's rather large.) My favorite features are:- Color copier: This is so much better than my usual home remedy of scanning my original and then printing a copy from my computer. The color copy is as crisp as the original.- Black and white copier: Again, far superior and less time-consuming than scanning and with excellent reproduction. It also beats using the copier at work!- Photo printing: I'm not going to knock off a star for this because it isn't sold as a photo printer. I compared two prints of the same subject side-by-side, one from my 340 and one from by new 600. The colors were comparable, but the resolution wasn't as good on the 600.- Fax: Quite frankly, I haven't tested that feature and probably won't use it. Most of my documents can be emailed. If the rare occasion arises when I need a fax, I can hook it up, but it isn't a very probable situation.- General printer: Copies, both black-and-white and color, are great.- Control panel: Well-lit, easy-to-use and easy to understand.- Wireless capability: Now that's the big seller for me since I tend to work at several locations in my house and prefer not to move into the office to print. The networked wireless printing function is flawless.- Set up: Hmmmm. This was easy with one exception. I was unable to set up the wireless function with an ethernet connection between my Mac and the printer, although that was the alternate set up procedure. It was necessary to connect directly through my router. After the initial set up, the ethernet cable is disconnected and the wireless connection takes over.- Scanning: I'm in the process of scanning all my old photos and it's nice to have one machine that can do everything without having to drag out the old scanner as well.I'm quite happy with this product and highly recommend it!

These NoteTabs are thicker than I expected.  They are nearly as good as the tabs I use in a 3-ring binder.  They can be used to mark pages, or you can divide up a book or other media that doesn't have the ability to add normal dividers.I've used post it notes in the past, but these are preferable because the sticky part is clear, allowing you to see the text under the tab.  You can also remove them and reuse them, or write on them.  I love these for text books or reference books where I want to make a note, but don't want to write on the page.

I have school age children that use markers to complete school projects and decorate personal items.  Each school year I average buying a set of markers every couple of months or when a new project is assigned. The Bic Mark-It Collection Permanent Marker set has lasted through several months of use during the previous school year and will begin the current school year as they are still going strong.  This marker set has a nice variety of colors, they mark on any type material and they are easy and comfortable to hold.  What I like most is the plastic storage case/container.  It is very sturdy as compared to the containers our previous markers came in (cardboard that tears after a few uses or the flimsy plastic bags with the snap closure that also tear)-so far we have been able to keep the entire set together without loosing any, something we have never been able to do in the past.

Does it matter where you buy your mailers? Sure it does...these are exactly as described, tough, roomy, good adhesive, and you can pack and mail with confidence that your contents are protected. You not find a better deal than these, I promise, I looked. (Especially on the local big store office supply shelves)......These are as advertised, no switching! I recommend!

Back in the day, EVERYBODY had a Trapper Keeper.  I got my first one when I was in first grade- it was blue with hot air balloons on it.  (I'm not sure why a 1st grader needed a Trapper Keeper, even a nerdy one like me, but the folders made a GREAT place for the scratch-n-sniff stickers the cafeteria gave out on special Sticker Days!)  And I love, love, loved it and took it to school every single day until I got a new Trapper Keeper for my birthday in fifth grade.  That one was the sandy-beach-with-seashells-themed Trapper.  I still have both of them.  Yes I do.So when I saw this Trapper Keeper offered in my Vine offerings, with the original font spelling out "Trapper Keeper" and the same border around it, but without the iconic pictures or designs, I STILL snapped this baby up.  Part of it was definitely for nostalgia's sake.  I have no immediately apparent need for a Trapper at this point in my life.  I've been out of graduate school for a dozen years now, with no plans to return to a schoolish setting.  But there was just something very beguiling about this sleek black Trapper Keeper... something familiar, and yet utterly different.  It was like seeing an old friend who's had some "improvements," if you catch my drift.Nah, this ain't my old Trapper Keeper.  In place of the Trapper Keeper designs and photos, this one encourages you to add your own instead.  That's kind of cool!  While this incarnation of the Trapper Keeper is not as rigid as the old-school version, I have to say that this is an instance of something being better than it used to be.  The areas on the old Trappers that saw a lot of flexion and therefore a lot of wear and rippage, such as the fold-over flap where you'd open and close it, and along the spine are now either refinforced and a more unibody-design (referring to the spine here), or the flap has become fabric.  The velcro closure from the '80s is now a heavy-duty snap.  It's serious, but not so difficult to use that a nerdy first-grader couldn't handle opening and closing it, to stick scratch-n-sniff stickers from the cafeteria on the plastic index dividers inside the Trapper.  Do they still make scratch-n-sniff stickers and hand them out on Sticker Day in cafeterias?  I hope so.In the front cover, there are two flat pockets that you can slide in thin documents.  On the back cover, there's a pen or pencil loop, made from elastic.  And my model came with 5 colored plastic full-page index dividers.  I don't think the holes will be ripping out of those any time soon.The really cool thing about this Trapper Keeper, besides having a "Hello, Old Friend!" moment, is that they took a really cool thing from back in the day and made it even better, even more customizable, and even more durable.  This ain't my old Trapper Keeper, but it's even better!

This may be true of almost all binders, that when you get the 1 inch size they also cut down the width of the binder, but you need to know when choosing a binder for your project.  Be sure to measure what you are going to put inside of it, especially the width of the page. When I put a hole punched 8.5 inch wide sheet of paper in this, it has about .5 in room left to the edge of the binder.  If I put a sheet protector in it, the sheet protector hangs out a tiny bit.  Anything bigger that a sheet protector (like a tab attached to a sheet protect) is definitely too wide for it.  With sheet protectors, it's still usable, but not ideal if you actually want to protect the contents. The rings snap closed very tight -- that's good.  D rings are definitely the way to go.  The binder itself is okay, a few bumps in the plastic.  I like that the clear plastic cover on the outside is a little short, making it easier to get an 8.5 x 11 sheet out.

This is a good Dry-Erase Board. I have had no issues. I use it to keep track of my weekly mile goals (bicycle). It is a bit too big for my fridge but it might be just right for most. I like it, it seems somewhat well made. The quality is ok. The magnets are easy to stick on and they are strong. I have had no issues with the board sliding down.

This Brother MFC-7360N Multi-Function Laser Printer with works great with Vista 64 Bit. I have it connected via the USB port, so I cannot comment on how well it would work with networking. So far I have found nothing that I do not like about this printer. The built in flatbed scanner works great also. I think it is bargain at this price.
This is the right ink for our printer.  Sometimes when you need to add an extra item to fill an order, add ink to your cart.  We only use HP and online it can safe money and time.

These boxes go together easily and are sturdy once together.  The viewing window is handy if you want to know what the box contains, or can be turned away if you don't.  They hold a reasonable amount and easily slide out of view under the bed (low enough to fit nicely even under a very low bed).  Alternately they are attractive enough you could store them on a shelf in your office for easier access.I typically use plastic boxes for storage, and for important documents I actually will continue to use plastic (at least if I will be storing them in the basement), as in the event of a flood, the contents of these would be ruined rather quickly.  But for upstairs storage these work great.

Bright pink, blue, yellow and green ("Limeade") labels (10 labels per sheet).  These colors really stand out.The adhesive is a nice blend of sticky, yet easy to remove from any surface (they easily peel back off from paper).Easily printed on by hand or with a laser printer or ink jet printer.These won't adhere to cloth (well not for more than a few seconds if you flex it), so you can't use them as name tags.

These white board pens have a broad tip, so there's no fine writing here.  These are great if you have a big whiteboard and want to write or draw a large, bold message. I wanted to use these on a calendar whiteboard with small squares, and the broad tip doesn't leave much room to write more than a time and two words for an appointment.The four colors are good for organizing or highlighting specific notes.  They are low odor, and I don't notice the smell at all.  Although the colors are bright, they wipe off clean and have not left a mark on my whiteboard.  I like the transparent barrel so that I can see the ink level.  Overall, good quality pens.

The Epson Workforce WF-3540 Wireless printer is a great printer, producing high quality color images. I have only tried printing from my wireless laptop and not my other devices (namely my Kindle Fire, which I haven't been able to find printing capabilities connected to). It's a heavy machine, and not small, but it fit with relative ease on the top of my own office desk. Set up was relatively easy too.The print quality for this machine is stunning, especially compared to a HP printer (within the same price range and with similar features) that my family owns. Scanning documents is relatively easy, and I love that it allows individuals to save OCRs as PDF files. My only quip with the Epson Workforce is not that with the results it produces (which are superior, in my opinion), it's the price of the ink sold for this machine. Yes, it promises to reduce the amount of ink you'll need to print with, but it costs a lot of money: nearly $40 for the multicolor and  $20 for individual color packs, (which could run $60 or more, if the packs were bought separately instead of the multipack).Anyway, with that small flaw, I still love this printer.

First things first.  The packaging for this huge stapler is very hard to open.Secondly, not only is this stapler huge, it's heavy too, and larger than I thought it would be.  It does come with 2 small boxes of 500 staples each.Installing the staples isn't any harder to do than any other kind of stapler you might use.I wanted to order this stapler though the Vine Program, because I already have a very small stapler that works for one or two pages, and a regular sized stapler that maybe works if you are trying to staple about 10 pages, then this larger stapler will work for about 50 pages or so, which I will also need from time to time as I do print out newsletters that are hard to staple, or hard to really secure the staple to that many pages if it's more than 10 pages.I did notice that if you are not trying to staple alot of pages with this stapler, the staple will come out to where the points are sticking up from the pages on the front of the page, but on the back it will be secured.It was easy to put two finger on the top of the stapler and staple.  You don't need to put alot of pressure onto the top of the stapler, like you need to do with normal staplers.  The head of the stapler has a cushiony feel, so that it isn't like most staplers where the entire stapler feels the same way.There is a leaflet of 4 small pages including the cover which shows the stapler, which also shows that this stapler has a 2 year warranty and, a 30 day money back guarantee. I've never seen any stapler that comes with any kind of warranty, not to my recollection.  This stapler does seem very sturdy.Another good thing about this stapler is what they call "A Cease Fire" Safety Feature, which prevents the stapler from being fired into the air.  I says when the stapler is not in normal use or not in contact with a solid surface, the handle locks so the stapler will not fire a staple.  It never hurts to have some kind of precaution.Iam happy to have 3 kinds of staplers-- A small one to handle a few pages, another stapler to use for a medium amount of pages, and then this huge stapler that can handle the rest as far as how many pages it can handle, up to 65 pages, which is alot of pages.Iam very happy with this stapler. To me it has alot of good features.  Normally I don't think about staplers, or how many pages it can handle, but it's nice to know that I will be prepared to staple pretty much anything that will need to be stapled.

I like the fact that you can set it up to answer your cell phone calls on it as well. I can't count the number of times I missed a call on my cell phones once it was in the other room. This allows you to have your cell calls go through the house phone and you don't worry about not hearing your cell phone.You can only receive one call at a time though.the sound quality couldn't be better. I would really recommend this phone. You can also buy additional handset later it you find that you need more handsets.

When I first opened the box, I thought oh, how whimpy and didn't really think I was going to like it.  The magnet really does a great job staying put.  I thought that it might slide down the cabinet as mail built up but it hasn't budged one bit.  The only thing that could be better is that the opening is narrow at the top, and the unit is hard plastic so you can scrape your knuckles when going to retrieve mail from it.  Now, I start at the top and spread it apart with my fingers and then slide my hand down to get mail or receipts down at the bottom.  Works great and I have no hesitation in recommending it.

As far as features, this printer is a vast improvement over my older Lexmark and Canon.  I love the color copying and duplex printing features.  Photos come out very well.  However, the price of a new printer on a great deal is not that much more expensive than the replacement ink.  I haven't bothered with remanufactured or filling my own in some time since the resulting printing was disappointing.  I have this Canon and another Pixma MX300.  Walmart had a new Pixma MX320 (newer) for $70 while the replacement ink at Staples cost $40 for black & $27.19 for color (for MX320).  I could have a newer printer including ink for the same price.  The Pixma MP610 ink was $57.49 for all colored ink and my first purchase of remanufactured black ink was $14.29.  These printers seem to use ink rapidly.  If one doesn't mind the cost of ink or is content with remanufactured or do-it-yourself refills, this printer is highly recommended.

These envelopes are actually quite pretty in person with raised, embossed details and bright, vibrant colors.  The problem is that I was expecting six patterned envelops and there are in fact only three  You get three plain white ones too, but those are meant to be used out outer envelopes for the three patterned ones. So even though it says six, you really can only send three.The other problem is that they are very thin.  I tried a few different items to get an idea and couldn't fit a small shirt into the largest envelope.  Books fit fine, as long as they weren't really thick hardcovers.Personally, I'm going to use the three patterned envelopes as stocking stuffer packages at home, and the three plain white envelopes to mail out books to friends.$12.99 for 3 too-thin patterned mailers and 3 plain ones is WAY TOO MUCH. I won't be buying any more of these.
I use this for my printer at university. It is cheap enough to where I don't have to buy the off brand. It lasts a good while more or less.

I have a small office with three printers. In the last two weeks two of those printers quit working. They were about four years old. When I got the chance to get the Epson WF-3620 printer I was excited, as it seemed like an excellent replacement. This is not a large office type printer and should work well within the home environment.First thing you will notice is the weight of the printer. It is listed at 24.7 pounds and  seems to be a little heavier than the Canon it is replacing. Not a large printer, it measures 19.2 X 21.1 X 12.9. The printer MUST sit firmly on a hard surface; otherwise the paper tray may get into a bind and be hard to close.The set up was easy, however like many electronic gadgets and computers items the written instruction that at one time filled pages are no longer given with the printers. The printer comes with a DVD which will direct you to an update download for the operation and drivers. I am using a MAC. The file is large and takes several  minutes to download. Once downloaded the rest of the set up is easy. I opted for the USB connection, as some of my wireless set ups kept getting mixed up in the small office space and does not always function properly. If you have only this printer as a printer and you can go wireless I personally think that would be the way. The printer also has Wi Fi and you can therefore print from your iPad if you have Wi Fi set up in your location.The scanner is a flat bed type with 2400 dpi resolution. You can scan to your PC. I do not use fax so this feature was not hooked up.I am not going to get into all the specs as you can read them on the product page however let me touch on a couple of features. There is the claim that this printer has “Performance Beyond Laser”. Don’t know about that as my first few pages came out at just about the same quality as pages from my older printers. I have now printed several sheets and I cannot say that printer has either laser speed or quality, however the quality is very good and serves my purpose. The specs claim 19 black pages per minute and 10 color. I never seem to achieve those levels however the printer is quick. I have not yet printed any photos on this printer.There is a large, 250 sheet capacity,  paper tray plus a rear tray. In the front there is a paper tray for this printer and I inserted 250 sheets of paper into the tray. The “size sliders” on the tray work really well whereas my older printer you had to tug on the slides to get them to move. The 2.7-inch touch screen makes for easy navigation of your needs. There is auto 2-sided print, copy and  scan. The automatic feeder worked real well with easy feeds, no sheets sticking together and no jams. If you run into a technical issue or question you will more than likely have to go to the internet and download the users manual. The printer comes with very minimal paperwork.I think after “playing” around with the black and white resolution and the color resolution I can get the printer to working closer to laser quality however for now it is being used as just another printer. By the way it only uses 4 ink cartridges where one of my older machines used 8 to 10 cartridges. This should be a real ink and cost saver. The printer comes with four standard ink cartridges, however please note that the initial charge of the printer took up a large percentage of that ink, thus I don’t expect to get the full number of printed sheets from those cartridges. It is always  a safe bet to have another set of ink cartridges available as the ones packed with the printer will run out quickly.The printer appears to be a quality product and should last me a long time.

This is the best printer i have used along with the epson 845. I have used the canon mx870, mg5220, ix6520 and several hp deskjet but this epson comes top in terms of water resistance and steadfastness. It drys immediately it comes out of the printer but it jams on heavy paper like papers as thick as 300lbs.

The unit was up and running with correct time and date showing in very short order, step by step instruction paper is quick and easy to follow.Instruction sheet leads you through all the needed setup items, although one item on the sheet is wrong..The "To adjust the LCD contrast" section has you looking under the menu key for setup/contrast when it should be setup/screen/contrast.Right off I have to say the worse thing I found right away was the size of the lettering for the buttons on the front, very small and with the reflections on the surface you have to really look hard to read them.Once you do press a button, you can then read the items on the LCD screen which is large enough to see well.. keeping in mind that it only shows 13 letters at a time so you need to let it crawl past the entire phrase to know what it is.Nothing real bad, but you do have to hit another button to start the scroll and then read at the slower speed as it moves across the screen.I suggest you hit the "home" button and let it speak the phrase showing on the screen, it's much quicker.I think one of the nice features is the "Favorites" where you can store what you might use the most without going in all the other menus.The volume even on highest setting will have you trying to put it up to your ear to hear well, I think the use of an ear piece (mono bud type) is in order most of the time.Note the speaker is on the back of the unit and you can have it covered with your hand or table which cuts it down even more.It says that the LCD has a "backlight" but it's actually illuminated from each side of the front with LEDs, you can see okay, but it is darker in the center of the screen.  Backlight (glow) would be much better and more what people are used to these days.Owners will no doubt try to use this in many ways.. do you listen to the translation and then try to repeat it to the person you are speaking to ?Do you let the other person listen directly to the unit?And then when they answer you of course, you are on your own to understand them.. it does have translation for yes, no, numbers, days, months,seasons,time etc. but the other person would have to be willing to take the time to go through the process with you.Comes with batteries installed which is nice touch, and a place to attach a wrist strap but no strap is included, would have been nice to include as I feel electronics this small can slip to the ground when least expected.If you are using this out of the country as your helper,you would be in trouble.  I suggest you buy a wrist strap right off, also a bud type earphoneThe one phrase I find the most useful is "Does anyone here speak English" (insert your own language) which just might be your best bet right from the start, should have a large button just for this one 8-)I'm sure these translators can come in handy at times, I might just try to teach myself by listening to and learning the phrases before I need them.And lets HOPE it's a misprint at the end of the paperwork when it says to prevent a malfunction do not exceed temperature range of  -10F to +40F 8-)

Quick thoughts:These pens are small; which is great if you want to jot something down, but horrible if you are a person who consistently writes on a white board.The colors flow with minimal fade. Meaning that you don't have to go over what you wrote to get clarity. (Not as deep in color as the Quartet Enduraglide)The eraser is a nice touch for erasing a sentence or two, but comical if trying to erase a whole board.The magnet is powerful enough to hold the pen, so you should have no worries about the pens sliding down a magnetic surface.The lids of the pen hold firmly to the pen body when being used.I use these on my fridge to quickly jot down any missing items we might need on our next grocery trip. Being able to keep them handy on the fridge is a great convenience.

We use index cards to create our own flash cards for studying.  Each kid is different so we have to constantly adapt to the way kids learn, this means, we make different aids for each kid.  These cards are the right size but don't last very long if handled too much - and with kids, they can get worn out fairly easily.  Generally speaking, they seem to be thinner than what we bought at the store a couple of years ago - we purchased a bunch during school year, but they are definitely much better quality than the other kind of index cards made overseas.  They are less expensive at our local store and once in a while we can get them at about a third of the price here.
I love that my boys (4 and 6) can maneuver these erasers accurately and efficiently. We recently bought novelty erasers which are fun but don't work as well as these.

The Smead travel organizer includes two letter size folders, and a small ticket-sized velcro-closure pouch.  The two letter size file pockets have a flap on the side to keep papers from falling out.  The top is still open, though, so if held upside down or dropped, papers could possibly fall out.  The thin size does slide easily out of a brief case or laptop case, but its flexible plastic would not handle being placed in a backpack or purse very well.  This has no firm structure to it, so the more often it is bent, the faster it will fall apart.Each one seems sturdy enough to make it through several business trips, and there are two in the package.  I like how it keeps everything you need in one location, which is especially nice for airline travel.If you are traveling weekly, it might be better to seek out a leather travel organizer that will last longer.  The Smead Travel Organizer is a good option for the occasional traveler, or someone embarking on a long-awaited international trip.

As a student, I selected the Avery NoteTabs in hopes they would help organize my reading and studies.  I currently usePost-it one inch wide flagsto indicate important pages in my textbook.  This system works for me; however the flags are too flimsy for page turning.The Avery NoteTabs I selected are shaped like the tabs found on file folders.  The three inch length is about three quarters the length of a file folder tab.  Using the NoteTabs, I can easily turn to specifically marked pages.  If the NoteTab is positioned incorrectly, it easily lifts and re-sticks to a new location without lifting ink or leaving a sticky residue.  As a page marker, the NoteTabs is an excellent tool.Avery claims these NoteTabs will work "with most writing instruments," but includes a disclaimer stating "Results may vary depending on ... type of ink."  I tested the NoteTabs using a pencil, gel rolling ball pen, ball point pens of various colors, and a highlighter.  The paper coated tab accepts writing better than the clear sticky section.  However the clear sticky section area smudges and transfers small spots of ink unless left to dry a short while.  The pencil smeared on the paper tab section as well.  Additionally the pale pastel tab colors provided plenty of contrast with the ink.As a simple page marker, the Avery NoteTabs work great.  Writing on the see-through area is not as good as Avery claims. However with the right pen and a little drying time, they should work.PROS:Thicker more effective tabsEasy to remove and repositionDoesn't lift ink, leave residueCONS:Written text smears and bleeds
This stuff is great, however the only downside is that it does not fit every fountain pen out there so be cautious.

I have used manila folders for years. I've bought the same type in the past with conventional sized tabs and light to slightly medium paperweight. When used regularly over time they would tear at the spine or at the tab and then have to be replaced. This is especially true if you put a large amount of papers in one. Thia manila folder is much thicker so will last longer without as much likelihood to tear with extensive use. If you write on the tabs with ink rather than pencil there is enough room to change what is written. There is plenty of space on the tab to write detailed info. so you are able to find what you are looking for much easier. They don't take up anymore space than conventional weight folders. I will be using these in the future.

I have used the blue medium point gel pens for as long as they've been manufactured. Then I bought the red ones. Now I do a lot of research and proof reading and have expanded my color palette to include the eight colors offered in this assortment. I have found that when you make corrections to someone's text, that if you continually use the same color for the corrections, for some reason the human brain becomes conditioned to it and begins to accept it as part of the text. Switching the color of your written corrections seems to cause the brain to notice it more easily and send the right trigger to the brain of the reader.Good product at a great price.

I was excited to see tape with FRAGILE on it since we mail packages often.  However, I have to say the tape may be a little too fragile itself.  I wouldn't trust a really fragile package to this tape alone since it is thinner than the standard packing tape.  But, I still enjoy adding one go around with this tape to tell all those that handle the package to do so carefully.

I'm a big fan so far.  Using them as a bluteooth extension of your cell phone is very cool.  And it works even if you don't have a landline.  Now I just have to convince my wife to get rid of the land line all together.

I needed a lap desk for my 17" laptop. This one has filled the bill.It it comfortable. It has room for my 17" laptop PLUS a mousepad. There is zippered storage underneath where I can keep my mouse and cords when I travel. There are 2 deep organizers on top for pads, pens, cell phone, etc.I am very picky about how I want things to be, so the fact I am pleased with it speaks volumes.

I use this printer and this low volume cart at the office for printing envelopes only. I can print a few hundred envelopes with it, and the print is crisp, black, and 100% reliable. I've never had to clean the heads or do maintenance for the print quality. I have installed only Epson brand carts. For low volume printing, say 150 pages of text a month or less, it is a worth while purchase. There is a high volume version of this cart but in the price vs pages printed ratio there is no advantage to that cart.
These are nice, colorful mini binder clips that are a must for any office environment. They do what they are supposed to do: hold papers together.

Post-it Pop-up Notes Dispenser is nice looking dispenser for Post-it notes that out-of-the box includes 50-sheet pad of notes.Although looking cool this dispenser isn't completely functional because the notes papers aren't so easy to be taken out from it.Also, its cover doesn't completely fit resulting in slight move each time new note is pulled out.Although this dispenser would be nice add-on on your desk I suggest you should try to first before purchase to avoid being disappointed.

BiC continues to produce better and better writing instruments at a great price. As the name correctly implies, the Velocity Bold Ball Pen provides a bold solid line. The rubber grip is just the right distance from the easy-glide ball point to make for comfortable writing.The pen writes about as smoothly as any pen I've ever used, including those costing hundreds of dollars. I'm growing tired of hearing and reading so many individuals--musicians, in my experience--complaining about "labels," their main beef consisting of the supposed threat that any general descriptive term--smooth jazz, free jazz, modal jazz, mainstream, hard bop, cool bop, etc.--poses a threat to their singular individuality as artists who of course defy (some even maintain "transcend") all labels.Well, in some cases the label-resisters have a point, and these 3M labels are a case in point.  I don't plan to use them in consort with a software program (pre-printed return address labels are too cheap to bother with making your own), but I'm finding them quite useful in sticking on drawers, shelves, envelopes and files.  They have just enough room to permit me to jot down a descriptive word or two and, most importantly, they stick!Both 3M and Avery are forever producing a continuing stream of little inventions and improvements designed to make life's little labors even less so. Some of the items prove more expendable than others. But given enough time, you might be surprised at the many uses you'll discover for a product that was never delegated for the precise employment to which you put it.  In fact, science and progress usually proceed in precisely that manner--coming up with "inventions," and even solutions and cures, through "serendipity" as much as intent.  (Quick example: MAO inhibitors were originally anesthetics that, by accident, were discovered to have an antidepressant effect.  Or nitric oxide (not to be confused with nitrous oxide, or laughing gas) was once thought to be a chemical with limited but critical importance to the enlargement and blood flow of the major arteries serving the heart.  It was by pure chance that someone discovered that the same chemical could be used to enlarge other parts of the body, primarily in the male species.  I won't name the product--the odds are that you'll see at least one commercial for it on TV tonight.The lesson: labels have their uses--they help us keep stuff organized; but they also have their limitations, as any creative artist or scientist will readily attest.

Back in 2006 I had purchased theLogitech 2.4 GHz Cordless Presenter (Black)and gave it a glowing 5-star review.  3 years later, I was given the opportunity to review this new Logitech R400 Wireless Presenter and thought wondered how they could one up their previous product.A comparison of the aforementioned presenters, along with the R400's big brother, theLogitech Professional Presenter R800, there are many similarities in features.The Basics:- Units fit well in hand.  Buttons are well positioned- Forward/Back buttons to navigate through slides- Battery indicator- Uses AAA batteries (no need to search for hard to find batteries, especially if you are away on a conference).  One set of batteries are included!- Compact padded storage case- Power on/off switch so that you can conserve power- All 3 units operate on 2.4 GHz frequency- USB Receiver slides and snaps into the Presenter for easy storage- Black out screen - Can black out the screen (good for when you want to have people focus their attention on you instead of the slides)- Laser Pointer (the older Presenter and R400 have a red laser, R800 has a green laser)o Green laser pointers are supposedly easier to see on Plasma/LCD screens and in brightly-lit roomso Laser pointer works independent of the power on/off switchBesides the difference in color of laser, there are a few distinct differences:- Range - old presenter and R400 have a range of approximately 50 ft.  R800 has a range of about 100 ft.- Range indicator - The R800 shows the signal strength so you will know if you're still within range- Timer/Alarm - The old presenter and R800 both have LCD timers and alarms to notify you how long your presentation is and when you should wrap up.  The alarm will silently vibrate the presenter at 5 mins, 2 mins, and at 0 mins.  The R400 does not have this feature.- The older Presenter and R400 are thin and light.  The R800 is a bit thicker to pack in the added features.I tested the R400 with MS PowerPoint 2003 on my WinXP laptop, and it worked as well as can be expected.  There are a couple reasons why I have chosen to give the Presenter 4 stars rather than a 5.- All the buttons are slightly concave.  The only way to tactilely distinguish the buttons is the tactile nub (which is really small) that is on the slide advance button.- Does not have one of the smaller mini receivers found on many of Logitech's newer mice.Bottom line is that the Logitech Wireless Presenter R400 is a great product for those of you that give occasional presentations in perhaps a small classroom environment, or for those of you that do not need all the advanced features.  If the timing of presentations is a big factor in your job or your grade, I would recommend going for theLogitech Professional Presenter R800

Canon PIXMA MG5420 Wireless Color Photo Printer with Scanner and Copier[12/13/2013 NOTE: I suggest also looking at the Canon PIXMA MG7120 if you are interested in the MG5420][12/22/2013 NOTE: I added a section below noting why the MG5420 is superior to the MG5520 in my opinion]OVERVIEW:----------If you don't care about having GRAY or ETHERNET, but want great PHOTO QUALITY in an inexpensive all-in-one style (copier, scanner) ink jet printer, this can be a quality/value sweet spot for you in the Canon PIXMA line giving you a lot of bang for the buck.  This is the replacement for MG5320, only available since December 2012.If this seems right for you, consider looking at the slightly more upscale Canon MG7120 features before committing as the cost difference isn't that much.PROS:------- A well regarded consumer magazine considers these MG5000/MG6000/MG8000 series printers the best photo quality for all-in-one (copier, scanner) ink jets.  This model is the entry point into this line.- The new ink tanks for the MG5420 (and the new MG6320 and newer MG7120) now also come in an XL size which can reduce the page cost significantly.  The inks themselves in the new tanks are the same formula.  This was not available for the predecessor MG5320/MG6220 models.- The MG5420 (and MG6320/MG7120) has 2x the number of black ink nozzles as their predecessors MG5320/MG6220.  This allows more efficient use of black ink and greater dot accuracy.- It is a bit shorter/squatter than its predecessor MG5320, which for some is a nicer form factor if on a desk, for example.  I think they both look fine, but it is clear from reviews that the new look has gone over well.- Like the newer MG6320/MG7120 (and unlike the last generation MG5320/MG6220), this has the new handy separate 4"x6" and 5"x7" photo paper drawer at the front.- For copying/scanning the top comes off easily (unlike the previous generation MG5320/MG6220).- With 10+ years of having a number of their products I have always found Canon to have great customer service, which for U.S. customers appears to be based out of Maryland and Virginia.LESSER PROS:-------------- 5-15% faster printing than last generation depending on b&w; vs. color, quality, etc.- Can print directly from CF memory cards unlike the last generation, if that is important to you.- Wider selection of devices that can print directly to it than the last generation.CONS/WARNINGS:------------------ Like its predecessor (MG5320), this has one less color than the next step up MG6320/MG6220, it does NOT HAVE GRAY, which is for improved black and white art and photo results and to better darken colors.  I can't tell the difference gray makes with color pages, but some reviewers can.- Like its predecessor (MG5320), there is NO ETHERNET connection like the next step up MG7120/MG6320/MG6220 has.  Ethernet allows a solid, simple shared/network wired connection that stays up even when computers are down.  I personally think getting this is worth the relatively small additional expense for a MG7120/MG6320/MG6220 if you have more than one user on the network, but that is just me.- Does not have the option of coming in white, which the MG7120/MG6320 ones do.- As of 2014 this is no longer new (end of 2012) and as such one hopes most issues found with it would have been fixed by now.  However, if you are buying a used one, this may still be a concern.- The inks for this model (and the other newer ones, the MG6320/MG7120) are relatively new and different than for the previous generation before that (MG5320/MG6220) and thus can be harder to find in stores, however enough time has passed now as of 2014 it is no where near as tough to find as only a year ago.- For copying/scanning, the lid telescopes up for books only to the thickness of around a cellphone (like its predecessor the MG5320).  On the other hand the top COMES OFF easily now with the MG5420, just like the newer MG6320/MG7120.- This doesn't come with the MG6320/MG7120's touch screen content-sensitive interface which is getting rave reviews, however, I find this older interface style just as easy.- No built-in fax, if this is important to you in an all-in-one.  Perhaps you want to get a dedicated one of your choosing near a phone line anyways, however if you are looking for a built-in fax the MX922/MX892 printers do.  This comes at a cost of not getting the higher end scanning of the MG models, though this may only matter to you if you are scanning negatives, MX922/MX892 scanning meets most other needs including most graphics needs, just as well.SUGGESTIONS TO CONSIDER:----------------------------- When doing text, choose the HIGH QUALITY setting (and perhaps set it as the default) in the printer page set-up, it really makes a difference.- See below consideration to select it not to automatically shut-off to reduce ink wastage.- Consider choosing to print black & white or grey scale when color isn't necessary, otherwise the printer may choose to layer colors to get black instead.  Canon feels the black is better with the color layering though, you decide :).- If you need something NOW that you will use a lot NOW, and the GRAY and ETHERNET is potentially useful you might consider looking at the older MG6220 since it uses inks that are easy to find at stores and online.  The MG6220 is pretty cheap now, too, since it is being replaced.- If you need something NOW that you will use a lot NOW, and you don't care enough about GRAY or ETHERNET, you might consider looking at the older MG5320 since it uses inks that are easy to find at stores and online.  The MG5320 is pretty cheap now, too, since it is being replaced.- If the color GRAY or ETHERNET connectivity (they come with MG7120/MG6320/MG6220) is potentially useful to you, you might consider looking into the MG7120/MG6320/MG6220, which are otherwise somewhat similar.- Use Canon paper when you need optimal results with their ink, and test matte vs. glossy.  Matte is much less expensive and may meet most of your needs.  Let me know in comments if anyone finds a comparable quality and yet significantly less costly photo paper for this printer, I'd like to test it out.- In case of POWER OUTAGE, it is sometimes necessary to unplug it for A FEW MINUTES and then plug it back in. This allows capacitor discharge.- The Canon site has lots of easy to find product comparison information for these inkjets, you might consider reviewing it before committing on a model.- As soon as you can after getting your printer, print samples of full color, b&w;, borderless photos, print on a DVD if that's important to you, etc.  Determine if you have a lemon before you get too busy with other things so you can exchange for a good one while it is easy to do.  These are complicated machines with lots of parts.INK USAGE:-----------Anyone researching the ink jet printers will likely be concerned about ink costs.  Here are 5 things you can do to mitigate this with the MG5420:- Buy the XL versions of the ink, this is supposed to reduce the cost per color page to a very competitive 13-14 cents per page (vs. 16-19 cents).- As noted above, choose to print black and white or grey scale when that will do just fine to avoid black made from layers of colors.  Canon feels the black mixed from colors is better, you be the judge.- Turn off the automatic shut-off.  Standby mode uses 0.9W, so on standby even all year uses around 8kWh/yr., so around $1/yr depending on where you live.  This can help lessen the number of the longer cleaning routines after start-up and often at shutdown.  It runs the cleaning other times, too, which is good as it keeps things from clogging.- Avoid printing pages with solid or heavily colored background in color when possible.- Some fonts use 20-40% less ink than others.
