For example, when I take ink from a MG5320 and put it in a MG6220, the low ink warning bars show the ink as vastly lower.  This helps exaggerate the appearance of high ink usage.  Actual ink usage is high enough that this bug is pretty unwelcome.  If it wasn't for a leading consumer magazine's highest photo quality rating for all-in-ones and their estimated page cost that wasn't crazy, and lots of other favorable reviews, I think this bug could have been much worse for MG6220 sales and other models in the family.  This might make you feel a little better about ink usage in the model family 5000/6000 after reading the ink comments for the 6220.NOTE #3:  Just an informative, probably not very useful factoid :).  This model range of Canon inkjet doesn't do a big cleaning/purging after it prints, you are usually hearing head realignment.  However, it does quietly "prime the head" to keep the heat from ink clogging the print head and this uses a little ink (even for B&W;).  This is much less ink than with the big cleaning/purging routine that is much rarer if you set the printer not to auto shut-off.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------INK USAGE CANON DATASHEET:------------------------------As it is pretty difficult to find, here below is Canon's published Page Yield per Document numbers (I rounded a little) for MG5420.I'm not sure how much of the difference between these numbers and users experience is due to the cleaning routine, difference between test and real world usage, etc.Here at least you can see real world expected usage ratio between standard and XL cartridges and compare to costs to determine the better value.----------Mixed Text/Graphics, A4/Letter, Plain Paper, Adobe Reader 10ISO/IEC24711 Test Method, ISO/IEC24712 Test Pattern:PGI-250 __ 300 pagesCLI-251 BK 1800CLI-251 C_ 330CLI-251 M_ 320CLI-251 Y_ 340PGI-250 XL __ 500 pagesCLI-251 XL BK 5500CLI-251 XL C_ 700CLI-251 XL M_ 680CLI-251 XL Y_ 700----------Color Photos, 4"x6":PGI-250 __ 2400 pagesCLI-251 BK 380CLI-251 C_ 120CLI-251 M_ 130CLI-251 Y_ 130PGI-250 XL __ 5600 pagesCLI-251 XL BK 1130CLI-251 XL C_ 260CLI-251 XL M_ 310CLI-251 XL Y_ 270----------vs. MG5520:------------Here are some of the more notable differences in MG5420's favor:MG5420:- Print Color Resolution: 9600 horizontal x 2400 vertical dpi- Print Most Granular Dot: 1 picoliter- Scanner Resolution: 2400 horizontal x 4800 vertical dpi (optical)- Print 4"x6" Photo speed: 21 seconds- Copy speed (FCOT): 14 seconds- Printing on DVD/CD'sMG5520:- Print Color Resolution: 4800 horizontal x 1200 vertical dpi*- Print Most Granular Dot: 2 picoliter- Scanner Resolution: 1200 horizontal x 2400 vertical dpi (optical)**- Print 4"x6" Photo speed: 44 seconds (110% slower)- Copy speed (FCOT): 20 seconds (40% slower)- No printing on DVD/CD's*The MG5520's 4800 horizontal x 2400 vertical max dpi COLOR PRINTING will meet MOST NEEDS. The Pro photo inkjet printers (PRO-1/PRO-10/PRO-100) even max out at 4800 horizontal dpi (though have finer vertical stepping capability), for example. It is therefore also moot to argue enlargement benefits of over 1200dpi scanning of paper photos as the detail is likely not there for over 1200dpi.Some Pros of MG5520 over MG5420:- MG5520 will automatically turn on if it is off when a print request is sent.- MG5520 doesn't require a wireless router to print from a mobile device, it has an Access Point Mode which allows direct printing to the printer without need for a wireless router.- MG5520 allows you to print directly (no computer needed) from Facebook, Twitter, Flickr, DropBox, Evernote, and more, via apps downloaded to the printer.Summary:I don't think the few ancillary pros of the MG5520 outweigh MG5420's superior features, though the info is there to make your own call. The Zebra stylus-pen combination that is a decent stylus and a decent pen, but not an excellent example of either.Pens tend to be a personal choice, so opinions are going to be subjective and differ from person to person. If you are not fussy about what pen you use, you will likely be very happy with the pen side of this item. I've come to like the Pilot G2 0.7mm, and I was actually surprised to find that the pen side of this item was pretty decent to use. Sure, it's not the same, but for situations where you would like to have a stylus handy and you're just jotting down a few notes in a meeting or while traveling, I could see carrying just this.The stylus side is pretty much standard. I've only used one other stylus, the AmazonBasics model which retails for around $7. I'm not the biggest fan of using a stylus, so I might not be the most thorough reviewer when it comes to their use. However, the stylus on this pen seemed to be about as useful and I didn't have any problems with getting it to be recognized by an iPad 4 or a Google Nexus 7 (2013 model).As with all combination items, it's not going to be the best at either use, but it's a suitable compromise that provides two uses in a single item so that two do not have to be taken along. It's a little high-priced for the convenience, and since I'm not a big stylus user in the first place, I'd rather pack my Pilot G2 and use my finger on the tablet. If you really like to use a stylus, this might be just what you were looking for!

I have an Epson Artisan 837 at home that I love, and a Workforce 3520 I use at work.  I had an XP-810, but didn't use it because I liked the 837 better.  And while the XP-810 is an improvement over the XP-800, I still will keep using the Artisan 837.One of the most annoying things on the XP-800 was that the cool feature it had that made it unique in my experience, the auto-extending paper try that would extend itself for a print job, didn't auto-return as well.  You were forced to shove it in, and I never liked the feeling of doing that.  I always wondered long term what would happen to the motor and gears.  I don't even let my son push around cars by hand that have a motorized drive, for the same reason.This printer improves on that - when you shut it off, it asks if you want to retract the paper tray, and if you tell it yes, the motor draws it back inside again.  Definitely an improvement over the previous model.Setup has an automated wizard that will include setting it up on the wireless network for you.  From watching the computer and the network status, it appears that, during the windows driver / software install, if you have not set up the printer on the wireless yet (which I generally already have done manually, but this time I wanted to test the feature), your computer will drop your current wireless network and connect to the printer.  Apparently then it will configure the printer for the wireless network that your home or office was using, saving you the trouble.  However, for me it didn't work.  There was a lot of waiting while the computer was working, and after I figured it failed, it progressed to the next point, and I thought it was going to work.  However, then it sat again, and ultimately failed anyway.  All told it was about 10 minutes of sitting there to see if the automatic process could do what takes me about 30 seconds manually.  So I ended up having to join the wireless network myself for the printer, but once that was done, the install proceeded fine.I really wish they supported wireless scanning.  In order to scan with this, the only option is a USB connection.There are two black cartridges, one for photos and a larger one for the majority of black and white printing.  I like inkjet printers that have setups like that.  Cartridges were easy to put in and the caps on them had good tabs to grab so you can pull the tab off without getting ink on yourself.  No tape over the ink ports on these, just the plastic tabbed covers.I still don't like how the CD tray sticks out of the front farther than everything else.  I can understand that you need to be able to grab it to pull it out, but it just ruins the looks in my opinion having that projecting out the front on the bottom.Power cord is average length, and since all the components are internal, there's no brick, just the two prong power plug that goes into the back.  That makes cord placement easier when you don't have a brick like some of the HP's I've had.Paper try isn't very large though, so if you go through a lot of paper, you'll be filling it up more often than the other printers I have.The eject and retract for the paper try works well, but while upon opening it drops the little cover out of the way so it can slide out, and it also tilts up the display about 30 or 40 degrees, neither of those two things that get moved out of the way return when it retracts, you have to close them manually.  I don't see that as a problem since I'd be doing that anyway if the tray wasn't motorized anyway, and it's just pivot points, not forcing a motor and gear to move like pushing the tray in on the older model was.Print jobs do print quickly, and they look good. I have used way too many laminators at various jobs, and this one is definitely the best I've used yet. It far exceeded my expectations. It performs reliably.  It can handle heavy stock paper in the pouch without flinching. It doesn't take up a lot of room. If you're using this in a production environment, such as laminating badges at a conference, it's going to be the thing that you don't have to call the one expert in the room for, the thing that gives you the least headaches, because it's easy to use and it works.Three caveats if this is your first laminator, and this is true of all laminators.  First, there will be an odd peice of cardboard in the box. Don't throw it out. You need to run it through the machine 2 or 3 times after every use in order to clean it.  Gunking is a big problem with all laminators, and cleaning it this way will enhance the life and performance of your device.  Second, get good pouches.  GBC and Scotch both make good ones.  Even the best laminator will do a crappy job with a poorly manufactured pouch. Third, take the finished item out immediately and let it lay flat to cool. Otherwise it'll cool crooked and look horrible.It doesn't come with any pouches, so be sure to grab some 3 mil or 5 mil.

[Standard Vine disclaimer here]Ok, the Epson Artisan 1430 Wireless Wide-Format Color Inkjet Printer.First: It's HUGE.  I guess I must have missed that part of the fine print, but this thing is titanic.  24 inches wide, 7.5 inches tall, 12 inches deep... without the paper holders extended (Note: they must be open for the thing to work. There is no paper tray for automatic printing)Second: It's noisy.  Not the standard shook-shook-shook of most printers. There are some clicks, clacks, and quite a few high-pitched squeals.  The squeals aren't loud, but they are annoying.  Sent my cat running from the room.  [not such a bad thing, I suppose]Third: It prints beautifully!  I wasn't even printing at 360DPI and what I got looked just like it did on my computer screen.  So, as a photo printer goes, it does its job.Now, the real review:Setting this beast up was relatively simple. Helpfully, Epson put their Buick-sized printer in a study plastic bag with handles.  It easily popped out of the box and was a snap to move to its new home.I will, however, knock Epson points for their setup guide.  Only after you go through the-5-different-work-processes of getting the printer ready, do the instructions *THEN* mention that you may be prompted to connect your printer to your computer with a USB cable - USB A to USB B cable needed, *not* included.  I'm knocking points because they should really mention this up front. As a laptop user, it was easy for me to pick up my lappy and walk over to the printer.  If I was a desktop PC user and the two were not near each other, I'd be rather ticked. (It's wireless... is wireless set up an unrealistic expectation?)  Not to mention the fact that Epson does not supply a required cable.I set this thing up on 3 different computers: Windows 7, Mac OSX Snow Leopard, Mac OSX Tiger... all THREE of them requested the USB cable be connected for first-time set up.So: Huge, noisy, and poorly executed Setup guide: Minus 1 star.Now, once your printer is on your wireless network, any PC/Mac in range can connect to it without the use of a USB cable. HOWEVER, you have to install Epson's software on each machine.  And, of course, every time you install the software, it prompts you to register the printer.  Annoying since there are separate choices: First Time Setup and Printer is Already On My Network.Annoying software and not supplying a required cable: Minus 1 star.Worst of all, 3 of the 5 prints I've made using the Epson 1430 were wrecked because the printer pulled the paper in at odd angles and crumpled it up.  Yes, I fanned the paper out before loading it, I didn't overload, and I used the paper guide & paper supports correctly.When it pulls the paper through correctly, it prints wonderfully high-quality pictures.  It just seems inconsistent. Perhaps that will wear in?Wrecking over 50% of attempted prints: Minus 1 star.Epson does include a copy of Adobe Photoshop Elements 9 for Windows and Mac.  This is a really nice treat since I didn't have Photoshop installed on my Windows machine.Including awesome software: 1 star added back in.Anyway, you've now been warned of the potential pitfalls with this printer. I would really rate it at 3.5 stars because my first point deduction is really a half.  Still, I couldn't recommend this printer to a friend without a stern warning.

Yes, it cuts. I cut articles out of magazines and coupons out of the newspaper while I sit in a comfy chair 20 feet from a table.  I trim tiny pieces of paper that are too small to cut with this.  (You need more than one inch of paper on one side of the cut, to hold the paper down, and thin strips of paper will bend and twist when the blade hits them.)  I open envelopes and boxes, and this won't work on those.  (It works on envelopes until you hit a seam, and then it stops cold.)What it does do is cut one or two sheets of paper, and it does this exceptionally well. I've got a storage container that holds my gift wrap and bows, and there's plenty of room there for this mouse.  I'm not sure I'd store it on my desk unless I thought I'd be using it more frequently.

While I don't do much shipping these days, I do make soap, and as any soapmakers know, having a quality, reliable digital scale is very, very important in the process.  (Mismeasure the oils? Supercool:  if you're a shipper, this model comes with a USB port that allows you to take measurement data and download it via included cable directly to your computer. The instructions that come with the model are very clear, and I was able to download them in minutes.A couple limitations:*  It's only ten pounds. Not that big of a deal for small shippers/users, but if you get close, you'll want to be aware of it.*  For the price (around $40 at the time of this writing), it seems a little high for a ten-pound model, despite the nifty download thing.  There are other models out there that are definitely more cost-effective, so if price is important to you, this might be your pain-point.Overall, though, this thing does what it says it's going to do, and seems to do it very well.  I'll be using it more over the coming weeks for both shipping and soapmaking, and will update if there's any changes/new developments.

First let me start by saying that this printer is immaculately packed for easy removal from the box.  I have never received a printer that the cables are all stored in a reusable HP zippered accessory bag and the printer is in a LARGE canvas tote bag with handles to slide out of the box with not tugging, pushing or using your feet.The HP printer is a beauty in a sleek high black gloss finish.  It comes with power AC adapter plug, phone line, installation CD, quick reference book, HP photo paper samples  and two face plates (one English & one French).  It DOES NOT come with the USB cable.  This does not surprise me since most printers now-a-days do not include the USB cable.After removing all the tape used to keep the printer intact during shipment, I plugged in the unit as instructed in the quick reference book.  Since I have a wireless home network, I was able to connect to my network using the WiFi  Protected Setup (WPS).  After verifying the network name and entering my paraphrase (password) it was online in seconds.  I then followed the "animated" instructions on the LCD screen on how to install the ink cartridges and paper.  There is a one time initial installation that the printer cycles through that takes about 7 minutes.  It downloaded updates, this is all happening without having to use my computer.  The printer spit out a test page showing that the printer head had been aligned/calibrated.Now it was time to install the CD.  I am using it in a Windows 7 environment and the installation took about 8 minutes, so it is quite a large file.  I followed the easy steps to setup photo printing, fax number and registration and I was done.  The printer was ready to use.I have many printers in my home since we have a large family with a total of 6 computers/laptops, but this is my first HP printer and I can honestly say this is by far the nicest, fastest and easiest to use printer I possess.  The colored printouts are beautiful in vivid colors, no smudges or lines.  It does only come with "setup" ink cartridges so I don't know how long they will actually last without being replaced.  The ink cartridges "HP 564" series are quite reasonably priced.  Depending on which cartridges you go with,  the HP564 yield approximately 250-300 pages while the HP 564XL series yield about 600-700. It takes a total of 5 ink cartridges - black, Photo black (item #CB322WN), cyan, magenta and yellow.THIS IS A PHOTOSMART PRINTER (e-all-in-one) BUT IS NOT CONSIDERED A PHOTOSMART "PLUS" PRINTER.  This makes it confusing when searching for ink cartridges.HP564 Series**HP 564 Black Ink Cartridge**PLEASE NOTE THAT HP HAS CHANGED THEIR PACKAGING OF THIS INK CARTRIDGE AND IT IS NOW SLIMMER.  It will fit but will have gaps on both sides when placed inside the cartridge head.HP 564 Photo Ink Cartridge (CB317WN#140)Original HP 564 Ink cartridges Combo-Pack (Cyan, Magenta & Yellow Cartridges) in Retail PackagingHP564XL Series**HP 564XL Black Ink Cartridge in Retail Packaging (CN684WN#140)**PLEASE NOTE THAT HP HAS CHANGED THEIR PACKAGING OF THIS INK CARTRIDGE AND IT IS NOW SLIMMER.  It will fit but will have gaps on both sides when placed inside the cartridge head.HP 564XL High Capacity Photo Black Ink Cartridge (CB322WN#140)HP 564XL Magenta  Ink Cartridge in Retail Packaging (CB324WN#140)HP 564XL Yellow  Ink Cartridge in Retail Packaging (CB325WN#140)HP 564XL Cyan Ink Cartridge in Retail Packaging (CB323WN#140)HP 564xl Ink Cartridges. 5-pack Black, Photo Black, Magenta, Cyan, YellowBesides the amazing features such as WiFi, embedded bluetooth, apps (which allows you to print from the web without PC), ePrint, and several slots for memory cards  (Memory Stick, MMD, CF and USB-removable drives, the thing I love the most is that it only takes one series of cartridge to print photos or documents!  It does require one black and one black "photo" cartridge but at least I don't have to be pulling out cartridges whenever I want to print photos.The ePrint function is extremely easy to use.  All you need to do is have the printer connected to a home network and follow the onscreen LCD instructions.  The printer assigns you a unique email address.  Then go to the HP ePrint website to register and set up your security options.  You can set it up so anyone can send printing projects to your printer, or use just selected users.  You can send photos, Word documents, Excel spreadsheets, reports and many other file types directly to your printer by emailing them from your smartphone.  I am using my Motorola Droid.  It's that easy.**Currently the ePrint does not support MMS format (so no picture text messages). ePrint only works if you send an email using email clients such as Yahoo, AOL, Google, etc.  You would have to attach the picture to the email. Hopefully in time, there will be an update that allows pictures to be sent as MMS messages.Since I am using my Yahoo email account to sign into the ePrint website, I get a confirmation email that the job was sent to my printer.  You can always check the status of your jobs on the HP ePrint website as well.  All print jobs will stay in the printer's memory (queue) for 24 hours.  This is a great feature since you never know if the printer might go offline when you are not home.When I send projects to print from other computers (ie sending a report home from work), the project prints with no issues.  However, sometimes photo emails do not get processed and are stuck with a "pending" or "failed" status.  I believe these are due to some "issues" at HP's end since this technology is so new.  I think with time and new updates, these bugs will be fixed.  For the time being, HP recommends turning off and then restarting the printer to correct server connection issues/print jobs.  Also make sure files are less than 5MB in size, I get many failed print projects because they are larger in size.For my iPad, I downloaded "HP iPrint" which is a free Wi-Fi application on my iPad. Amazon Vine offered me theFellowes Mars ML 95 9.5" Home Laminatorto test and review a few months after I'd purchased this Scotch unit.  As it happens, I had not even opened the box on the laminator I purchased so I thought I'd offer a side-by-side comparison of the two, fresh out of the box.  Physically, the two machines are of similar size with the Scotch model having an input tray that increases its footprint.  They were built to similar quality standards with similar materials.  As they are both offered in the same lower end home office price ranges, I feel that they are a good pair to compare.The initial warm up took 7 minutes and 15 seconds for the Fellows unit, while the Scotch unit took an extra 15 seconds.  Both operated very quietly with self feeding rollers, though the Scotch unit started a light humming sound after it had warmed up.  Both initially emitted a light smoke/burning smell that dissipated after a while.  Both units are wide enough to handle letter sized laminating pouches.  I used 3 mil bags from both companies in both machines.  The pouches performed similarly with waves in the plastic happening in wide sections where there was nothing inserted in the sleeve.  The Fellowes pouches did impress me as being a little better quality than the Scotch pouches and the end result was slightly thicker and a tiny bit more firm feeling to me.  This end result was common to both of the machines I tested.  The Fellows machine was slightly slower than the Scotch machine, but not by more than a few seconds for a full sheet pass.Both units advertise that they operate up to 5 mil, as I only had 3 mil pouches to play with, I can not comment on effectiveness with thicker pouches. I can tell you that I used thicker card stock as my test materials with no issues.  The Scotch brand has some nice features that the Fellowes doesn't offer, such as the ability to accommodate a maximum of 10 mils.  Additionally, the Fellows does not have a feeder tray (not really a big deal), nor does it have a release lever or thickness adjustment control.The Scotch unit is full featured and economical.  Its versatility makes it the winner in this side-by-side comparison so long as it stays in a price range similar to other laminators of this size and ability.

I have achy joints. Instead of foam, like the new one, it's made of gel. At some point along the way, it got punctured, and gel started leaking out, so I taped it up. Then the gel started getting sticky, so I covered it in cloth (which is, now that I look at it closely, quite disgusting!).Having said all that, I was happy to see the new PlushTouch Wrist Rest as an option from Vine, and am glad to replace my old one with something better.Pros:~ It has a very nice shape, so there's more support for wrists when typing on the keyboard - 3" at its widest point - and a little less - 2" at its thinnest point on the right side for the keypad.  (To compare, my old gel pad is only 2.25" at its widest.)~ The foam is quite comfortable and supportive. I've been using the pad for a week or so now, and it seems like the foam will hold up well. I haven't noticed yet if my wrists feel any better, but they definitely don't feel any worse. (Yay!)~ It has microban antimicrobial protection. (I did mention my old gel pad is now rather disgusting, didn't I?) Considering how much time my hands spend on this thing, it's nice to know it's fighting away the germs.~ Non-skid backing keeps wrist support in place. This is a bit of con for me personally, as my desk has a long pull-out keyboard tray, and I often slide my keyboard, pad, mousepad and mouse back so I can use the surface to write on. Unfortunately, the non-skid backing tends to pick up all kinds of crud - pet fur, crumbs, and I'm not sure what else. I'm also not sure how to clean it.~ Other reviewers mentioned a bad smell; I never noticed anything until I held it right up to my nose; it's not exactly a pleasant smell, but then again I'm not likely to do that very often, or really ever again.Cons:~ The biggest con for me is that it's just too short. It's 18" long, which is too long for my keyboard, but not quite long enough for my keyboard AND mouse. My old pad is 20" long, so much easier to use for keyboard and mouse. There really isn't room on my tray for this wrist rest AND a mousepad with wrist support. I wish it was 2.5" - 3" longer; then it would be perfect for me.4.5 stars.

I had a Uniden cordless system for nearly a decade and loved it. The time has come, finally to replace it, so naturally I looked again to Uniden.Sadly, I am very disappointed. The look and feel of this phone is cheap and plasticky. It is ugly. But worse yet, the features I loved that have disappeared far outweigh the new ones.Details on feature pros and cons are below. Just one example of the terribleness of this design: The main thing I use on my phone menus is the "missed call" log. I access this many many times each day. On my old phone, a single tap and I was there--and the display showed name, phone number and time called. This phone is just CRAZY. You have to press FOUR keys just to get to the missed calls menu: Press Menu. Press "Down" key to select recent calls. Press Okay. Press Okay again to select Caller ID). Once you finally get there, the phone's screen displays a message that says "Please Wait" After about three seconds, the list appears...but even then it doesn't show the number, just the name. To see the incoming phone number and time called I must click the name...and only one number and time displays at once! The ten-year old phone displayed the list instantly, with all the info.I purchased this model "like new" from Uniden (box had been opened by a consumer but phone perfect condition) for $35. Not worth returning, so I'll be giving it away.For those who are interested, of the three phone systems I tested, including this one, and a Vtech, the best (or perhaps I should say least disappointing, was this one:Panasonic KX-TG4053B DECT 6.0 PLUS Expandable Digital Cordless Phone with Answering System & Range Extender, Black, 3 Handsets. I will be reviewing that one soon, but for now I'll say that the display ease-of-reading and the sound quality is better than this "Loud and Clear" phone.PROS*The Caller Announce reads aloud the name of the caller; works pretty well and voice is about as clear as the Panasonic.*LED display is easy to read but less good than the Panasonic.*Sound quality is acceptable, but not as good as the Panasonic.*Unlike my older model, I can see the number of an incoming call when I am on the line. That's great!*You can set a personal ring for specific people. Sadly, Uniden has removed the "silent" ring option, so you can no longer send a pest directly to voice mail without hearing the phone ring.*Great call blocking! This is the BEST feature of the phone: You can block up to thirty individual phone numbers, and also if you choose block private or unknown numbers. Unlike the Panasonic, you do not hear the first ring. I can't tell you how awesome this is, and I don't know how Uniden does it because the phone is not suppressing the first ring like some systems do...you still hear the first ring when a number is not blocked. Also, unlike the Panasonic where the caller hears a busy signal, on this phone they hear a message, "No one is available to take your call" and then a hang-up.CONS*Worst interface of any cordless phone I've ever seen, and a major downgrade from the functionality of earlier Uniden phones. Common functions take many key strokes (see above for how to get to your caller ID list!). Redial is simple but most everything else is a hassle.*The phone's electronics are very slow. I get the "Please Wait" message frequently, while my 10-year-old Uniden phone was much faster. Can you say cheapening it up?*Only seven ring tones and most are annoying as hell. C'mon Uniden, costs nothing to add a few ring tones.*Uniden removed its earlier WONDERFUL feature of being able to set a specific number to "silent" ring so the person goes right to voice mail. So when your boss calls, he gets a nice professional voice mail and you are undisturbed. Uniden must think the call blocking covers this issue  but it does NOT. Plenty of times I want to politely give someone the opportunity to leave a message but not be disturbed by that person.*Main base station's ring cannot be set to very soft. Your choice is loud or louder. That does not work for me. I like the phone handset to ring loud, since I can choose that ring tone. I typically set the main station to have a very soft ring, just in case my handset runs out of battery power.*The name of the person calling displays on this phone a couple of seconds later than on my ten year old phone. (I tested both with a stopwatch.) Why? Electronics should be better today, not worse. The two seconds does make a slight difference in usability for me, but mostly it's just annoying. Why slower?After extensive testing three phones (Panasonic, Vtech and this one) I can say the only reason to get this one is if your major priority is a call blocking feature that works great. This one is fabulous. I'll give Uniden that, and it is the reason I gave this phone three stars instead of two or one. The Vtech has no call blocking, and most phones don't. Panasonic does offer call blocking, but  you hear the first ring; what good is that if I still jump up to get the phone and it's a telemarketer?If great call blocking is not a killer feature to you, I suggest trying other brands of cordless phones. If you want good functionality and great sound, with a large easy-to-read display, go for the Panasonic. If a nice sleek look is most important to you, shop Vtech. But other than great call blocking, Uniden has gone way downhill and has nothing else to offer.

The printing of these labels was simple and painless - even on a Mac.  But the quality of the paper surface was lower than expected.  These are specified for Inkjet, but the letters are not crisp (slight bleeding of edges).  Paper is not smooth enough/too absorbent.PROS:--From opening the package to having printed labels in my hand was less than 5 minutes on my Mac (all templates are in MS Word).  Website is simple, clean, with easy-to-find information: no wasted time rummaging through endless drop-downs.  Click, click, click and you're typing in your template.--One sheet can handle multiple runs through my printer (all mfgrs. say not to, but let's face it:  most of us do this, right?):1) Printed 8 labels.2) Removing no labels, printed more.3) Removed 1/3 of printed labels, printed more.--Still no deterioration; I could probably run this through several more times.--Adhesive is as good as all Post-it adhesive:  I tried it on wood, paper, metal, plastic.  Unlike a post it, however, the entire surface has adhesive, so you have to "pick" it off w/ your fingernail.  This is so easy, though, that even the label corner is not damaged; nor does it stick up when you re-adhere it to something else.CONS:--The paper surface of the labels is not very high quality:  there is slight edge bleeding on the characters.  More than I would have expected.  My HP inkjet printer was set to Normal B&W.;OVERALL:  very pleased with these, and would definitely buy them.  Love 3M in general, and these do not disappoint.  Easy to format, print, re-print partially used sheets, and easy to adhere/remove/reuse labels.  Plus you could hand-write on these, too.They probably have the cheaper paper-surface to control costs/offer these at a reasonable price.  However four stars as the paper should, imo, be at least the quality of Post-it Note paper.  Then, I believe, there would be no bleeding.MAC USERS: MS Word template opened seamlessly in Pages.  I have Mac Leopard OS X 10.5.8 and Pages '09 4.0.3.--For those that are picky, the template is slightly off in Pages - centered left to right, but prints slightly below center top to bottom (when formatted centered top-to-bottom) on each label. This printer was easy to set up, though you need to know how to get your WiFi credentials out of your router in order to let it join a wireless network (there's usually a user-friendly program to set and display the password from a laptop or desktop on the network).It does drink ink a bit heavily, which I think may be linked to the ink not drying up during periods of inactivity like all my other Epson printers have done. I think it does a cleaning cycle every so often to keep the ink flowing.[EDIT 8/6/13] I recently went on vacation and flipped the "everything off" switch that powers down just about all my network bits'n'bobs. I returned after ten days to find I had to run several head cleanings on this printer. All but the light magenta print heads had clogged and the machine reported two cartidges as out of ink (they were low when I left). Lesson learned: never power down and live with the ink usage.[/EDIT]Don't fit standard capacity cartridges. You'll be going through them like nobody's business, especially the "light" colors. Dunno why the light colors get such a caning.The scanner bed is compromised by a daft bulge in the front panel that means a book must be backfolded against its spine to lie flat on the glass. This is beyond stupid. A star comes off.The scanner software lets you scan from a remote computer (which is of marginal usefulness unless you can move the system into the same room as the printer) and capture the scans to that system (which is very useful indeed).Paper must be of reasonable quality and must be loaded properly if jams and wrecks are to be avoided. The paper path is designed to present both sides to the print heads so care is required.Don't load creased sheets.Don't load paper normally good only for wrapping fish in.Don't reload paper after it has been through the printer once.Don't overload the cartridge.And use The Old Printer's Trick to break the vacuum between the sheets: grip the pack on one short edge, bend the pack and grip the other edge. Straighten the pack and run the bulge formed back and forth. Let go one end, straighten the pack, turn it over and do it all again. Square the pack and load it in the printer. This works much better than just fanning the paper, as it makes each page slip against its neighbors.You'll need some of these:Epson Claria T098120 Hi-Definition 98 High-capacity Inkjet Cartridge-BlackEpson Claria T098920 Hi-Definition 98 Extra High-capacity Inkjet Cartridge Color Multipack-Cyan/Light Cyan/Magenta/Light Magenta/YellowBuy two sets if you use the printer every day or print many photographs, otherwise you'll be driving all over the place one Sunday looking for a light magenta cartridge and cursing up a blue streak.

The bad news: I was recently laid off and became an unemployment statisticThe good news: Despite the relatively hefty price tag, I was given these boxes to clean out my cubicle.I'm no stranger to moving offices. At one of my former employers, we moved offices about once a year... one year I moved exactly 6 offices to the left.Every time I have moved, we have been given standard issue "bankers boxes" for moving. Assembly on the first one is always a little tricky and a test of your ability to interpret cryptic visual diagrams. (I think it is sort of like "map people" and "direction people" -- my brain just doesn't interpret the diagrams that well.The instructions for assembling these boxes were about as "clear" as others and they assembled about as quickly as other boxes.However, one of the things I noticed is that the way you carry the box has a significant impact on how well the "structural integrity" of the box is maintained. That is because only one side has a "double cardboard" edge. If you look at the stock photo -- the back of the box, because of the way the box is constructed, has 2 layers of cardboard. The front only has 1 layer/fold of cardboard. As a result, you need to pick it up from the "correct side" (double layer of cardboard). If you pick it up from the wrong side, the single-layer edge will "collapse in" against your stomach.The handles are strong and reasonably comfortable. I didn't have the sense that the bottom was going to fall out.I wouldn't use these to pack only books -- they are clearly intended only for light office stuff or "pillows and light linens" (a recommended use). However, having these boxes is a BIG step up from trying to steal boxes from grocery stores or used moving boxes (though maybe not as economically friendly). However, if I had to buy them myself, I would probably have not spent the money and looked for other alternatives (like reusable Rubbermaid plastic tubs which I have at home anyway)[NCJVR]

The most reliable and solid printer I have ever owned is a Canon Pixma i4500 which sits on my desk and is wired directly to my personal computer. It has been more dependable than any HP or Epson printer I have used and I have used and abused it for years. Because of my experience with my older Pixma, I had very high expectations of the MG5420. For printing, it performs quite well. For scanning, though, it is less than ideal.Setup of this printer is absurdly easy. I did follow the printed directions, not because I felt like I did not understand the device but because I wanted to determine if the included instructions are useful or if they are somewhat off in their guidance. They took me step by step through configuration, but it could have been summarized as "plug it in, turn it on, follow the instructions on the screen".This particular printer comes with a black pigment cartridge in addition to 4 color ink tanks. I like this configuration as it means I can print a lot more text pages.Initial configuration, while straightforward, is lengthy. It takes about 10 minutes of calibration and alignment (during which time it makes all manner of odd noises) before it is ready to go to work. Once it finished configuring itself, I plugged it in to the USB port and Windows 7 loaded drivers from online and it's ready to go. So, if the system has Internet access, the installation media isn't even necessary.I elected not to set up this printer on wireless, as it will be dedicated to a single machine and as such connected via USB. So, I can't really speak to it's configuration on a wireless LAN.Print quality is very good. I selected a high-resolution photo and sent it to the printer, and the printer dutifully produced a borderless letter-sized picture with fine detail, even set on regular paper and normal print settings. Color reproduction was slightly dull, though, and I will have to retry with photo paper and photo settings. More astonishing, though, is the print speed - my photo emerged from the printer in roughly 20 seconds, making this one of the fastest color printers I have used for printing photos.I then decided to scan an image with the printer. The scan was quick and painless. That said, the scan was very banded and the image was marginally acceptable. I tried another scan and got similar results - banding on the image and the overall quality was low. Other reviewers have had good success with the scanning, so I am hopeful that my particular unit is slightly faulty.I tried using the copy feature using a text-only document and the copy was nearly indistinguishable from the original. Because the copy portion relies on scanning I was unsure if the copy would have the same banding issue - it did not. So, this tells me that in the capacity of a copier this unit is capable of decent OCR work.My experience with this printer is mostly good. The photo printing and copying is good while the scanning of images leaves something to be desired. Overall, this is a decent printer for moderate use and is worth a look.

This is a very nice label maker.  If you are looking for a top of the line, desktop label maker by Dymo, with a color touch screen and a computer interface, and money is no object, this one is for you. This model would be especially useful for those who require their labels to be "artistic" or incorporate features such as automatic numbering and dating, special fonts, logos, graphics or be able to print from spreadsheets or data files.There are two leading label maker companies: Dymo (owned by Sanford Brands) and Brother. Each manufacturer requires its own propriety tape cartridge, so if you already have Dymo tape, you'll probably not want to switch to Brother, and vise versa. Of course, even within the same company, different models require different types of tape, so there is no real guarantee that the tape cartridge you are using currently will be compatible, anyway.This particular model, Dymo Label Manager 500 requires D1 tape cartridges. It will print 5 different width labels: ", 3/8", ", " and 1".  It comes with a "starter" roll of 10' x 1" black print on white tape.Set up is not difficult but it is multi-step. This labeler is powered by a rechargeable, Lithium Polymer battery pack which arrives only partially (very partially) charged. This battery has to be inserted into the printer and it has to be charged for about three hours before first use. The charging adapter supplied with the printer is only used for charging the battery; it cannot be used to power the label maker while charging.The next step is to snap in the label cassette which is extremely easy.Although not required in order to make labels, this printer offers enhanced functionality when attached to your computer.  In order to do this one must go to the Dymo web site, register the product and then locate and download the software (Windows or Mac) on to your computer. You then need to update this software as well as the software on the label printer. The printer then attaches to your computer via a supplied USB cable.You open up the Dymo label maker software, turn on the label printer and you are good to go.Here are some of the benefits of this label printer:1) The best thing about this printer is the large 3 " x 2 " color touch screen that displays WYSIWYG type and layout.2) You can control the layout, the font selection and insert characters, bar codes, and downloaded symbols and logos directly from the screen.3) The QUERTY keyboard is large and easy to use.4) You can select whether the labels are cut automatically or manually.5) When the unit is charging, a large, easy to read clock appears on the screen. This is something that my AT&T; desk phone does not do!6) This model accepts tape from " to 1" wide.7) The unit offers 10 fonts, 25 font sizes, 5 borders, underline, strikeout, outline, and bold.8) The unit prints in 300 dpi resolution. It prints extremely fast.9) The unit prints barcodes, symbols, diacritic marks, automatic numbering, date and time, days, months and quarters without being connected to a computer.10) The unit will store settings for up to 5 different users.11) The unit will save your favorite labels and they can easily be recalled.12) The software (v.8.4.0.1524) is easy to use. It has no trouble identifying the printer and can switch from various label maker models should you use more than one.13) The software has an address book feature that can interface with Outlook. This is very nifty for creating address labels.14) The software can print any font available on your computer. If you are a fan of Franklyn Gothic or Lucida Calligraphy....no problem.15) The software can accept information from Microsoft Excel, Access, and Text files as well as Universal Data Links.16) The software can interface with Dymo Stamps website.17) The software can download clip art and screen capture.There are some negative aspects:1) The door to the battery and tape cassette compartment is on the bottom of the unit. One is required to turn the unit over to access this compartment or to check on the size of the tape, etc.2) The electric charger cannot power the unit while charging the battery. This is really dumb.3) I charged the battery for three hours before first use. I made about six labels. The battery showed that it was half drained. I assume by this that the battery requires longer than three hours to be fully charged.4) The unit does not charge while attached to your computer via the USB cord.5) The unit times out very quickly. If you are not actively making labels, it will turn itself off within a minute or two. This is frustrating while you are using the software on your computer to compose the label and hit "print" only to find that the printer has turned itself off.6) The unit does not automatically recognize the size and type of tape cassette that has been inserted. You have to manually set this feature.7) Although the software offers symbols and logos the design interface is extremely limited. There are many options but fundamentally, this is a label maker.I enjoy using this label printer although I will probably never use most of its features. I like that it accepts 1" wide labels and the color touch screen is definitely a big plus when composing the label. Being able to connect to the computer is somewhat useful but not necessary for the type of labeling I do around the house. Because of its expense, I would recommend it to businesses, those who require logos or other graphics on their labels, scrap-bookers, and those who require access to data files for their labels.I also own two other label makers:TheBrother Desktop Office Labeler with AC Adapter (PT2030AD)which offers many nice, easy to use features and sells for about $30-$50 with an AC adapter. The down side is that this P-Touch has a poor quality, difficult to read screen, only accepts labels up to " wide and cannot connect to a computer. It does take regular batteries, works with an AC electric cord, and is relatively light weight and easy to carry around. It makes perfectly decent labels. It seems that Brother offers a wider variety of label types, sizes, colors and formats than Dymo.TheDymo Labelmanager Pnp Printeris a label printer that only works when connected to your computer. It has no screen or keyboard; it only prints what your computer tells it to. It is powered solely through the USB cord. It comes with its own Dymo Lite software but will also work with the full Dymo software version which Dymo offers for free on its web site. This is not a bad option if you only need labels up to " wide and know that you only will be composing labels on your computer. It takes up very little desk space and you don't have to worry about re-charging it or replacing its batteries.

The tape is standard Scotch Magic Transparent tape (Scotch 810) which they apparently now simply call Magic Tape, meaning it's not the yellowing cellophane tape which they now call Transparent tape, but rather the long-lasting tape that's safe to use on photographs and other items you wish to keep forever. You can write on it, Magic's other claim to fame. Here, you've got the 3/4" width that I prefer over the 1/2" variety. This one works well in case you just sealed an envelope, put on a stamp, and then realized that you forgot to put the letter inside. Open the envelope, insert the letter, and fold tape over the open edge...good as new and ready for mailing. The 1/2" width isn't quite enough for that.Dispenser - that's where this is different. Maybe you'll get the green one pictured here. We got the purple one. Our 6 year old said, "Ooooo, purple!" OK, I get it. Cool dispenser. But would I really pay $2.50 for 300" of tape when I can go elsewhere on Amazon and get three times the amount of tape for only double the price in a regular dispenser (that's $5 for 900" of tape)? This dispenser works, of course. You can open it up and refill it. You can tear tape off using the perforated edge. You can sit it upright on your desk and go, "Ooooo, purple!" If that's worth an extra buck or so, go for it. The packaging removes easily: pull the two halves of the plastic assembly apart as you would any Scotch tape dispenser, pull the tape off the spindle, pull out the cardboard, and reassemble. It takes less time to do than it does to read these instructions. The plastic of the dispenser is a little less thick than a standard tape dispenser. As a result, the dispenser feels somewhat less substantial than a standard dispenser.Whatever you do, avoid standard Transparent cellophane tape (in the red packages from Scotch) and stick with the Magic tape in the green packages. It's always worth the extra price. There's also the double-sided tape in the yellow package, removable poster tape in the purple package, Magic Plus removable transparent tape in the blue package, and the list goes on. A long time ago, I picked up a dispenser of Scotch packing tape in a standard dispenser; I've kept the dispenser all these years because it has a metal cutting edge rather than the standard plastic one. It works just a little better. But back to the review...So overall this is the best tape in a interesting color dispenser of novel shape. It does the job and is great for the 5-10 year old age group. The tape sticks, the dispenser dispenses, and overall the product works as advertised and promoted.

I was a little worried about upgrading to a multifunction printer - the usual axiom is that the more things you try to do, the worse you'll do them. This printer really does do it all, and does it all well. My only complaint is that there are a few undocumented functions which I'll cover below.Printing: it prints quickly and is the quality is very sharp. It supports just about every printing method you would want - raw socket printing, USB, internet printing, print over http, etc.Fax: It works as you would expect a fax machine to work (not a whole lot to say here).Scanning: In addition to the regular scan, there is also scan to PC which I really love. Stick a stack of papers to digitize in the paper tray, hit scan to PC, and a few minutes later a PDF (or tiff or jpeg if you prefer) file will appear in the designated folder on your PC. Easy as pie, and if you're working on your PC at the same time, you won't even notice. Since I run a small business, but hate keeping paper around, (so I want to scan everything for my records), I find this feature invaluable. You can and obviously should set a password on this feature so no one else can drop files on your computer remotely.Copying: You can do regular (1 sheet) copying, or bulk copying through the tray at the top. You can also set it to do 1->2 or 2->2 double sided copying. Really everything you'd want in a copier.Set-up: Initial set up was easy, and can be done with with a directly connected USB, connecting to the printer's wireless network, or connecting to a wired network and getting a DHCP address. However the manual included on the CD neglected one crucial piece of information - the username and password for the web console so you can change the settings. The username is admin, and the password is sec00000 - with that you can log in and set up your printer.

I wasn't in the market for a printer at all, but as soon as I got this baby hooked up I was using it all afternoon!  With the ease of set up, the unique options, and the relatively low price I would recommend this printer without hesitation.Personally, the appeal of any printer means that it's easy to set up and start using.  I found this printer very easy to set up, and I can't imagine many people having a problem with it, even if you're not very tech savvy.  The manuals are easy to follow, and the start up CD is intuitive.I printed some standard documents, and they printed in a snap.  This also prints on both sides of the paper sheet, and that appeals to me as someone who hates to waste paper as I print up documents and essays.I scanned both a picture and a magazine article that had some lines and angles on it, and they printed separately, quickly, and were clear as a bell.The real draw for me, though, is being able to remotely send pictures from your iPhone or iPod Touch to this printer, and print out your images with crystal clarity.  The printing is nearly instantaneous, and it's pretty great to be able to print your photos directly from your phone or other handheld device.  The quality of the pictures were perfect;  the photos from my iPhone were the same quality of a roll of film being developed at a photo developer.  It's also easy to print photos from any source, like a usb stick for example.  It has a usb port, and it works very quickly and concisely.The only complaints I have are minor.  The main gripe I have is the noise of this thing.  It's not a deal breaker, but I've never heard a personal printer that was so loud.  Considering the options I have with this printer, though, it doesn't bother me much.  Also, it seems like a fax being included would have been the cherry on the top.  It's wi-fi enabled, can take photos from your phone, and has usb hookups, so a fax should have been an easy addition.Perhaps all of the things I'm mentioning are just standard additions to printers these days, but I found this printer to be a really cool addition to my network center.  As I stated before, if the idea of sending pictures from your phone to your printer is enticing, and then having them printed out in a matter of seconds in glossy, picture perfect quality, you should definitely pick this up!

My daughter is a professional photographer, who swears by Canon products, so I thought she would be the ideal person to review this item.The color, and printing results are spectacular, really. The print plug studio software is OK, not great but OK - but printing from other photo software is easy.The printer itself is HUGE, and I mean huge - it also weighs almost 50 pounds so think about that before you buy.All the usual bells and whistles, wi-fi, mobile printing, High speed USB etc. etc.For a professional grade photographic printer, it's not that expensive either, not really - probably on the high end price wise for the casual user, but for a pro, pretty reasonable.The question, is, remains, and always will be INK..........Why printer ink is so expensive has always been a mystery to me, and often it works out cheaper in the long run (in some cases) to buy a new printer complete with ink every time you run out!My daughter uses a professional online print service.All her prints, pictures, blow ups remattings, photoshopped images and so on, are delivered (often within 48 hours) and are of impeccable quality. Price for price, print for print it is often cheaper to use this kind of service over owning, maintaining, and refilling a pro printer like this one.As an example this takes 8 ink cartridges, yes 8 - that's not a misprint. Price for a refill here on Amazon isCanon CLI42 8 Pack Ink Tanks for PIXMA PRO-100 PrinterI think the bottom line is choice and convenience. If you do a lot of home printing, and want exceptional quality, this is one way to go.Most pro photographers I know, can do without the hassle, and outsource to pro printing services.

I've been rather happy with this scanner thus far in its limited use. I'm an amateur photographer, and workflows are everything. You'll need ample drive space if you want to start scanning your photos and figure out if you want to preserve them in lossless (TIFF) or lossy (JPG) and at what quality. It's worth the investment to have something for home, even if you just relegate this to scanning.

I've tried several Epson printers. My favorite has been the 840, mainly because of its speed, but it is huge compared to the Epson Stylus NX530. It works as well as the 840, it's just slower. But it fits in a much smaller space, such as a shelf, and since it's wireless you don't need to worry about cords. For everyday home or light office needs, this is a wonderful printer.Set up is easy. It took about 15 minutes to install and all the features, including wireless printing from multiple devices, were ready to go. Both color and black and white print outs were crisp and vibrant. Pages also printed quickly enough for my needs. Scanning is very good. The images are nearly as detailed as the originals for things like photographs and you can't really see much of a difference from the original when scanning documents. Black and white and color copies also turn out quite nice. The paper tray is large capacity, so you don't need to refill it very often and the ink cartridges are lasting on par with other ink jets I've owned.My only complaints are the same as with my other Epsons and they aren't such a big deal that they make me dislike the machine. This is not the printer for photos. The color just isn't vibrant like you would get from Shutterfly or Walgreens or a professional photo shop or even from the HP ink jet I had ten years ago. If you want a photo printer, get something else. My other displeasure is with the touch screen. It does not take a light touch. I have to poke at it just right to get it to register my touch. It's nothing like a smart Phone or tablet in which the lightest swipe will get it done. Over time though, I've largely perfected my poke and I usually don't have to press the screen twice anymore. Like I said, these complaints are minor and overall this is a very good machine and gets done what I want it to do.

I was in the market for a scanner to do negatives, slides and prints and this one was recommended by a former colleague that had a side job working in a camera store, that did lots of scanning for clients. This was the scanner she had bought for home use.Figuring that anyone who did this professionally would be able to steer me to the best tool to buy for home use, I'm happy to say she was right.I have a great multi-function printer at home, that has a flat bed scanner, but you can't use those to do negatives and slides. Also since it was the family's printer it was not in a spot convenient to my computer to do one scan after the other.SEAMLESS SET UPThis scanner sets up seamlessly.  You have a CD of software and drivers and it takes only a few minutes to get the scanner up and running.  I also like the fact that the scanner lid holds it self up when you lift it.  That is a simple thing, but when you are scanning a lot of stuff, that is such a convenience.SCANNING SLIDES: QUICK AND EASY.First my boyfriend nabbed it before I even used it and scanned his entire family's collection of slides.  This scanner has an attachment that allows you to set in 4 slides at once, to prescan, then you do your final scan to create the file. It does a nice job of incrementing the numbers for you.  He complained that he needed to reset the output size with each scan, but I found the way around that was to use a custom setting or not use Thumbnails.  He had wanted the output size to be original versus 4 X 6".WORKHORSE.Next I started in on my Dad's collection of prints, albums and negatives.  I haven't even gotten out the slides yet.  So far I have done over 2000 scans with this.  I have this scanner, sitting on my desk, so it is convenient to use.  The scanner itself is not that much bigger than it's maximum size scan, so it does not take up much room.QUICK SWAP OUT OF WHITE BACKING MAKE IT EASY TO CHANGE FORMATSThis scanner comes with the plastic parts that set in the scanner to hold slides and film.  The white background comes out when you do these transparent media.  It is really easy to swap these parts in and out. If you have odd format sizes, as I do, you can set them on the scanner without the film guides, but they must be in the center where the mirror is.  So I used post-it-notes on the glass to help locate the negatives.  This works well and leaves no residue. Post-it notes also has a fully sticky tape that really works well for this.MORE USES THAN JUST PHOTOS, IF CONVENIENTOne thing I found by having this scanner so convenient, is that I have taken to scanning in recipes and articles (like yoga routines) that catch my eye in magazines and storing them on my computer.  It allows you to ditch all the paper and keep only what you need. You need to be rigorous in naming and filing but it also makes this more handy as you don't have to dig through a bunch of magazines to find what you want.  I had not anticipated this plus.COOL ASPECTI had stacks of old format negatives that had not seen the light of day in years.  When I scanned them the scanner took these negatives and converted them to the positives that prints could be made from, or pictures that could be used in stuff like photo books. I found this utterly fascinating watching the pictures appear magically. I know that is not so stupendous, but I found it utterly cool.  Also I had some albums that I just unbound  the pages and put the whole page on the scanner.  Using a pre-scan, I could locate the pictures I wanted to capture, and save separately.  If the page is too big, first I did one half and then the other.  This is great if you have fragile old albums that you don't want to risk removing the pictures from.  For that matter if you can open the pages wide enough, you don't have to unbind the albums.The color restoration option also took some horrible looking prints from the 1960s to passable.  That was merely checking a box when needed.SUMMARYThis was an entirely utilitarian purchase. I had tons of stuff that needed scanning and did not want to pay a fortune to do so.  This scanner fit the bill nicely and has lead me to use it for a variety of other items. It went from utility to fun and that was cool.

There's a lot to like about thisSamsung SCX-3405FW Wireless Monochrome Printer with Scanner, Copier and Fax, and one of the best parts was that it could be set up so quickly.  In fact, I had it printing from a Windows 7 notebook and a MacBook Pro within ten minutes of taking it out of the box, and that was a surprise in itself.The wireless connection was easy to set up, and once the unit was online and the paper was loaded, everything worked quite efficiently.  For those who want the quick facts, the good and the not so good, here they are.◆ Pros:+ Very solid all-in-one SOHO solution where space is at a premium.+ Extremely fast setup with either Window 7 or Mac OS X+ Connects via built-in wireless 802.11; USB 2.0; Ethernet 10/100 Base TX+ Fast printing, over 20 pages per minute (ppm); verified+ First print out in less than 10 seconds from ready+ High-resolution black & white printing; about 1,200 x 1,200 dpi+ Holds about 150 sheets standard 20 lb. letter paper+ Prints on plain paper, envelopes, labels and other paper stock+ Auto document feeder (ADF) holds up to 40 sheets+ Fax modem speed at 33.6 Kbps (not verified)+ Warranty: 12 months, parts & labor◆ Cons:- Built-in LCD display is a bit small at 16 x 2 line; can be hard to read◆ Details & First Impressions:The printer was packaged very well, and it only took a few minutes to unpack it from the carton and review the contents.  Its desktop footprint is very small; at 15.8" wide and 11.5" deep it takes up little more space than my Windows 7 notebook, and at 11.7" high it's not very obtrusive at all.  It weighs less than 18 lbs., so it's easy to move.  There was no real user manual, but here's one available online for download from Samsung.  Besides the printer itself, is came with the following:- CD software- A quick installation guide- A full network installation guide- French display panel sticker- An AC power cord- A USB cord- A phone cord (for fax)- A warranty bookletDid a brief overview of the basic setup, plugged in the power and the included USB cord (wireless would come later).  The instructions indicated to shake the toner cartridge, so I did. Paper loading was easy, and printing the first documents from a Word document in the Windows 7 notebook with embedded images and graphics was impressive, with clear and sharp details and good grey scaling.  Did the same with the MacBook Pro with equal results.Tackled the wireless setup next, using the included manual.  All went fine, but it's suggested that you have the details of your own wireless network handy for reference.◆ In Use:This all-in-one printer, scanner, copier and fax system is perfect for the small office & home office (SOHO) environments, especially where space may be at a premium.  It's extremely quiet in it's operation, more so than any office printer that I've encountered, and one can actually make a phone call without leaving the room when it's printing.Scanning was tried only on the Windows 7 notebook, and with the software installed it's quite simple once you learn the interface.  You just right click Smart Panel in the Windows task bar, select Scan Manager, select the printer you want to use, and then click Quick Scan.  Once the Quick Scan dialog appears, you set the Save Location, the File Name (default is the date and time the scan is performed), and the File Format, which will be the default file type for each consecutive scan. Your choices are TIFF, PDF, BMP, and JPG formats. After entering this info, click OK and then click Scan to scan the document to the PC.Will admit that I did not use the fax feature on this all-in-one unit except for about two minutes as a test to confirm that it worked, and for the primary reason that I personally have very little (if any) use for it.  Scanning directly to email can be done, which is something that I find quite useful, as do the people with whom I correspond. It's nice to know that it's there if needs change in the future, but it's not something that I've done in years.Copying documents is straightforward, and you can also prints multiple image copies from the original document onto a single page. The actual number of images is automatically determined by the size of original image and paper size.  Copy speed is the same as printing (about 15 to 21 ppm in letter format), and there are a number of different options that you can choose.  Just remember that your results will be in black & white.The original toner cartridge is limited, so plan on getting one soon.  This seems to be an industry-wide practice now, somewhat irritating, but that's just the way it is, so please don't shoot the messenger.  A new cartridge should give you about 1,500 printouts, and the proper replacement toner cartridge for this unit is theSamsung MLT-D101S/XAA Toner 1.5K Yield (ML-2165W, SCX-3405FW, SF-760P).  It can be ordered here on Amazon or probably picked up from your local office supply store.◆ Update 11/12/2013:I recently did some upgrades to my computers, taking my MacBook Pro to OS X 10.9 Mavericks and installing Windows 8.1 on a notebook PC. Expected to have to do some driver updates for this printer, but it wasn't necessary, as it was automatically detected by both new operating system upgrades, and both have functioned perfectly to date. Checking online, Samsung has updated some of the drivers/downloads in October/November 2013, so if you own this printer you may wish the check online for those.◆ Update 1/22/2014:Checking for the newest software updates at the Samsung support site, I discovered a note for the Samsung Mobile Print app. Going a bit further, found that it claimed to offer "wireless printing, scanning and file transfers let you do more on the go." This app requires Android Version 2.1 or later (Galaxy S, Galaxy Tab, etc.) or iOS Version 3.2 or later (iPod Touch, iPhone, iPad), and is compatible with Samsung network capable printers, such as this one. See the comments to my review here for further details, as this freebie is well worth it if you need mobile printing on the fly.◆ Summary:Color laser printers can be very expensive, as can be their toner cartridges.  This is a personal choice, but for color printing, especially when dealing with photos, I prefer using a separate photo-grade inkjet printer.  For document processing, a good monochrome (black & white) high-speed printer, especially if it's an all-in-one, is a far more economical and functional choice for daily needs.When looking at this printer sitting next to me right now, the first thought is how compact it is, smaller than my old HP LaserJet 4L from years ago, yet far faster, much quieter and with far better ergonomics and controls.  The second thought is one that dominates: this all-in-one is very quiet.  It's one of the easiest printers that I've encountered to set up, and the results that I've been getting are surprisingly good.  It's compact, fast, efficient and quiet, which makes it ideal for any SOHO environment.  If you need an all-in-one and can forego color printing, this for the money, thisSamsung SCX-3405FWis an excellent choice, and is easily worthy of a 5-star recommendation.JW ▪ 7/3/2012; Updated 11/12/2013, 1/22/2014

This is a fantastic machine.  I've owned it for over two years now, and it's truly a workhorse.  I have almost caught fire to a couple things before, but it keeps right on going. You have to be careful laminating small things like bookmarks. I'm cheap, and I buy menu sized laminating pouches because I can't find 12x12 pouches for scrapbooking paper.  So when I have about six inches of laminating pouch leftover, I use it for small projects (bookmarks, pressed flowers, whatever).  This can be tricky also.  You have to make sure you either use a carrier or the glue part of the cut pouch lines up perfectly so you don't get any glue on the rollers as it goes through.  I'm sure most people won't have this problem.  I just hate throwing things away.  3.  You have to play with the settings a bit to get the exact amount right.  If it doesn't seal, you need a higher temp.  If it wrinkles, you need to lower it.EDITED TO ADD:  3/12/14  I bought this machine 2 and a half years ago. Just an update to the review I wrote a very short time ago (at least... for a printer's lifetime).A few weeks after writing this review, black text started looking a little "off". The ink monitor showed that black was low, so I dutifully bought a new Genuine Epson cartridge. I put it in, did the magic new cartridge dance, cleaned out the print head, and... no black."Hm. Must be Photo Black! I don't know why it's blending them, but I'll give that a shot." So, another cartridge, another new cartridge incantation, and... no black. Thinking "Wow, what a waste of ink it would be if I kept doing these head cleanings on all five cartridges!", I decided to take out all but Black - which caused the printer to freak out and cry about not having its whole collection.Well, on a printer that's fairly new, I'll just RMA it. Sorry, not so much with Epson. They won't just take your word for it, so there's a solid hour of time I get to spend troubleshooting with someone who thinks this is my first printer. Wonderful.And while "Epson won't print black" is an incredibly common search term that produces tons of hits, none of them go anywhere useful. Basically: everyone's Epson seems to do this, and the solution is getting Epson to replace it. Why this never happened on my Workforce 840 is probably luck, if I had to guess.But wait... my story gets better. Epson sent me a replacement. I got to trade my shiny new (albeit broken) printer for a refurbished model that was scratched everywhere, and had mysterious "splashes" all over one side. I was kind of sad that I had a printer that looked so trashed until... YAY! Epson replaced my broken printer with... ANOTHER BROKEN PRINTER! This one wouldn't even power on properly.So what did I do? Why, I called Epson! (Did I mention that it's not toll-free? I get that most people, myself included, have wireless phones or unlimited long distance these days, but still, it seemed pretty chintzy.)This time, it only took twenty minutes. I described the problem, which the first person immediately confirmed as being a hardware problem. He transferred me to someone else, who took somewhat longer to confirm that, yes, there was a hardware problem. Great! Try again, right? Mmmmm... no. For reasons that the support guy couldn't articulate, he couldn't send a replacement. Someone *might* call me in 24 - 48 hours, but if they don't, I should call back, unless I want to wait 3 - 5 business days to see if a replacement just happens to show up. (I'm not even kind of making this up.)P.S., hope you live near a FedEx depot or Kinko's, because they're the only places you can drop off the broken printer. Lucky me, the nearest Kinko's is almost across the street from the nearest FedEx depot -- 20 miles away. And since I now have to return the first printer within 7 days to prevent a charge on my credit card, and the replacement replacement printer may or may not come, I get to go twice! Maybe I'll visit both places!***Original Review Follows***Between my Canon Pixma MX850, MX860, andEpson WorkForce 845(not to mention several others), I've settled in to some requirements for any decent multifunction printer, and I have to say, the XP-800 has hit just about every mark:1) Hybrid supportOne of the things I've traditionally disliked about Epson multifunction printers is their penchant for leaving Mac users in the cold. Even the 845 had features that worked in Windows (e.g. "Scan to PC") but not OS X. Fortunately, Epson has come up with great Windows *and* Mac drivers -- AND they're apparently paying penance by including Google Cloud Print (so Chromebooks can print, too), e-mail-to-print, AirPrint... Seriously, hats off on this one. Everything that works in Windows 8 works in OS X, and just about every mobile device under the sun can print.2) SizeThe XP-800 is smaller in every dimension from any other multifunction printer I've owned, yet it still manages to pack two front-loading paper trays! There's a catch, though, in that it protrudes nearly 10" when the tray comes out for printing -- and the tray never automatically retracts. It's probably the most confusing design I've ever seen on a printer. Yet, it still takes up less space than either of my Pixmas.3) Print qualityEver since the Epson Stylus 740, there's been a certain sharpness of text / softness of color that even a casual observer could notice. "Did you print this on an Epson?" has been asked more than a few times, and I'd wager, rarely in a negative way. While the text quality on the XP-800 is more than decent, I did notice that the characteristic Epson "look" was missing for the first time since the late 90's.4) Ink managementEpson ink seems a bit on the expensive side to me, and yet, the XP-800 cartridges are very competitively priced. Once thing I did notice though: the XP-800 is chewing through ink like crazy. Having the C/M/Y/K/PK tanks is certainly welcome, but not if very casual printing means buying a new black cartridge almost monthly. I'm not 100% certain that the ink isn't at a 50% factory fill and that the ink meters are just relative contents-to-full. So far, though, it's looking like the XP-800 might be expensive to run.All things being equal, I can't fall all over myself with praise for the XP-800, but it's definitely a competent multifunction. If you have non-Windows devices (and especially if a Chromebook is on your horizon) you owe it to yourself to have this printer on your short list.

I live in a nice neighborhood, but there have been some recent, strange disappearances of package deliveries. I'm well protected with an alarm system and a more persuasive physical deterrent if someone makes it through the door, but I want to be able to see who approaches my home when I'm not around. The Lorex wireless system seemed to make sense, mostly because of the architecture of my home. I don't have a basement or an attic, so laying video cable from cameras to a DVR won't easily work for me.So, I got the Lorex system and was immediately impressed with the quality look and feel of the camera and the receiver/display. To test the unit before permanently installing it, I plugged the camera into an outside socket near my front door and then turned on the receiver in my house about 35-40 feet away. Between the outside camera and the receiver was, of course, one exterior wall and one interior wall. No significant amount of metal or electrical wiring is in this interior wall, however, at this 40 foot distance, I had to hold the receiver up to get a signal from the camera. I moved the receiver to about 30 feet and the signal was good, but would occasionally, momentarily tell me that it couldn't receive a signal from the camera. When I moved the receiver to the room where my computer is located, (where I really want to place the receiver) approximately 65 feet from the camera and the addition of one more interior wall, no camera signal could be received at all.So in its initial test, the system won't work for me. According to Lorex, the wireless range might reach up to 180 feet indoors, but I couldn't make it one third that distance. I can't very well use this system. With such a limited wireless range, I would have to place the receiver so close to the front door of my house that anyone forcing their way into my house could simply remove the SD card from the receiver. In order to connect the receiver to SKYPE, it needs to be hard wired to a PC, and that wouldn't really solve the problem anyway.Other issues with the system:- The receiver settings are a bit non-intuitive, but once you get the hang of moving around the screen, things seem to fall into place.- The motion detection recording has a slight delay in kicking in. I recorded my wife returning home and all I saw on the replay was her moving past the last 30% of the screen. Had she been a burgler, I wouldn't have been able to identify her. There is a setting to increase/decrease the sensitivity of the motion detection, and I had the daytime sensitivity set to Medium. The only setting for the nighttime motion detection is Low, so it is questionable how well this would work when the sun goes down.Lorex is known for consumer friendly monitoring systems, and their setup manual is well organized and easy to follow. Yes, the onscreen controls are a bit odd, but once you get your system setup correctly, you won't have to mess with that often. The display panel is clear and bright, but don't expect studio quality recording from the camera.... it is a security camera and nothing more - slightly better than what you see on liquor store holdup videos recorded in 1998 and played back on cops and robbers programs.Other users report getting good range from their systems. I could possibly have a lemon, as my house is pretty wifi signal friendly. But based on my 30 minute test, this dog won't hunt.
