My first printer was a Dot-Matrix; black dots on the page that formed letters and numbers. Then somewhere along the way came the ink jet color printer; then laser. And now we have the choice of all black or color printing.To the printer. Before connecting it to the world remove the tone cartridge, give it a back and forth shake and put it back in the printer.  Now it's time to tell it how you want it to connect. Because my gateway(AT&T;) does not have a WPS button, I had to connect it manually. Manually being, boot up your computer, turn on the printer and install the disc that came with the printer.It asks how you want to connect the printer to the computer. I chose wireless. Next step is to hook up the supplied USB cable to the computer and printer. The software will walk you through the install step by step. When it connects wirelessly you are instructed to remove the USB cable.  Now it will install the driver and other software of your choice. Last step is to print out a test page and you're done.This printer replaced a Lexmark ink jet wireless printer. The router is about midway in the house and when I would click on the print button for the Lexmark, it would take quite a while to start printing so that you wondered if the printer was working.  Not so with this one. You better have the paper tray out or you will be picking up paper off the floor. Before you can move your finger off the mouse it's printing. But I have scanned an email, signed it and copied it back to the computer to email it out and that worked great, after figuring out where the scanned copy was in the computer.Of course, print in full mode is very clear and fast. It's a Laser.  In ECO mode, the  printing is still very clear.  I printed out a 6 page on-line tip and hints on how to kill ants.  Besides saving toner (which is hard to tell, because the printing is still very clear), it printed two pages on one side of the sheet, which gave me a total of 3 pages. As far as enlarging, I haven't needed to try that, because everything I've printed has been right on.I'm very pleased with this printer and have to give it 5 stars. Nowadays, setting up a new printer can’t get easier. Unboxing and setting this printer up to get ready for some printing, scanning, and copying took about 15 minutes total. I did not have to install any software or driver on my Mac; all I had to do was connect the printer to my home internet.Basically, I took the printer out of box, powered on, put the inks (combined color cartridge and black cartridge), then waited for the printer to print out alignment testing, and then I scanned that paper as instructed on the color LCD screen on the printer. Then the printer showed that the alignment and calibration was successful. One last step was to connect to my home WIFI. My network name was hidden (not broadcasting) and there was option I can manually type in the SSID name. As I expected, the printer did not recognize 5 GHz N network, but had no problem connecting to 2.4 GHz network. Once the printer was connected to the internet, it asked if I want to enable ‘webservice’ and ‘auto update’ so I tapped OK. So all this process took about 15 minutes, and I was glad I didn’t have to go through the HP software installation process from the enclosed CD.Printing documents and photos, scanning, and copying all worked great as expected. Printing one of the pages from the printer’s TimesDigest app took 24 seconds (b/w, full page with multi colums) and printing a 4x6 sized color photo from my iPhone took about 70 seconds. Scanning a color document took about 10 seconds and copying a color document took about 37 seconds (b/w document took 22 seconds). I’ve tried many different brands of printers and compare to others, and there was no significant speed difference on this one. However, I noticed this one scanned slightly faster than others.Print quality in normal mode looked very clear and sharp and even in draft mode still looked wonderful to me. One thing I noticed was the black ink level downed about 10~15% after some 30 pages of full black and white documents printing.Scan/copy quality also looked great and was so easy to operate, this is probably the best home wireless printer under $100 with many convenient features.Some highlights I’d like to mention from this printer are: first, how easy it is to setup and use. The color touch screen LCD on the printer makes things a lot easier to setup and operate. The printer being wireless is another advantage. There is no need to wire next to the computer; I can just put this anywhere I want and wireless range seemed very good as well. Once it’s connected to my home network, it was already ready for Apple’s AirPrint feature. My iPhone and iPad recognized printer immediately, and I was able to print from my mobile devices without anything to download and setup. The only thing I had to do to print from my Mac was adding this printer in the System Preferences -> Printers pane. HP Envy was already showing on the list, I just had to click on ‘ + ‘ button. I printed a news article from Safari and had no issues and loved double sided printing. I actually didn’t expect double side printing because of the thin form factor, but I was wrong. This printer has double side printing feature,and it was quick and easy, and it saves paper.Secondly, HPConnected service is quite convenient and has some nice features. This printer can be connected to internet and managed online. I can email documents or photos to this printer from anywhere in the world and it prints out. Anyone with this printer’s email address (changeable, and can limit the access as well) can send emails to print out. I am actually thinking about buying this printer for my parents so they can effortlessly receive prints of their grandson from their home. I could also subscribe HP’s Instant Ink plan so my elderly parents don’t have to go out and try to find the right kind of ink when it is empty. I can send 50 photos a month for only $2.99/month. That’s very cost effective in my opinion (compared to more conventional way to send physical photos to far away parents or family members) and time saving because I don’t need to drive anywhere to pickup the photos or pay anything for shipping if ordered online. I just keep thinking about different ways I can make use of this printer and that makes me really excited.There is also app catalogue on HPconnected website, and I could choose with app (they call it Printables on the printer’s LCD screen) I want to put on my printer. There are many useful apps for both kids and adults. My son just learned how to print coloring pages already, and my wife liked the coupon printing app. I could schedule when to print out NY times digest and that’s like NYT paper delivered to me for free (well, except cost of ink and paper).Lastly, I love the design of this printer. There are a few mini or portable printers with very small form factor, but those usually have limited functionality because of the size. However, I was really surprised how thin this printer is yet with all the great features. The whole size is about my 24” cinema display with the thickness of 5”. I was surprised it could still do double side printing and has pull out paper loader/tray. The design also looks slick. Compared to my older HP eprinter, this one has much improved design that doesn’t look or feel so plasticky and cheap. It looks quite nice to put next to my desk of brushed metal toned computers and monitors.Overall, this is the best home printer in my opinion. This printer offers more features than any other home printers and it is really easy to use and operate/maintain. This printer is working very well with all of my i-devices and multiple Macs with ease. I found no issues over a couple weeks of usage. Ok, this tape is awesome. But I can't believe 3M would market this for boxes & shipping! LOLWe've been shipping both small & large packages all over the world for 15 years, and always use a standard 2mil clear packing tape (by the case, it typically costs 70-80 per roll). We have never had a problem - never a break, never a tape failure.We regularly ship by container to & from Asia / Africa / Europe, we've shipped 70 and 80-pound boxes of books across the country, and we are not brand specific about the tape we use (sometimes Uline, sometimes Office Max/Depot, and sometimes generic from eBay or Amazon). The secret is in packing your box square & tight (peanuts or filler if necessary), wrapping tape around the entire box at least once, and covering seams.That said, this tape is almost 3x thicker, and probably 50x stronger. Fiberglass threads, *impossible* to tear by hand, and strong adhesive that will never fall off. (Don't try to tear by hand, by the way - you risk cutting yourself on the fiberglass threads).I think it's clever that 3M would try to get consumers to pay $22 per roll for packing tape (instead of 80), but it's really not necessary for most projects, and definitely not necessary for shipping or moving boxes.HOWEVER ...(a big "but") ... this is excellent tape for specialty projects. Perfect for reinforcing pieces on radio controlled devices (planes, helicopters, etc). Much better than duck tape, no question. It's ideal for appliances repair, tool repair, & countless machinery and industrial applications. We use it at the office when we want a quick & easy permanent solution, like bundling data cables, furniture or shelving repair, etc etc.Any handyman or maintenance department would probably want to keep a roll of this on hand. We estimate one roll will last us 10 years (that's one roll shared between office & home). You don't need much, and it's not really an everyday thing.The fact that it's nearly transparent is so cool. Keep in mind, this has no stretch at all - when using on a small surface, it will wrinkle & fold over, not stretch into a smooth surface.

I've had a hard time finding cordless phones that have all the features that I am looking for. Foremost among these is talking caller ID. Panasonic is the only mainstream manufacturer that has phones with this feature. Although the KX-TG9344 is not perfect, it is the best of the phones I've looked at so far.It utilizes DECT 6.0, which is the latest technology for cordless phones and is supposed to have greater clarity and privacy without having interference issues like the older 2.4 GHz phones. Not sure if this is primarily a marketing gimmick or not, but the Panasonic sounds clear and has good range. The screen is nice, and the handsets are smaller than previous generations of cordless phones (which is a pro or a con, depending on your personal preference).Regarding the talking caller ID, it's a godsend not to have to get up to pick up the phone only to find out you have a telemarketer on the line. You have to subscribe to caller ID with your phone company, and not all the caller labels are always understandable, but the nice thing is that you have the option of putting in your own labels for folks in your address book. It usually takes a couple of rings for the talking caller ID to kick in, which is a bit of a drag.The only things I wish the Panasonic had are a speed dial feature and larger "talk" and "end" buttons. I'm so used to hitting one key to call frequently-dialed numbers in my cell phone, that not having this feature seems strange on a cordless phone. Regarding the buttons, the two most frequently used buttons are "talk" and "end". Is there a reason why these aren't any bigger than the other buttons on the keypad? May be a case of form over function.Minor gripes aside, the Panasonic stands out among the current generation of cordless phones. Having three extra handsets is also a major plus - means a lot less running between rooms to pick up the phone.

Prices range from $40 for a four-pack to $83 for a 12-pack, depending on where you purchase. I was very satisfied with the quality of Presto Bankers Boxes and was not troubled that much by the assembly issue because it's one I face with anything that requires assembly.

The Lexmark MS610DN is a good mid level networked workgroup printer. It's comparable to theBrother HL6180DW Printer. It's a little faster but without built-in wireless networking and the toner is more expensive than the brother. Lexmark makes theMarkNet N8352 802.11b/g/n Wirelesskit for the MS610DN at about $40 additional.Setup was simple and mostly consisted of removing various pieces of tape, a couple pieces of plastic on the imaging unit, placing it on an appropriate flat surface, plugging in power and network (assuming you are going for a network install), and loading paper into the generous 650 page paper tray.Drivers installed easily and found the MS610DN on the network. The printer also has a web interface which is pretty useful. I've only begun to explore the features of the MS610DN but one that is of interest is the ability to setup forms in the printer. I'm thinking about building my letterhead design for head and foot of the page. The instructions are on the Lexmark web site.The printer comes with 256MB of RAM memory, but has a slot for a DDR3 SODIMM RAM module. Lexmark sells these for $80 but I tried a SODIM from an old netbook to max out the printer at 1.25GB. These 1GB DDR3 SODIMM modules can be found dirt cheap and more memory means more document information can be stored in the printer and more complex printing can be performed. Here is one on Amazon similar to the one I had on hand:1GB Memory DDR3.Duplexing seems like a pretty standard feature these days and the MS610DN seems to actually print close to half its one sided print speed when print two sided. Not many printers achieve this feat. Nice!One thing caught my attention enough to look for more detail. The printer comes with a "Return Program" starter toner cartridge. When I read about the return program cartridges this caught my eye: "In addition, the cartridge is designed to automatically update the memory in your printer to protect against the introduction of counterfeit and/or unauthorized third-party cartridges."The included starter cartridge is a return program cartridge. This seems to mean it will alter the printer so it will not longer work with third party toner cartridges. It seems at least Lexmark requires you to agree to this if you use the included return program cartridge. I can understand why they would want to lock-in customers to buying Lexmark branded toner...Lexmark toner is more expensive than comparable toner from Brother. With heavy use the toner is much more costly than the printer itself over the lifetime of the printer. A 5K pageLexmark High Yield Return Program Toneris currently $129 here on Amazon. ABrother TN750 8K Page Toneris currently selling for $75 here on Amazon.There are 3rd party cartridges available but I've not gone through my starter yet so I can't say if they will work after an official return program cartridge has been loaded. I'll update the review when I find out!Print quality is very very nice monochrome printing.  Time to first page is impressive.Like with any laser printer it's not a good idea to plug it into your UPS unless it's really beefy - FYI. I've had some clients kill their smallish UPS battery backup by doing this.Since it does not have wireless built-in but does have that return-program starter cartridge and high toner cost adds to the total cost of ownership the MS610 gets 4 stars. It would get 5 but the return program feels like a vendor lock-in to me, though I tend to purchase cartridges made by the manufacturer anyway. I don't like feeling coerced.Hope this helps someone.

The vital specs: it's 18" long, 1 " wide at its most narrow and 2 " wide at its widest point (it's straight on one side and has a slight convex, smile-shaped curve on the other).  It's overall " thick, with the hard plastic base making up " of that and the gel portion making up the remaining ".  It's made in Taiwan.It weighs in at almost exactly one pound. I first saw the CANON LS-82z calculator at my local bank.  Itwas anchored to a table, so no one would take it, and wasthere for people to tally up deposits and/or withdrawals. It isso little, so useful, so -- well, cute -- that I found myselfanthropomorphizing it, (that is, turning an innanimate objectinto something which is living...at least in my imagination,and falling completely in love with the adorable littlecalculator at first sight, (and use!). I wanted so much to takeit home with me, (as a calculator -- AND pet!)  Perhaps it'sdue to the fact that I live in a no-pet building that helpedfoister these, er....feelings in me, but the fact is that it ISa rather small and compact little calculator, (only 3.5 x 4.5 x1.2 inches in size), has easy-to-use hard, (but not too hard)plastic keys, and a nice big 8-digit display!  It also seemedjust the right size fit in my hand...though, of course, tetheredas it was to the table in the bank, I couldn't try it out.  No --I did NOT hear the little calculator say, "Take me home with you!"-- but it was fun to IMAGINE it was saying this.  I also knew thebank had probably searched very carefully to find the right modelcalculator to put on the bank table. So -- with this free advicethat this was a good calculator, (which the bank had unknowinglygiven me -- and every other bank customer!), and my own immediateliking to it -- though I knew I couldn't take the bank's modelhome with me, I did the next best thing: I wrote down the modelnumber, and looked for it on the internet.  Sure enough -- therethe calculator I had seen in the bank, (or maybe one of it'sfirst or second cousins!), was there on Amazon!  Immediately, Iliberated....er, that is, bought...two of them, hoping, (in myimagination, that is), that these little calculators would finda happy home in my condo!When the calculators arrived, I took one out of its proteciveplastic casing, and immediately put the number "107734" on it.Then I turned the calculator upside down. As with any calculator,the word "heLLO!" appeared on the screen.  (There's a whole bookof these calculator tricks, which I mean to look up on Amazonas at the earliest opportunity!)Well, the little Canon LS=82z does fit nicely in the palm of myhand, and works just as well in my home, as it does at thebank.  The keys are HARD plastic -- which means they do NOT getsoft and difficult to use after a while.  However, "hard" doesnot mean "difficult" here -- the keys are a pleasure to use!They are small enough to keep the size of the calculator down,but big enough for adult hands to use.  And -- this IS a solarAND battery calculator.  You can always test this on any calcu-lator.  Just be sure the calculator is on, and showing numbers.Then put your finger over the solar-battery panel.  If thenumbers fade, then the calculator is a solar-powered calculator,only.  If they do not fade, then obviously a battery is in thecalculator, too -- as is the case here.It's true this calculator has only a three-key memory, and somepeople find this a great inconvenience.  To me, it's only a veryminor inconvenience, and one I can easily live with.  The "change-sign" (from plus to minus, or vice versa), key is strangely printedon the same key as "%".  Sadly, there seems no way to use the"change sign" function, as directions are not given on the back ofthe package, and there are no other directions given.  I don'tchange the sign, often -- so again, this is a minor inconvenience,for me.  But if you must change signs from plus to minus, or viceversa, often, I sadlty must suggest you "adopt" another calculator.The biggest disappointment, though, is that, although this ISpowered by a battery, (presumably a button model), as well as solarpower, THERE ARE ONLY TWO SCREWS, ON TOP, IN THE BACK OF THECALCULATOR.  This means that it's all but impossible to take thebattery out, and one will be left, eventually, with the choice ofeither using this as only a solar calculator, or getting anothercalculator altogether.  A mean thing to do to both calculator...and user.Still, I plan to use and enjoy my litte LS-82z. And if I anthropor-morphize once in a while, what of it?  Sometime back, an entireTV show, ('WONDERFALLS'), was based on this idea of anthropormorph-ism.  It stayed on the air only a short time...but during thattime, made money for everyone connected in its production!

First on the negative side and related to installation. It was difficult and the documentation really skimped on installation issues even when you went online. You might have some intital wireless problems but fortunately for me I know something about networking but still took me an hour to work through them. What really lost a star besides the installation problems was was lack of clear documentation on two-sided printing. You have to enable two-sided printing and you may miss the box that asks you to do that. For the life of me, I don't know why it wasn't a default. Also, instructions on proper installation of the duplexer was very poor...a simple picture even on the web site would have helped.Now on the plus side: First, the printer doesn't look flimsy but much more well built than it's 5000 and 6000 cousins and has more features than the 7180. Those printers above the 7280 are big monsters that are wider and higher and don't do much more than the 7280. While substantial looking and non-flimsy, the 7280 gave me more desk space since I got rid of my old fax and scanner. One deal breaker for me: the printer had to had automatic 2 sided printing whith the 7280 has at no extra charge (watch out for the "two-sided printing capable"---which means you spend about $70 more for a duplexer...the 7280 has duplexing when you buy it.Besides wanting a duplex printer, I wanted to replace fax and scanner to unclutter my desktop. I also needed it to work well with my MacPro desktop, Imac, and Macbook pro. My earlier printer was OS compatible but software for it was almost an afterthought for the MAC. I was pleasantly surprised that OSX was strongly supported on this all in one.  It comes with several software tools for editing scanned images and the TWAIN driver plays nice with the New CS3 Adobe PhotoShop. It also has an acceptable (free) OCR software that can output to Word.  There is really some nice integration here with the software which usually isn't the case for Macs but I think HP wants to make Apple happy. What about the quality of the printing? Good to excellent and fairly fast but not the 30 pages per second in B&W.; Scan quality? I think fair to good. I think some calibration might be needed if you were using it for serious scanning but the scan isn't bad and relatively fast.Once you get the duplex to work 2 sided printing is easy (more on that later). The printer comes with a small color screen and actually it is useful to do the various tasks such as faxing, scanning, and of course printing.  Once you overcome the problems of installation, I have a totally wireless printer (802.11g) as well as a Bluetooth printer if you spend $20 for a Bluetooth dongle so two ways to get wireless and of course the printer has USB and Ethernet capability. It also has a media reader and when you put in a CF, XD, or SD, etc. your window opens and you can copy the files to your computer. You can use the Mac Finder windows from the Mac OS, or the interface that comes with the software that mimics a MS Windows file explorer.  The software is simple to use. Even with the little onboard screen you will be surprised how much pre-printing manipulation you can do.I started out hating this printer a bit during installation now it really shows me how versatile it is at a reasonable price.One last feature a surprise for me: the automatic document feeder...get it! I am used to opening the scanner lid and placing my document but putting several sheets of pages to be scanned and then have them fed in and scanned automatically is a feature I didn't think about but really is something I can use to speed the scan and copy process up for multiple pages. That feature used to be only available on expensive machines.Update on Mac 10.5 (Leopard): as of this time not all features work if you upgrade to 10.5. For example, when you  try to use the ADF and use the scan menu button to scan to software on your MAC you no longer get any selections. You get: !No Scan Options. Refer to device documentation to troubleshoot. Wrote HP been ignored so far. If you upgrade to OS 10.5 you can still print and scan but the onscreen menu and ADF on the printer are not fully functional with the new OS.

No matter, I will continue to use them proudly and defiantly.

I have three electric and one manual sharpener in my house.  This is the one the kids can use, ages four and five.The Panasonic's (KP150BK) problem is the hole on top; the kids are just too short to reach up and hold it in place; they can't even see the hole.The Bostich's (EPS8HD-BLK) problem is the motor is too strong; the kids stick the pencil in and the motor grabs so hard and fast that the pencil just spins around in their little fingers.And the old-fashioned Boston manual sharpener is just waaaay out of their league.  They can't even reach the crank, and when I do stand them up to it they have zero ability to hold a pencil and turn a crank simultaneously.  Perhaps in a few years.But the X-ACTO (1675) is just right.  They can dial the size guide large enough to let them insert their pencils (which isn't easy when you're an uncoordinated little kid).  Then they just hold it in place for a minute or two and the pencil comes out sharp.  Though they never push hard enough to get the "all done" L.E.D. to light up blue, the pencils get sharp enough.The unit seems fairly well constructed for clear plastic; it fell from the counter to the floor with no harm done.  It's heavy, weighing in at 3.5 pounds.  At 7" deep by 5.5" wide and 8" high, it is easily twice the size of the next largest sharpener, so plan to devote a good deal of shelf/counter space to this beast.Indulge me for a bit of a rant, here: when I was a kid we had a single, ancient, Boston hand-crank unit in each classroom, and it stood up to dozens of daily uses, year in and year out.  And they're still for sale (though no longer Made in America).  I'm not sure why classrooms these days need anything else, but I am sure that any motorized electric device with all its little parts could not possibly be as durable as something simpler and human-powered.  With all the talk about "sustainability" these days, what better way to demonstrate the principal than by using muscle power, instead of electricity, for something as easy as pencil sharpening?  Regardless, it's hard to believe a $40 plastic product can hold up to the abuse a classroom full of grammar school kids can dish out.Bottom line: if you want something for home, for kids who are too young to use a crank, this is a really good bet.  Beyond that, less so.

The Epson Expression Premium Inkjet also prints flawlessly from a tablet or smartphone (my iPad connected almost instantly on the first attempt to the printer). You can also easily print documents from a remote location using the Epson Connect feature.I thought the setup process was relatively simple, as is the case with most printers. You should read the instructions before installing the 5 ink cartridges (some cartridge shaking is required), but the process is easy to understand if you read the directions.  The 3.5 inch touch screen works perfectly and the "Save to Memory" feature is a nice option I have not seen on cheaper printers I've owned.  Overall, this is another outstanding Epson printer offering for home/light office use.

I have been impressed with this Fellowes Venus 2 laminator. It heats up quickly, and using it is really simple. I haven't found anything yet that doesn't come out perfect. No unsightly air pockets that have to be smoothed over or wrinkles. If you haven't used a newer style laminator, you will be very happy with the performance of this one compared to older models that sometimes had problems. Kudos to Fellowes for getting this one perfect,

Nice and sturdy, these strips are well constructed and easy to use, can be cut to size, removes easily without marring the wall surface, and holds a pretty hefty sized yet lightweight items. Good price for 6 strips.  I'd buy a larger quantity if it were available.
This is a little easier to use than most I used it already and loved it I will definitley be buying more :)

This is a 3" box that can fit inside a file cabinet drawer.  I am using to hold a set of three file folders together.  I can pull this box out of the drawer to work on those three files together as kind of a portable mini file cabinet.  Then it goes back in the file cabinet drawer when I'm done. It serves the purpose well.But it seems overpriced for what it is.
Its good quality ink and last as long as most printers inks do never had any problems with them just wish they lasted longer.

I first jumped at these because they have so many uses. The fact that there are 750 of them means that I won't be running out anytime soon. They come mounted on a stiff paper sheet designed to coast through your printer and provide very clean labeling. I initially thought my most useful application would be labeling myPyrex Storage 14-Piece Round Set, Clear with Blue Lidswhen I want to store leftovers, or when making large batches of food for future use. I also used them last night for labeling Saran Wrap enclosing some pre-made pizzas; although I wouldn't put these labels in the super sticky category for such uses. They did hold on even after being frozen.I also have a lot of file folders, and I got tired of throwing them out when I no longer needed a folder with that subject written on it. Of course for industrial applications you could wrap it with a slice of scotch tape. Scotch continues to amaze me in its plethora of purposeful products.  How one company can produce so many quality, cost effective and multi-use products amazes me.  These little gems fit the 3M business plan perfectly.  They work and work well.  They are unique and have multiple uses.  I have an extra entrance key and keep it in a "secret" place.  Before these its location could be seen with ease but now it is out of sight enough to be secure.  The grip for the key has bee quite effective even after numerable uses.  The same top notch holding ability exists for my "I've fallen and can't get up" device.  It is a pain to have that device hanging around my neck while getting in the way.  Now, it is attached to my mower or moved to another location where it might have a chance for use.  So far it (the device) has been unused except to test. Kids don't want to have a binder for more than one school year.  Binders are notoriously thrown in the dumpster at the end of the year.This binder, although well-built, looks like it could make it through the first semester. There's not much to add to all the positive reviews here. We had in the office all kind of printers for about 20 years, and nothing comes close to this printer!Cheapest among all competitors, cheapest toner, prints very fast, first page out is like 7-8 seconds, and although it's quite noisy when printing, it's expected for such a fast printing machine. Also, the tiny LCD, is not tiltable (like on my HL-4150 2-Line LCD), and if the printer does not sit low enough, you will be unable to read it. That's a bad design flaw. Why laser printers are so back-dated is beyond my understanding.And as always, with all Brother laser printers, it feels a bit flimsy, it doesn't have the quality feel of, let's say, Samsung printers.I am not using WiFi, so I cannot comment on that. I have had no issues whatsoever with electricity or breaker. Everything works as it is supposed to.Bottom line: do not overlook this machine. It's highly recommended and should be on top of your list.

Back in my school days I remember the Trapper Keeper as a status symbol.  It was the school ground equivalent of a Mercedes Benz.  A lot of dough for a simple device with a fancy name.  Fast forward 30 years later.  My Son has no idea what a Trapper Keeper is.  When I first show it to him he says it is cool but when he opens it up he is wowed by how sparse it is. Wow, I thought, when I first saw the Wilson Jones Cut and Sewn Binder, that binder looks nice.  Words like "stylish," "fancy," "elegant" and "professional" popped into my head.  This binder would make a great gift for someone who is graduating from high school and preparing for college.  Professionals would appreciate it.  I've been using it for taking notes.  I have approximately two-hundred sheets of Mead notebook paper and five Wilson Jones index dividers stuffed into the one-inch notebook.  It's a little bit crowded but I will be removing sheets when they are no longer needed.  For example, I take notes when reading a novel.  After my review has been completed, I remove the notes.  This frees up space.The binder is easy to open and close.  It is also very sturdy.  The binder walls are thick and have the appearance of sewn leather.  I love my navy-blue binder; however, the binder is manufactured in several other muted, antique colors that are attractive, elegant and stylish. They can be used for holding notes, pamphlets, brochures, receipts, etc.  There is also a holder for one's business card and a holder for a pen or pencil; most notebooks don't have these added features.What grabbed my attention was the black cord that wraps around the entire binder, keeping it closed.  It has Wilson Jones' insignia hanging from it.  This definitely gives the binder an elegant touch; it has the appearance of being very expensive even though it is reasonably priced on Amazon.  I simply adore this binder.  Not only is it easy to operate and very durable but it is also easy to clean.  I saw an insect larvae squirming inside the binder, which disgusted me.  I squished it, causing a stain.  Fortunately, a paper napkin dampened with water was able to remove all traces.  I breathed a sigh of relief because I didn't want this attractive binder ruined.Joseph B. Hoyos

A long time ago, during one of the jobs I had, we were taught about ergonomics and if you do a lot of computer work, the things you need to do is stand up and take breaks, stretching your hands and arms but also having ergonomic wrist pads, chair, desk and a foot rest.I have to admit that when I was younger, I didn't pay too much attention to it at home and noticed I was exhibiting symptoms of RSI (repetitive stress injury) on my hands and so I invested in ergonomic things that I can have at home.Now, things have changed a little many years later.  My keyboard is so thin (for my Mac) that I don't use a wristpad, my once ergonomic desk(s) which I tend to keep upgrading, keep busting but the thing is, I practice caution with my hands but I admit that I am not living as ergonomic as I should.Recently, I've been working long hours in my office and despite getting up every hour, walking around...the truth is I work in my office longer than most people do.  My legs feel numb.  It's because I've been putting my feet on the chair rests and I have had no foot rests.  I remember how the foot rest was so beneficial to me at my old workplace but felt that was the lowest priority as most injuries are to the wrist and arms but I started noticing that my legs were feeling numb (and even had it checked out medically).Aside from having to walk more and not stay in the same seating position for hours, I needed to purchase an adjustable footrest and sure enough, I gave the 3M foot rest a try.Unlike previous foot rests I used with the removable rest and the metal bar which swivels, this foot rest also swivels but it's nice and wide, made of steel and has a good grip as well.  It's not heavy but it's not one I would want to drop as it is held by screws and such (unlike the two piece which if dropped, probably wouldn't matter because there are no screws, bolts or anything like that).But for the most part, for SOHO use, it works perfectly.If you are a programmer, graphic designer or a person who is constantly working on the computer for hours (or like me, sometimes 16 hours or more some days and nights), for your health, it's important to keep ergonomics in mind and if you find your thighs or knees hurting each time you get up and your job requires many hours seated, I highly recommend a foot rest.  The last thing you need to deal with is improper seating and stationary positions which can hurt blood circulation to your legs and lead to blood clots or anything fatal.Definitely recommended!

The QL710W label printer combines an intuitive and stable software suite, with excellent print quality and speed, and wireless connectivity - resulting in a full featured professional grade label printer for the home or home office.What's to like:[1] Installation and setup are fairly straightforward[2] The accompanying software suite is very intuitive, stable, and full featured.[3] This printer writes with heat on thermal paper - as a result you will never have to worry about ink.[4] Excellent print quality - with clear text and graphics. Its palette is a fairly limited gray-scale, so clean high contrast images work best.[5] Well written documentation. In addition to a printed Quick Setup guide, you get PDF guides for its software and for networking.[6] It is solidly built, and looks sleek and professional.Setup:#####I setup the QL710W on a Windows 7 x64 bit Core i7 based machine with 6GB RAM, and it worked without fuss or incident.Set up consists of installing a label roll and threading the tape to an output slot. The software is comprised of a contact manager, a free form graphical label editor, and printer drivers. Once the drivers are installed, you have two options when connecting to this printer:1. you can connect it directly to your computer via a USB cable, or2. you can use it as a wireless printer. To configure it with your network's SSID and passphrase, you must either use Wifi Protected Setup (WPS, not advisable due to security concerns), or you must use the USB cable. I used the latter, and the connection was established in a couple of minutes.What's really cool for a techie nerd like me?Once the QL710W is up and running on your network, you can talk to it using a web based interface. Simply navigate to it using an internal IP address (the one assigned by your router's DHCP server)!How cool is that?Software Suite:###########The QL710W does not skimp on its software offering:1. P-touch Editor 5 - a free-form label editor.You pick a label size (with choices such as Standard/Large/Small Address Label, CD/DVD label, 2" Binder spine, etc.), and then go to town with your edits. Among others, you can:# add and style text (font, size, style) as well as add effects such as shadow, outline, and layouts that are vertical, circular, and curved!# add images (an assortment of clip art is supplied, and you can always import images from files);# add screen captures using a SnagIt style interface# add barcodes from a variety of protocols (UPC-A/E, EAN8/13, ISBN-2, POSTNET, QR Codes, etc.)# add the calendar for a given monthIf that weren't enough, it can integrate with Microsoft Word, Excel, and Outlook!Finally, a minimized mode (called Snap mode) lets you capture content via screen shots or drag and drop for later editing.Suffice it to say that this software is probably worth the sticker price of this unit!2. P-touch Address Book 1.1 - a contact managerYou can manage contact information and print using preset layouts. Of course, if you wish to edit a layout, you are taken immediately to the P-touch Editor, with a full arsenal of tools at your command.Conclusion:########Its older sibling, the QL720NW, adds an Ethernet interface as well as a serial port. However, for general home office use, the QL710W is a sufficiently powerful machine, especially when considering its accompanying software suite. Printing speed in particular is to be seen to be believed.There's a lot to like with this well designed printer making it truly a 5-star product.Happy Printing!

EXCELLENT HARDWARE:  The Epson V500 is a versatile, powerful scanner.  When it was first released, the capabilities were really remarkable.  However, the speed and quality bar rises quickly - there's little point to buying model that's more than a year old, as you gain a lot by going with a newer model.CHALLENGING SOFTWARE:  However, to get the most from the scanner, software is an essential link in the chain.  Generally, Epson has always tended to produce the best hardware, but somewhat bloated and cumbersome software.  Luckily, the hardware drivers and wide support allow it to be used with a variety of image-processing software.MIXED DOCUMENT FEEDER:  I think how you view this depends on your expectations.  It's difficult to make a device that performs like a several-thousand-dollar office machine for home use.  If you expect relatively light use of fairly smooth and clean originals, then you may be happy.  Take the limitations of the machine into account.

It's gift-giving time, and the wrap-challenged such as myself are looking for something to make wrapping easier.  There are some things for which gift bags just don't work.I had high hopes for the Scissor Mouse.  I ran it across a wide swath of paper and...nothing!  I tried it again and again, with teeth incresingly gritted, but the paper wore out before the first cut was made.Then I discovered you have to thread the paper through the little feet on the bottom of the gadget.  Now, we're in business.  It's still kind of hit or miss, but once it gets going, it's great.  It's very fast and makes a clean cut.  The mouse fits comfortably into the hand, and just like a computer mouse, is controlled with the index finger.  The blade is perfect for even the thickes wrapping paper, and doesn't touch the surface underneath.There is a problem in making the initial cut.  Unless the paper is seated exactly right, the mouse won't work.  After I figured it out, I handed it to my husband, who never could make it work.  Even understanding that the manufacturer installed a kind of safety feature, I think the thing would work better with a lethal blade and some kind of removable protective cover.Verdict?  When it works, it works extremely well, but it's very hit or miss.

(REVISED, May 2012) After moderate use for one year this device gave up and died and is now landfill junk. Nowadays, almost all the all-in-one printers have very similar functions: printing, scanning, copying, faxing (not a main feature anymore, so some have this function and some don't), wireless connection, two-side printing, LCD control panel. Also, all-in-one printers at this price range can print out good photos, but never be able to match the quality from those high-end models.So, what factors to be used for finding a relatively good one from this over-crowded market? Every person has different needs. Personally, I use following criteria:First is reliability. Some printers last longer before printer heads get clogged. One of my last printers last only for 3 months, while my previous Canon PIXMA IP-4500 printer lasts for 4+ years while being used on daily basis. Only time can tell if this Canon PIXMA MG5420 has a longer printer head life. But I have high hope on Canon.Second is the cost of ink cartridge. The Canon MG5420 comes with 5 separate ink cartridges, with the cartridges in XL (extra large) size. This is by far the largest cartridge size I have ever seen from Canon's entry-level All-in-One printers. This is far better than some models with all colors packaged into a single cartridge.Third is the printing speed. Somehow, this printer is very very slow to get ready for printing. When it gets over the warm-up time, the actually printing time itself is pretty fast. So, if you print big job, you won't feel the slow. But if your printing job tends to one page now, one page later...etc, then you need to be patient with this printer.Forth is two-side printing. Don't be surprised that some all-in-one printers are still one side printing only. This Canon MG5420 is duplex-printing capable.All in all, I don't see any special feature that really makes this Canon MG5420 printer/scanner stand out from the crowd. If the slow warm-up time does not bother you, then I would say this is a fair entry level All-in-one at this price level.

With the release of the wonderful 630 Epson printers of 2010, and then in 2011 with the 840 Epson WorkForce series, for 2012, it's time to see how Epson has continued its reign of printing excellence with the latest WorkForce model, the WF-3520.And as always, to help those who are planning to purchase a printer, I will do comparisons with the WF-3540 and the WF-3520 and give you information o see which version works for your budget.In 2011, Epson introduced the touchscreen interface with the 840 series but while touchscreen, the screen was amber, the layout setup was a bit tedious but this time around Epson is introducing full color touch screen display and icons to help you find a certain section for quick access (ie. Copy, Fax, Scan, Wi-Fi Setup, etc.).With this latest upgrade, you get double-sided printing, scanning, copying, much better wi-fi capabilities, option to used a wired version (if you don't have wi-fi or wi-fi is bugging out on you), SD and MS Duo card interface and has a single front tray that can hold 250 pages each plus a rear feed for envelopes and specialty media.With the new printer, the new iso page per minute is 15 pages (black ink) 1-sided and 9.3 pages (color) 1-sided and 7.4 black and 5.4 door via 2-sided.  The printer also uses the 127 series DURABrite ink cartridges.Also, included is a 30-page duplex auto document feeder to quickly copy, scan or fax stacks of 1 or 2-sided documents.For fax, you can fax documents directly to/from your computer and high speed faxing in black and color as fast as 3 seconds per page, speed dial storage up to 100 numbers plus fax memory up to 180 pages.EPSON Connect allows for convenient mobile printing from smartphones, tablets and more (NOTE: iPhone and iPad users, there is an Epson app available.  I don't have an android device, but I would assume that Epson would have created one for the android).The Eco Features including saving up to 50% on paper supply with automatic 2-sided printing/copying and uses up to 70% less power than laser printers and is Energy Star qualified.I. INSTALLATIONA CD-ROM with the drivers is provided, but you can also download the latest software upgrade or latest software straight from Epson's website.Installing to PC and older Mac's was easy but for those using Mac OS 10.7 or 10.8, your computer will detect the printer (after you set up the wi-fi for it) and it will download the appropriate drivers from Apple.Last year, I complained of how long it took to download the software but this time around, took less than five minutes to download the software and print.  Also, last year's WorkForce 845 release was buggy when it came to Wi-Fi use.  Sometimes I had to switch over to wired mode because the printer wouldn't be detected.  BUT this time around, the WorkForce 3520 had no problem in being detected and printing.  So, I was very pleased with that.NOTE: A USB printing Cord is not provided, so you will need to use your old printer USB cord, or USB that came with an older external CD/DVD/HD drive or purchase a USB cord for a direct connection.The device does come with a phone cord for fax use.II.  FUNCTIONSPrinting was absolutely quick.  I conducted several tests from printing an 8.5 x 11 hi-res image, to printing one of articles from Adobe InDesign and also Adobe Photoshop for full color printing and it was quick and looked absolutely great.I felt that Epson was quite truthful about black and white and color printing as the  WorkForce WF-3520 was very quick.  It's important to note that printing was the same between the WorkForce WF-3520 vs. the WorkForce 840 in terms of pages per minute.Single-sided printing was very quick and both earn high marks for printing single and double-sided in color and black and white.Also, what is important for me is that if there is a paper jam, you can easily remove the rear to fix any problem. But truthfully, I haven't had paper jams with a WorkForce printer, so I'm quite pleased with this printer after several weeks of use!Scanning was easy and is wireless.  Although I do prefer to use a flatbed for larger scanning purposes for my work, many will find the scanner to be quite suitable.  But there is no doubt that scanning at 300DPI is quite fast using this WF-3520 and makes me even reconsider using my Epson Perfection that I have used in the office for years because of its size.  But people should be pleased with the quickness of scanning especially at a higher DPI.  It's important to note that I was also able to scan from Adobe Photoshop via import->images from device.III.  Going with the 3540 vs. 3520?Noticeable differences is that the 3520 is single front tray and the LCD touch screen is much smaller at 2.5 inches, while the 3540 uses a 3.5 inch touchscreen.  While the icons on the 3520 are shown in the touch screen, number pad is on the right while the 3540 will feature the number touchpad onscreen.Because the 3540 is double tray, it has a capacity of 500 pages, while the 3520 has a capacity of 250 pages.Both are easy to install ink cartridges, both are easy to startup and get printing immediately.  And both are considerably easy to scan, copy and fax.But looking at the prices on Amazon, the price difference is small.  With the 3540, the price is currently at $149.99 while the 3520 is at $131.99.  An $18 price difference.  So, unless the 3540 goes up in price anytime after this review, for $18 difference, I would go with the 3540 hands down!  But if you have no need for a double-tray printer and want to save the money, definitely go with the 3520!JUDGMENT CALL:The Epson WorkForce 3520 is may not be a dramatic step-up from the solid WorkForce 840 in terms of printing.But in terms of functionality, the 3520 easily surpasses the 840 in terms of its ease of use for its LCD color touchscreen.  It's a fairly easy printer to set up and to use right off the bat.  Installation of ink cartridges, paper is quite easy.  Especially loading paper from the top section, everything was easy to do.Can I think of anything negative?  Hmm...I wish Epson included a USB cable for those who may have wi-fi problems or don't have Wi-Fi and need to plug the USB cable directly into their computer.  Other than that, this printer is quite magnificent, I was able to print, copy, fax, scan with ease.As mentioned earlier, what I love about the recent WorkForce printers is the way it uses paper and loads, unlike many other cheaper printers in which paper gets stuck and you get the awful paper jam, I never had to worry about it with these type of printers.  Grabs paper easy and had no issues at all.  You also have access to the rear if you do have any problems.  But have not had any problems with WorkForce printers in the last few years in terms of paperjam (which I have had problems with other printers from major manufacturers).With the $18 price difference between the WorkForce 3540 and the 3520, there really is no need to get the 3520 unless you want to save $18 and you don't have space for a double tray printer.  But with its functionality and ease of use, especially the fact that the 3540 is such a major workhorse that delivers in terms of printing, copying, scanning and faxing... for it's price right now at less than $150, that's fantastic!  Otherwise, if you do want to save money and have no need for a double tray, the 3520 is great, but if you can, definitely get the 3540!Overall, Epson managed to surpass its WorkForce 840 printer with the WorkForce 3520 in terms of functionality.  Both are similar in terms of printed pages via black and white and color but ease of use, no Wi-Fi issues, ease of use with both Mac and PC and also tablets and smartphones, makes this WorkForce 3520 a magnificent release for those looking for a budget printer within the $100-$140 range.  But still, I would consider the WorkForce 3540 because it's only $18 more (at this moment on Amazon)!Still, a wonderful printer for its price and functions and is highly recommended!

In my time I've probably punch-bound 10,000 books - literally.  For myself, clients and for resale. I've done all of this on a commercial punch-binder I purchased way back in 1978. Let's take a look at the punch-binding process and what makes it work - and what doesn't. There are basically two parts to the binder.1) The hole puncher2) the combThe puncher is the part that sees all the wear and tear. You're punching a bunch of rectangular holes in several sheets of paper at one time. If you're ever used a hand-held hole punch and tried going through a bunch of sheets, you know how hard it is. So these machines use long handles and gears to increase leverage. The more sheets, the beefier the punch has to be.  This puncher is pretty light-weight as punchers go. Seven standard sheets is the max - you can't fit more than that. That's using standard paper.  If you use heavier paper, it's less sheets.  So a 90 page report with a front and back cover would take at least 15 punches (assuming heavier front and back cover stock.). With this model, punch slowly - it's easy to knock your knuckles on the counter-top.The best way to do this is assemble the book is on a counter-top or table, with the binder in the middle. But the book/report to be bound the right of the binder, face-up.  Take several pages, punch them, and put them on the left of the binder, face down. Repeat until done. Take the pages and tap the "spine" end on a hard surface until all pages are aligned, then bind them.  Do a couple of practice runs to get the hang of any binder - you can re-use the spines.The KEY setting is the position of the paper guide on the left of the punch - since you can't move the hole punches, you re-position the paper, moving it left or right so the punches are centered on the edge. The guide accomplishes this.  That's another reason for some test runs.Actually binding the paper takes a little practice. There's a second, smaller, lever that operates the hooks that open the plastic spine on the comb - it's easy to put these in upside-down, but since you can't bind that way, you'll know if it's wrong.  Sometimes you can do the entire book in one run, but usually you do several pages at a time.Insert spine, spread, slip pages over open spine until all pages are in place, close spine.  The spine has a "memory" - it closes automatically when tension is released.What separates different binders is the number of pages punched at one time and how many sheets can be bound. They all accomplish the same thing with the same decades old technology. This one punches 7 pages and can bind 90 sheets. If you're doing school reports, home projects and the occasional binding project, why spend a ton of money?If you plan on doing more frequent binding, I'd get a different model. For "occasional" use, this is ideal.Others have stated that the punch handle is plastic - it's not.  The punch arm is metal with a plastic sleeve wrapping a metal handle - it's not going to break. My commercial model has the exact same design, but with heavier duty materials. One more point to clarify - the manufacturer photo shows it punching, not binding.Before I forget - one neat trick - If you cut the combs with scissors, you can make custom sized smaller books.See all my photos for details and tips.

For some, just grabbing any paper and shoving it in the printer works just fine.  That may be OK for draft copies, but if you want excellent printed results that are worthy of letters that stand out or for presentation work, thisGP Ink Jet and Laser Paper, 8.5 x 11 Inches Letter Sizedoes a commendable job.  It's packed in three reams of 500 sheets each, so you get 1500 sheets per carton.Some may prefer the medium-weight 20 lb papers for general use and because more sheets will fit into the printer's paper tray.  I've long preferred the 24 lb heavyweight paper because of its more solid and authoritative feel, and it's not as transparent as the lighter weight papers.  Contrast is the key element between the toner or ink and the paper, and the whiter the paper, the better your printed results will look. The idea behind the erasable folder is pretty interesting. The folder has a laminated area where you would normally write. It's like a mini dry erase board. The erasable function only works when you write in marker. You can't use pencils or pens. This means that you are going to be limited by what you write based on the thickness of your marker tip. I tried both Marks-A-Lot and Sharpie type markers on these folders. You can't use a standard pencil eraser, this requires a "white polymer" eraser. The white polymer marker worked easily on the Marks-A-Lot but took a little bit of elbow grease on the Sharpie. I had a pack of Lysol wipes at my desk, so I decided to try those. It was the same, they pulled off the Marks-A-Lot easily but took a little effort with the Sharpie. The directions indicated that you could also use tissue and alcohol. While this did succeed in easily removing the ink, it will smear so you have to be extremely careful if you don't want to end up with ink smudges on the non-erasable portions of your folder. I surmised that if alcohol worked, hand sanitizer (which is more readily available at my desk than alcohol) would work as well. It did work, but with even more "smudge factor" than pure alcohol.These are fairly flimsy manila folders. One thing I found odd is the fact that the erasable tab is only on one side of the folder. If the point of these is to promote being green, it seems like they would bother to put the erasable film on both sides. (Personally, I generally use both sides of a manila folder, flipping it "inside out" if it still in good condition after I'm done with my first use.) I guess in theory, you shouldn't need to turn the folder inside out if the label area is erasable in the first place. However, if you take notes on the folder itself, being able to flip it is a big help. While I will gladly use the package I have, I won't purchase these. For me, normal manila folders, used on both sides, are more cost effective. In the rare instances where a folder is still in usable condition after two uses, I just use an address label sticker to cover up the old information. The cost for these is just not worth the benefit.
