I used to love my PIXMA MP520 which was a simple all-in-one, as this is. When that broke down I had replaced it with an Epson Artisan 725 which I picked up for less than a hundred dollars from a B&M; office supply chain store. With the Epson, the colors always seemed so muted in comparison to my former Canon printer even when printing in the highest quality standard so I was happy at the thought of coming back to Canon. The MX432 I now have returned the vivid colors I loved with my old Canon printer. The reds are redder and blues are bluer with Canon printers than on Epson the way I see it.Though the colors are more vivid, the ink (using cartridges cl-241, pg-240) smudges a lot more than Epson. I print a lot of mailing labels. Even after leaving the printed label to dry a whole day, it'll still smudge where I run my hand over back and forth over the inked parts of the label when I'm gluing/taping it onto packaging material.Also, my old Epson never had to have printing parameters tweaked to print full html pages off the web without having anything (webpage urls at the top/bottom) cut off.. the Canon always cuts off the beginning of urls at the top/bottom when I print out webpages so I had to tweak the paper size settings to 8.3" x 11" instead of letting it print from the default standard size 8.5" to get it to print without cutting things off. I tried printing with the "borderless" setting, and that'll let you leave the paper size the standard size but the color changes to where it prints lighter if you try to print on plain paper, so changing the paper size was the way to go to print on plain paper and keep regular colors.I have a problem with the way this printer prints gray text on webpages. It is so washed out it is very difficult to see, even if it's an easily visible shade of gray on your browser. A lot of online order confirmation details and emails I deal with have gray text, so this affects me on an almost daily basis since I've always printed these out. I never had a problem with printing gray text on my old Canon or Epson.One thing I do like about Canon printers that hasn't changed is it allows you to print a decent quality page in "fast" mode which saves a lot of ink. I've printed out several Internet coupons in fast mode which have no problem scanning at retailers. I also really appreciate the fact it has a smaller footprint than the Epson.Though I looked forward to coming back to Canon printing, I am not thrilled the welcome back machine was the MX432. I wouldn't prefer this over my Epson, even with its more muted colors.

I remember back when all-in-ones, especially all-in-ones at this price point, were awful. It was like in order to get something decent, you HAD TO buy each machine separately. Now it seems like many decent printers throw in some scanning, copying and faxing capability, and do it fairly decently, for no extra charge. Then you get it hooked up wirelessly to your network (archaic not to have that these days if you have a network, especially with being able to print from your phone or from Google's print feature even if you are far, far away from your actual network) and you can do quite acceptably with almost any printer.Last year I got a printer that is about double the price-point of this one (the Epson WorkForce 635) so my main question with this one was "is it worth it to pay (slightly less than) twice as much for the other one?" Comparing them side-by-side I guess the answer is that it depends, but the pricier one is a little nicer with a nicer display a few extra bells and whistles AND high capacity ink cartridges, and you know ink can be a big expense. I think personally I would pay a little more for a printer because you can really get more quality and value for your money, BUT if you just want something really inexpensive that works, this printer can get the job done without too much trouble.

My mate fashioned my very first wrist rest from a piece of plywood, a foam strip and a vinyl cloth scrounged from one of his theater sets. I do love the shred stacks and stacks of paper there's just something therapeutic about I think I might have a condition :)  that being said I think this writer is a decent shredder for the price (at the time of writing was just over $100). The motor seems strong it went through 9 pages and didn't bog down like some shredders can. It even did some thin cardboard that I had lying around (I'm talking thin cardboard not your normal box type cardboard) and a handle that pretty decently.I will talk about the CD shredder because it little strange. I think generally the most shredders that do CDs they run the CDs through the same grinding mechanism as the paper. The shredder does not do that it shreds the CD in its own slot which cuts the CD into 3 pieces now that's fine if you want destroy the CD so it can never be played but I think a lot of times people who want to shred their CDs one on cut up a little bit more disability keep in mind. But the fact that is not running through the same years as the paper means that those blades will last longer so it's a trade-off. But I don't see a lot of people shredding CDs much anymore as were moving toward digital  downloadable content.So all in all I think it's a decent shredder got power in the bin holds probably 100 pages of shredded paper which isn't a lot I like mine to hold a little bit more but emptying out is pretty easy with the handle on the top it works out just fine.One that's all folks I hope you enjoyed/found this informative have fun shredding!

A special eraser for a dry erase board might seem unnecessary, but I've always hated how messy it is to use a paper towel; little flecks get everywhere!  In addition, I've had my dry erase board for a few years now (I use it to plan my workouts), and I found that my board was becoming discolored over time--although I've only ever used dry erase markers on it, the various colors were leaving ghosting effects.So, I was very interested in trying this product.  The white side is the actual eraser, whereas the blue side is supposed to be designed to provide a comfortable grip.  This part seemed a bit wasteful to me--why is half the eraser unusable?  The instructions explain that you can use water on the white side to remove permanent stains from your dry erase board, so this is what I decided to do.After dampening the eraser, I ran it across my board a few times, and it worked!  My dry erase board wound up looking practically as good as new.  (I did have to wipe off the dampness and excess residue with a paper towel, however.)  On the other hand, the eraser itself wasn't in very good shape, as it retained all the color from the markers.  Therefore, I decided to rinse it under water.  It did come clean, but little white pieces also began crumbling off--after just a single use!In the end, I'm glad I had the chance to try this product, and it did work well for me.  But be aware that your eraser might not last very long, especially if you will frequently be using it wet.

With this weight, along with the additional weight from your hands when in use, you really should not install this to those cheap particle-board-type desks.The included instructions have very little text. Instead, diagrams illustrate how the various parts fit together. The diagrams are very easy to follow and the installation is pretty intuitive. However, the challenging part is to handle this 20 lbs stuff. You should get a second hands to ease the installation efforts. Drilling the holes for the screws is the only part that should take some extra cautions. Fortunately, a paper template is provided in the package to be taped to the desk to ensure holes are drilled at the right locations. By the way, to complete hide the tray when you push it all the way in, you might want to install the tray about 2 inches back from the edge of the desk.The slide mount is pretty beefy, you can really lean on it without worrying breaking it. Overall, the adjustments works fine. It goes up, goes down, goes in and pulls out. It does swivel also. However it doesn't slide out far enough to swivel more than 30 degrees.In summary, except the "EXTRA" heavy duty metal parts, I really don't see too much advantages of this tray when comparing with others. For home use, I probably will skip this one and pick the "3M Knob-Adjust Keyboard Tray with Standard Platform, 17 Inch Track (AKT60LE)" instead.

I am really happy that these extra large labels (2 to a page) are so useful.  Today I accomplished three activities using the labels that will keep me buying more for a long time.  I don't print out postage labels such as those shown in the picture, but I wanted a big label for other reasons.  For one thing, I wanted an easy way to cover labels already on received packages to enable easy reuse of the shipping box. I've used smaller labels but it usually takes several plus you can often see through them.  You can't see through these at all.  I can print my address information on the label or just write on it, but I don't have to worry about getting a pre-existing label off a box anymore.  I packaged something up this morning that took much less time than usual because of these great labels.When I print labels to mail my children's picture book manuscripts, I can style the label with a little of the artwork to attract attention.  I did that this morning too and they turned out really well.  I can also make unique labels for mailed gifts.  This is especially nice when the actual gift box is also the shipping box and can't be gift-wrapped.  My picture software includes lots of frame templates that I can print on the label with the address printed in the frame 'opening', or I can add some art or a border.  Makes for a nicer looking package.The third project I really had fun with today was also gift related.  I printed some especially chosen art on two labels and used them to cover a small box.  I sometimes make jewelry and reuse small boxes I've saved when I give the jewelry as a gift.  I've never liked the idea of a store logo being on the box and now I can cover it up.  The pretty covered box needs only a ribbon and is itself a gift the recipient can reuse.My software doesn't have this label number as a choice for printing, but it has a half-fold card print style that works perfectly.  The labels print well, release cleanly from the backing, but stick well to the chosen package. Labels this size are great for many purposes in addition to the expected use and I'm delighted with them.

I didn't even know how much I needed this Lapdesk w/ built-in stereo until I tried it. I was always putting my laptop on the floor, bed, couch and it usually got overheated after a while. This product fixes that problem, plus the added bonus of a great stereo sound system.The padded mesh base of the Lapdesk is very comfortable on your lap. There's enough cushioning and there's no heat transfer from the laptop because the internal fan keeps it cool. There's also no worry about the laptop overheating when it's placed on the carpet, bed, etc. The fan is very quiet and turns off automatically when you turn the computer off. (You can also turn off the fan manually) Two rubber tabs are included to raise the computer even more to let additional air circulate.The base raises the laptop to a comfortable level for typing and viewing the screen whether you're using it on your lap or setting it on the floor. Two rubberized, pull-out tabs in the very front of the base secure the laptop and keep it from sliding forward.Both my 13" and 15" (a PC and a Mac) laptops fit perfectly and felt very stable and secure on the base. No sliding, slipping or wobbling at all, even with my Mac Book Pro which has a smooth bottom.The built-in stereo speakers are such a great feature because the speakers in my laptop have a barely average sound. When I played songs from my music library and some movie DVD's, the sound quality from the Lapdesk speakers was very impressive. I'm always watching movies on my laptop and now the sound quality rivals my HDTV. There are also easily-accessible buttons on the right side of the base to raise, lower or mute the sound.The Lapdesk connects to the computer via a single USB plug and uses the computer's power, so there are no other plugs or adapters needed. There's also no software or installation required which I appreciated. I don't notice any significant drain on my computer's battery life when using the base.This product is extremely well-designed, ergonomic, well-made and has the kind of helpful features people who use their laptops often really need. My laptop hasn't left my Lapdesk since I got it. Well worth the price. Great product! 5 stars.

I was excited to receive my Epson WorkForce Pro WF-4640 after my last printer (the Epson WP-4530) suddenly died out on us. I will admit, this printer is perhaps more machine than I need for my everyday printing, however, it was important to me that I get a high quality printer as I often need to print documents, spreadsheets and pictures from my home computer. I don't have a fax, but definitely will use the scan and copy features. The main differences between the two printers I'm comparing are that this new one holds more paper in the tray (580 to 330 sheets) and the size.The color touch screen is a big larger on this one as well (4.3 to 3.5 inches).The set up process of the printer was quite easy but, it was a bit heavy at 37 pounds so get some help if you need to lift it or move it.  It has a large footprint so make sure you have enough room for it. All of the parts attached quickly and, after pulling off the tape and powering on the machine, it was all quite simple.  After the printer did its “initial ink charging” which took about 10 minutes, I popped in the installation CD to my computer and after an additional 5-10 minutes, and a very easy wireless connection process, I was ready to print, and these pages printed within seconds. No more sitting there waiting as the printer takes its time pushing the ink back and forth across the page. Also gone are those annoying printer lines that often ruined my pictures if I did not have the printer on the highest quality setting. Even on this printer’s lowest setting I was quite impressed with how my pictures and documents turned out.The only down side that I have to this printer is the lack of directions. There is a VERY SMALL manual that comes with it but is not really helpful.  he printer claims that I can print from my phone and or wireless device however there were no clear instructions as to how to go about doing this and it will require me to do extra research.Overall I am quite happy with this printer and being able to once again print from home will save me both time and money.4.5 stars

I've been using Post-it sticky notes for years and have enjoyed their paper products, finding them superior to other products of the same type which I've bought at stationery stores.  The adhesive really does seem to stick longer, and I'm anticipating the same with the Post-it Super Sticky Removable File Folder Labels.  Since I've only been using them for a few days, I can't comment on their longevity, but for now, I'm sold.I was first impressed by the buff color of the backing paper, different than the usual white backing which has teased me in the past when I've opened a package only to find that someone had put the used label sheets back in the box and the sheets were label-free.  That will not occur with these because of the contrast of white labels on beige.  I personally like the rougher texture of the paper, and have found my favorite font, Marker Felt in all caps in a 24pt, which actually looks nice in the event that the ink bleeds a little.  I'm using a Canon iP1800 with Canon ink and the bleed has been extremely minimal.  Visiting the 3M website as recommended in the literature, I downloaded the template instead of searching through Word to identify the correct one for my Mac.  In about five minutes, I'd gone from opening the package to printing off my first sheet for year-end tax preparations and applying the labels to the file folders.  If only the filing was so quick!I created another sheet of labels for kitchen canisters and as long as I keep them dry, am inclined to believe they will have a long and purposeful life in that application.  Yes, there are other sizes and colors available in the Super Sticky Removable Label family, but I have these and was eager to continue in the fun printing and sticking mode.  These aren't shiny like my other little label maker labels, but they will assuredly be easier to remove when it is time to wash the quinoa jar and having the option to replace the label on the sparkling clean jar is appealing.It is recommended that partially printed sheets not be fed through the printer and I haven't tested that warning.  I also print on the paper which separates the two columns, with nice large numbers that I've cut down and placed on storage.  Not wanting to waste a thing, I've also used the outer edge of sticky paper with handwritten words since the printer will not sufficiently print on that space.  The rounded edge as opposed to squared edges allows the individual labels to be removed very easily, but I do need to cut off the little residual notches from these bonus label strips.  It's also recommended by the manufacturer to store these flat in the package and my own personal recommendation is to assure that they remain in the original package so they are not mistakenly used for permanent applications like postage.While at the 3M website, I registered for their Post-it Perks program.  I look forward to trying more of these products soon.

I had stacks and stacks of papers and stuff sitting around, unorganized.  Receipts, photos, stuff in piles... important stuff, unimportant stuff, piles and piles of stuff. And then these amazing manila folders from Smead showed up.  My life was changed!  I began to get organized by labeling the folders with various categories; reciepts, pictures, lists, reference materials, places I wanted to go, places I had been.  Little by little my desk was becoming a thing of beauty. Wow, I had no idea there was actually a faux maple surface down there, how nice.These ubiquitous file folders are made from sturdy, thick, almost-card-like paper stock in the famous Manila color. Some of you out there may not know this but the name "manila" comes from the fact that when these were first made, they were created with "Manila hemp" or what is known as the abaca plant, a native of the Philippines. It is not related to true hemp, pot or Mary Jane. However, Abaca, like true hemp, has multiple uses like rope, textiles, furniture... and paper. Even the Philippine currency is printed on it!The label area on these is large and makes a nice landing spot for various labels, either stick on or simply written. The tabs are either left, right or middle, which if you are really super-organized, can come in handy. I usually don't pay that close attention.  But, since I own a business and have to keep track of things for tax purposes for 7 years, it's nice to have these around. Having recycled my current ones for over a decade, it's nice to have some sturdy new ones since it seems like every year the folders get thicker with stuff!  Thanks, Smead, for making these sturdier! There's just not much more I can say about these folders other than the fact that every time I look at one from this day forward, I'm going to think about what Manila really means.

I purchased the Canon CanoScan 8400F in the hopes of scanning about a thousand 35mm negatives, but I no longer think this is possible.  After scanning the first 5 rolls, my experiences are as follows:  First, in "automatic" mode the scanner is unable to determine, about 70% of the time, which positions in the tray actually contain film (each position takes over a minute to scan resulting in wasted time).  Next, after waiting 15 minutes for a scan, the resulting pictures (of the negatives that ARE present) are too dark about 30% of the time, requiring a re-scan (after manually configuring the brightness or sometimes just pressing the scan button [for 2 seconds] again).  Next, about 10% of the time the scanner doesn't seem to know the dimensions of the plastic tray, and the resulting pictures end up needing to be manually cropped to remove parts of the tray.  About 5% of the time, after walking away and coming back 15 minutes later, a popup message on the screen says that the scanner found no negatives in the tray, when 8-10 were actually present (and were properly aligned).  In "automatic" mode, sometimes I also ended up with a picture of the tray itself, instead of scanned negatives (perhaps the scanner didn't detect the backlight).  About 90% of the time, it was impossible to remove all of the dust from the negatives, requiring another re-scan or editing of each photo before printing.  After this experience, I am very glad that I now use a digital camera, because scanning negatives has not been a positive experience.

Courtesy of Amazon Vine, I have the pleasure to review FAVI's wireless presenter and I have used it for over a month in office.I will start with the pros first: the radio has a good range, even in an office environment crowded with wifi and other wireless devices. In my case I can get about 30 feet away from the laptop and it is still reliable. It also has an integrated laser pointer that is relatively bright even at 30 feet. It also features intelligent power management: it turns on only when the USB receiver is pulled out.But the current implementation is marred with a number of problems. First, the trackpoint (mouse) is totally unusable in my opinion. The stick is very stiff to push; couple that with a relatively slippery / oil-attracting rubber coating, you will strain your thumb in no time if you have to depend on it. The USB receiver has an irregular shape that is wider than the USB standard and it can block an adjacent port. Also, in order to get the USB receiver, you have to open the back cover. This gets old very soon. (Why can't we have a slot that is externally accessible?) Finally, the blue LED on the receiver is relatively bright and it will light up whenever the receiver receives an event such as a click or a pointer movement. (Fortunately this can be "fixed" easily by taping a small piece of business card on top.)For the current asking price, it is a decent device. However, it has very strong competitors even at this price point and I am not sure I can recommend it. Sorry, FAVI.

I love scanners.Years back I gave up on keeping a physical file cabinet, and began scanning all incoming bills, receipts, etc.  OurFujitsu ScanSnap S1500Msheet-fed scanner has been great for this kind of high-volume work.Before we switched to all digital cameras, we built up a pretty good collection of shoe boxes full of print photos, too. These new Avery NoteTabs are fairly functional but I just don't get the point.They consist of a pastel-colored "divider" part (a tapering 2.75" x less than .5")  connected to a semi-clear rectangle (3" x 1.5").  The divider is like a thicker version of a thin Post-It Page MarkerPost-it Page Markers, Five Assorted Ultra Colors, Five Pads of 100 Strips per Pack (670-5AU)but without adhesive on the back of it...basically it is a tab divider.  The "clear" part does have adhesive all on the back of it, so it totally sticks to your page:  The back of the package says that it "Won't damage documents or lift ink" with this caveat--"Results may vary depending on paper thickness and type of ink."The same sort of caveat applies to "Works with most writing instruments."  Of course it works with ballpoint pens.  I found it also worked with Sharpies and quite a few of my permanent markers.  But it was less successful with gel pens (especially Jelly Rollers) and other (not necessarily permanent) markers:  these either didn't dry for a minute or two...or continued to smear forever.I guess these are basically designed for students or businesspeople, to be used vertically with books or reports (as shown in the tiny picture on the package). The package says they can also be used as highlighters, but then you'd have to place them horizontally somewhere on the page, which sort of defeats the purpose of the divider tab.So, they are fairly functional but I guess I just don't get the point of them.  How many people need a divider combined with a clear "Post-it" that doesn't have enough room on which to write something substantial?  If I want to remember something in a magazine, for example, I'll use a Post-It Page Marker sticking up from that page and write the point on the part of the Post-it that sticks out.  Works fine.  Plus, you get 500 Post-it Page Markers in a package for about $5.50.  This package of Avery NoteTabs contains only 36 and probably won't be much cheaper.I'm sure some people will immediately see the use of these and find them worth the money.  No offense to Avery, who makes some fine office products, but I think I'll "stick" with my Post-it Page Markers.

The HP B8550 is my first Photo Printer; I'm more of an amateur, with a passing interest in photography.  I print out the occasional 8x10", but more often, buy my 4x6" prints from Adorama or Shutterfly.  The B8550 is probably overkill for my needs, but it's nice to have a printer of this capability.Others have said that $299 is too expensive for a home photo printer, but from my viewpoint, $299 is an excellent price slot for a mid-range photo printer.  $299 is pretty reasonable considering its capabilities.Initial thoughts:The printer is much larger than I thought it would be, about 2 feet in width!, but since it's advertised as being able to print 13 x 19 prints, it needs to be.  It comes in an iPod white plastic casing that feels pretty solid.  There are multiple feed trays, a USB and power connection in the back.  At the front, are various CF/SD/Media slots which enable you to directly connect your camera to the printer without the need for your computer to be turned on.  There is a popup-mini 2.4" LCD screen which enables you to view the pictures, along with various external buttons for adjustments.It uses multiple ink wells which have an expiration date of ~ 2 years (June 2010), just to keep in mind.  Replacement could be expensive, at $28 a pop for retail on Amazon.  That could run you $150 just to replace all of the cartridges.  However, I'd suggest eBay as a potential cost-effective alternative.  You can get about half a dozen replacement, genuine HP, ink cartridges for $30-40 (total!) there.Biggest complaint about the 8550 as others have mentioned- no USB cord!  While it's a $299 mid-range machine, a USB cord only costs a few dollars to the manufacturer, and would go a long way towards convenience and initial setup.  However, I did appreciate the inclusion of 4x6" paper samples with which to test the printer.Print quality- surprisingly fast, gorgeous pictures.  I did notice a slight difference with say, pictures printed from a professional printer, but these are pretty darn good for a home printer. For testing, I didn't print anything larger than an 8x10, and my camera is kind of sucky, but from what I saw, the print quality is fantastic.  Which brings me to my next point- you won't be saving any money using this to print 4x6s; save this one for the 5x7, 8x10s, and larger sizes.So here's the summary.PROS:- Capability to print up to 13 x 19 is handy.- Fast, good quality print making for the home office- Can buy cheaper ink cartridges off eBay.- Ability to use the mini-LCD without turning on computer.- Solid build qualityCONS:- No USB cord.- $28/retail ink well is still pretty expensive.- Some installation quirks.The lack of a USB cord really bothers me, and I'd give it 4.5 stars, because the print quality is fantastic for a mid-range printer.  However, I don't want to round up and give it 5 stars, so 4 stars it is.  You can pick up a cheap USB cord from Amazon.

Between the quick start guide and the installation wizard, Canon really takes the guess work out of setting this printer up.Once installed, printing using either of my Windows 7 x64 computers went very well. The resulting print jobs looked very good whether in color or black and white. The text is sharp and clear, photos are vivid and realistic.There is an app for Android phones, Canon EPP, that you can use to print from Android devices. Only one catch: it only prints photos, no documents. It seems a pretty glaring omission to produce an app that only prints one kind of document, in my opinion. Photos printed using the app were OK, but they didn't fit to page as I would hope. I believe the app is likely intended to print to photo paper.The biggest problem I have with this printer is that when it goes to sleep and I send a print job, it always errors. The printer won't wake up on its own. I have to completely power cycle the printer before my print jobs will run. This problem makes the printer very annoying to use, because I'm not often next to the printer when I want to send a print job. I haven't yet found a way to fix this, but will update the review if I do.I haven't yet tested the fax - mostly because I need to figure out how to make my Ooma VoIP work with faxing. I'll update the review once I have done this.The scanner works very well and scan jobs can be launched from the PC or from the front panel of the scanner. The resulting scan jobs look as good as the original document or photo do.Canon bundles several different software pieces with the device, each of which create their own folder in the Start -> All Programs menu. As far as I'm concerned, this is messy programming and it would have been far better to program the installer to put all of these shortcuts in one folder for the Canon MX452 rather than have four individual folders each with only one shortcut. There is one folder for the "Print History", another for the manual, another for user registration, then another for the Utilities. The Utilities folder contains 7 subfolders: IJ Network Scanner Selector EX, IJ Network Tool, IJ Scan Utility, My Image Garden, My Printer, Quick Menu, Speed Dial Utility. Having each of these in a subfolder means it takes more clicks than it should to get to the program. I also don't understand why some of these tools were not combined in one piece of software as other manufacturers do. This just seems unnecessarily tedious and user un-friendly.All in all, I'd say this multi-function device deserves only three stars. While it does a great job printing and scanning, the software is organized poorly and the fact that the device won't print after it goes to sleep is a big issue.

Amazon delivered on time as usual. Fantastic printer it is amazing what this thing will do, I see features I saw on $5k bucks HPs when I was working years ago. For only 100 bucks this machine is a steal...Ok, set up is not that bad. There a little quick setup booklet comes with it. Read the unpacking instructions very carefully (don't forget to shake the toner cart).There is a very good installation cd comes with it. NOW, there is two comprehensive manuals on cd. One is the printer manual (140 pages) and a Network manual (50) pages on how to setup wifi. Save your a major headache and read the network manual on how the wifi works before you try the disk install menu, it leaves a few things out. Remember there are two wifi modes. One is a generic mode open to anybody and two is a home network with security. Go into your wifi router and copy down network password, name, security type. While you are in there look at the range of IP addresses your router will assign.It is best to use the static mode in the printer. Set a static IP address that is well away from all your dynamic devises (computers and such). Because when you install wifi printers in windows you have use a hard IP. If the printer has a dynamic IP your computer will not find your printer when everything resets or reboots up.There is a online browser menu that allows you to set or change printer parameters. http://192.168.1.120/printer/main.html  Note: the IP address is the address I assigned the printer. The default login is admin/access.I highly recommend reading the big manual cover to cover. This printer will do a lot of things like offset printing duplex so you can use ring binders (wow).All parts and buttons are explained. The back left panel has a light that comes on when printer in connected by wifi. Also, there is a small hole that can do automatic wifi set up if you router has that capability. Use a paper clip to set it BUTTT, Read the Network manual very carefully.There are clear instructions on what the panel lights mean and how to do maintenance checks with the lights. The drum and toner maintenance is well covered.The printer prints envelopes and labels. It's all in the manual. The duplex printer mode is  automatic and you don't have to think about it. The duplex can be turned off in the printer properties menu (web see above).For the non wifi folks the printer has an RJ45 (network hardwired to switch) and a regular Usb (printer needs a small end  D type). No cables come with printer. You need a usb cable to install WIFI. Oh, the standard power cable does come with it.If you do any kind of printing you got to be nuts not to buy this printer for this very cheap price. No more crappy ink cartridges,,, YEAAAAAA.

Shredders need lubrication!  I found out the hard way when our Fellows shredder started acting up (not running items through, stopping, reversing, et cetera).  I always thought it was a bit of bunk, needing to lubricate shredders, but it's true, they do need it.When you think about it, paper is drying.  It absorbs oil, water, etc, so when you run it through the shredder, it's going to eventually suck up any lubrication on the cutting wheels.You can use vegetable oils, but that is so messy.  This product comes in a large bottle (suitable for an office environment) with a spout that can be cut so that just the right amount comes out.  And it works great, just running a small bead on the wheels.The shredder, which was balky before, now works as God and Fellows intended.  Fellows makes a superior shredder, and their oil keeps the machine in good shape.This is a keeper and is highly recommended!  Shredders are a must these days, and good ones are expensive.  It's worth a little bit of money to keep it going great.

Well, with handwriting being taken into consideration.Yes this is a fountain pen--which does not work as 'straight-out-of-the-box' as a normal pen does. However, everyone should own a fountain pen because our ability to write is handicapped by all other pens except fountain.Have you ever tried to use your hands with big, bulky gloves on? Whenever the latter is done you always wish you could take them off and use your hands to get the precision that wearing a glove lacks. This is the difference between a regular pen and a fountain.This particular pen, the Pilot MR, has a eloquent design where the entire outershell is made of stainless steel. There is a subtle hint of 'lizard' print around where you would expect to put your fingertips as you write--it does not detract or look conspicuous. Think of the addition of the 'animal print' as would understated lines in natural leather on well-made shoes.As a reviewer noted about the steps to use this pen, know that you should not really use the cartridges steadily as it is much more fun, and economical, to buy a big bottle of ink and refill as needed.**Instructions (abridged) **The pen does come with a cartridge and for that you simply unscrew the pen from the base, and pull out the metal plunger (the proper term is 'converter') and put the cartridge in. Easy as a regular pen.However the converter is what you want to be using for the future as it can be reused and reused with you only needing to buy additional ink. If you want to skip the cartridge here are your converter steps:Unscrew the pen from the base.Dip the pen (submerge it in ink) into the ink reservoir and squeeze the plunger to suck up the ink. You can now begin using the pen.*It would be much more helpful to be able to use the 'piston' type converters however I was unable to find one that fit this particular pen. With those you only need to dip the pen into the ink and screw the converter (moving the piston up)end so that you always have a full converter.****************Filling aside, the pen moves well on paper and does not 'catch' so that it does have a very smooth nib. Using the cartridge, the 7mm was a little too thick for me however when using the converter the lines were more thin similar to a 5mm.Well made pen that will make all your writing better (though this would be helped even more by improving your handwriting in general).Everyone should own at least one fountain pen.

The quality of the prints out of this printer is fantastic.  Rich blacks, even grey tones, even color gradations with no banding, fine details, everything I've thrown at this printer it has done well!I've been looking at pigment printers for a while now.  My biggest motivation has been that when visiting galleries and art shows notice is being given to prospective purchasers that the prints have been made with archival pigment inks.  My work has risen to that level, and though it may be fine to hang a print on my own wall and reprint it as needed, if somebody is going to pay good money for a print they want it to last.  I've sent a lot of work out to be printed, but sometimes the quality has to suffer a bit when I can't crop the print exactly as desired, the brightness and contrast are a little off, or the colors are just not quite what I envisioned, this printer solves all of those problems.I've spent two full days printing on a variety of media; glossy, lustre, photo rag, and metallic and they all look marvelous.  It was very easy to get exactly the looks I wanted with little fiddling as the colors match like I haven't seen before, and I was using custom created profiles for each paper type with my Canon Pro 9000 Mark II.  That printer is quite good, but this one blows it away.  I've never seen my B&W; prints look so good outside of a darkroom, subtle small differences in clouds, for example, come out just perfect, and black is really black.To the details:  It took me about two hours total to set up the printer and start using it.  You really need help to lift this monster, it weighs about 60 pounds.  I just glanced at the getting started instructions, everything is pretty straight forward, pull off all of the orange tape strips that secure everything, install the twelve ink tanks, and the print head.  Turn it on and it primes the head, then just hook up the USB cable and print.  I also installed the software that came with the printer, found out later that it is really not necessary, I'm just printing through Photoshop CS6.  The driver is much improved from the version I have been using, it now correctly allows you to choose color matching and media types.  I'm using OSX Lion by the way.  I did try the print software that came with the printer,  I can see how it might be useful for those without PS, it allows for a lot of the same options, but will not print from a PSD file, so it has to be saved as a JPEG first.  It also has some layout functions that some people may find useful, I tend to just print one print per page.  One thing that I haven't had to do yet is to print a clear coat over sections of a print or even over the whole print, there are options to do that, but as hard as I've looked, I can't see any unevenness or bronzing on my prints.The printer takes about 8 minutes to print a 13"X19" borderless print, 6-1/2 for an 11"X14".  Part of that may be the slow USB2 connection, I have yet to try the Ethernet connection.  As far as ink usage goes, about 25% of the ink tanks are used to prime the print head.  I've printed about 25 4X6, 10 5X7, 10 8X10, 5 11X14, and 5 13X19 prints since then and the ink levels do not seem to have dropped any further.  The ink cartridges are unique, they look like an 8-track tape that plug into the front of the printer, with a verification light to tell you the right one is in the right spot.  I don't see how you could possibly refill them.  When I was printing large quantities of signs and posters I refilled cartridges as a normal course, since I've transitioned to quality over quantity I've just stuck with Canon ink and paper, with the exception of RedRiver metallic paper and Epson Luster paper.  I never really got the quality I was looking for with third party ink, too much variance between suppliers and even from batches from the same supplier.  (I spent a lot of time creating profiles using Spyder Print.)  After I run through some ink tanks I'll update this review to try and express some kind of idea of print cost.  One thing I do to mitigate that is to print on 4X6 until I get the brightness and color balance for the environment right, and then go ahead and print bigger sizes.This is the fourth Canon printer I've owned in the past 10 years.  I tried a couple of other brands, but was really put off by inaccurate and finicky paper handling and the awful problem of clogged pint heads.  In all fairness, I destroyed 2 of the printers using them in a high volume fashion with cheap ink.  The Pro 9000 Mark II I've had for 2-1/2 years now with no problems, and if anything this one is made even better, it is solid throughout.I can really see this printer improving my work, to the point where I'm now going to be able to confidently sell prints, no longer being at the mercy of print labs in achieving a perfect finished product.  Yes, the printer is expensive, too expensive for most people's daily work.  However, if you really want prints you can sell, display in galleries and art fairs, and even in local establishments, the expense is more of an investment, well worth the money.Update 7/4/2012 -  I went ahead and switched the printer to an ethernet cable connected to a router. at the same time I also installed the printer on a Win7 computer with no problems.  Printing takes significantly longer on my Mac, an 11X14 went up from 6-1/2 minutes to 8-1/2 minutes due to spooling.  I also lost access to the printer utility so I can no longer check ink levels, for one thing.  Speaking of which, I hadn't used the printer for a couple of days, and when I turned it on it went through an ink readying routine.  The level of the Grey, Matte Black, and Chroma Optimizer tanks now read 50% used instead of 25% used as stated above.  I now also know why I haven't noticed the need to use clear coat (chroma optimizer), I had it set to AUTO when I installed the printer.  There does not seem to be any way to turn it off.  I suppose I could make a tiny manual mask in a corner.  At $35 a cartridge for clear coat I don't want to be using it if I don't have to.On the bright side, I was showing off some prints and sold a 13X19 metallic without trying, they really are breathtaking.  I guess I'll have to order a set of ink tanks and a bunch of paper and re-print a lot of my old shots.Update 7/7/2012 - This is downright alarming!  After printing about 6 more large prints (11X14 and 13X19)  I checked the ink levels this morning and now all of the cartridges show 50%.  Ordering ink for sure right now.Update 9/30/2012 - This is sickening.  I haven't used the printer hardly at all since my last update, turned it on and it went through another 'prime' cycle.  Now one cartridge is completely empty, 9 others are down to low with warnings, and 2 are at 25%.  Just ordered over $400 worth of ink.  Basically, the printer ate up over $150 of ink just sitting there looking pretty.  If I'm going to continue to use it, I'll have to batch up prints to be made and do them all at once.  By the way, contrary to what was mentioned elsewhere, the cartridges that ship with the printer are full cartridges, not 'starter' ones, so that is not the problem.Update 2/13/13 - It seems that turning the printer on about once a week and printing out a test sheet mitigates the huge sucking up of ink when I leave the printer unused for a while.  Of course, I've gone back to using my Pro 9000II dye based printer quite a bit as well.  Most of my photography is very vibrant, a lot of HDR, and it just pops a little better with dye based vs. pigment based ink.  I've also noticed that few papers have profiles for the Pro-1, although it seems that the standard Canon profiles seem to work fine on a variety of papers.

I was recently gifted this printer instead of purchasing it myself. I am an artist/photographer & I needed a high end wide format to serve my client's needs. This printer does have a learning curve, that's for sure. It is much more sophisticated than your typical all in one or photo printer. I am warning you about this if you are the impatient type or want a printer that works "badda bing" right out of the box without reading a manual. No such luck!Like all ink jets it eats an enormous amount of ink, even more so since you are printing photos (which rely on several layers of color) rather than text or color on plain paper or card stock (which only requires 1-3). I'm guessing you're looking at this printer to do high quality photos or art. If not, a lesser priced photo printer will do the job without alot of fuss. That being said I learned a few things that may help you as well.The basic(s) of matte & black is that the glossy is designed for photos and the matte for matte (or art type) paper. Those who intend to switch back and forth often will find it a nightmare to switch out ink. Find another printer (such as an older 1800, 1900, 2400) instead. If you can stick to one type of paper for awhile, you'll be fine. If you only print photos you will find bliss! Easy!Epson does not allow you to print glossy on matte if that is the paper profile you're using. When you choose the type of paper for printing, you're limited to that profile, period. You can work around it by choosing "glossy photo" with matte paper to bypass that problem. How the end result looks depends more upon your paper than your ink. You can do a test on 4"x6" paper to see. I honestly recommend using that small size to test any prints. You will use alot less ink. Another thing is that the printer needs to charge the nozzles before printing each time if you turn off the machine. All pigment based printers do this. Don't turn it off. Leave it on, it's an Energy Star...it consumes very little electricity. Again, you'll save ink.Nozzles drying out is another consideration with this printer. It is "micro piezo" nozzle design gets clogged if you;A. Don't print at least something (like a 4x6 inch)print each week or soB. Live in a dry climate with low humidityC. Have a dusty environment.Once the nozzles clog, you're looking at using a boatload of ink to clean them. Not fun. Simply print something small to keep the nozzles clear, and if where you live is super dry, consider a room humidifier. It will help alot and keep the dust down too. Epson has all sorts of ICC profiles ready to download on their site for various paper types. Just Google and you'll find them. You can also use ICC profiles from other paper manufacturers (I like Moab). Go to the site & download what you need at the paper site (not epson). A variety of different Epson paper types come with the software as is, but if you want to do something more sophisticated you'll need these profiles. I recommend doing some tests to save ink between #3, #4, and #5 (you'll find this option in "quality") as far as "detail" or "fine detail". This setting also determines how much ink you'll use. I normally use a #3 and it looks awesome. Not much difference to the eye between 3 and 4 for me. My prints are standard 8.5"x11".Who on Earth uses #5? This is an "exhibition quality" (museum) setting. Maybe you will (?). Test the ink quality to see what you can get away with. You'll save $ in the long run. If you get any banding (or move the printer,take it for a car ride, send it in the mail) align the print head. Make certain you're using a very stable table for it to sit on. If the printer shakes much you'll be aligning the head more often. BTW, if you're getting banding on your prints it usually has to do with the speed/quality settings. Use lower quality (dpi) if you want fast prints, or turn off the speed setting.I love that the color accuracy is great between the monitor & printer. The R2880 prints in "epson RGB" or "adobe rgb" (photoshop) without need for calibration nonsense. However, with photoshop the color can look strange if you're not accustomed to setting it up to work with the R2880. Again, you can google for steps to take to calibrate between adobe & the printer. If color if off, it's due to photoshop, not the printer. Test in in a basic program like Paint or PSP and you'll see. Some people suggest not using adobe rgb, that one is your call. You can find vids at youtube to walk you through printing from photo shop to epson. Very helpful!What the R2880 really has going for it is this;*Extremely fine detailed beautiful prints, usually better than a photo lab*Black & white photos are gorgeous (much better than earlier printers R1800-R2400)*Wide format prints (roll paper is more cost effective for this)*The ability to print on pretty much any media including canvas & card stock (earlier printers either don't or don't work well)*You have the type of control over printing that you usually hand over to the lab.*Prints are archival as long as you use acid free paper*Ultrachrome pigment ink cannot be compared with earlier printers or printers from other brands. The color has a "pop" and depth that can't be matched.It's true, the small cartridges are a pain & don't last long. A full set of 9 X whatever you pay (around $13.50 per) is what it will take. Honestly, if that's beyond your budget, you will never be happy with this printer. There are much simpler models that are cheaper to run. Another reviewer mentioned that the R3000 was a better choice since the cartridges are bigger. True, but at $50 a pop some may have a tough time with that. It will run ya just under $500 for a full ink set for a R3000. No thanks!I had a few snafus, but emailing Epson got a response in less than 24 hours and their suggestions worked. You can also call their 1-800 number for help. I prefer to email, it's less of a hassle & there's little misunderstanding as long as I state the problem clearly. You can find a PDF (I'm not allowed to post a link) if you search "print quality issues and how to cure them march 2008" that will outline whatever could possibly go wrong with your prints. This goes way beyond what you'll find in the manual regarding troubleshooting. Otherwise try checking with youtube for the homemade vids for info. They help make the manual much easier to understand if you're a newbie, and have tips and shortcuts. The vids for the paper loading were extremely helpful. I'm not really thrilled with this bubble mailer, but it has its uses.  Nearly every other size "0" mailer I've ever used (and I've used them all) fits a VHS tape with no problem but this brand is just a little bit on the "too tight" side.  While I can get them in there with a bunch of wiggling, it's not an easy fit.  Even a standard DVD case is a bit too tight.  The adhesive doesn't seem very strong so I always reinforce it with tape if I have anything of significant size or weight in the package.On the plus side, the sides are "gusseted", which means there is a seamed edge of about 1/4" up each side.  I find this to be desirable in a mailer one intends to use for shipping as those without gusseted edges can "blow out" and the contents can easily be lost.  The exterior kraft paper, while not offering any moisture protection (in fact it seems to absorb humidity), is fairly strong and combined with the interior bubble layer provides adequate protection for most needs.  The bubbles are "firm" and of good quality.  Believe me, these little details can mean the difference between a damaged product and an undamaged product for your buyer or shipment addressee.If one is filling out the addressing information manually, I would advise the use of a felt tip or "Sharpie" type marker as a ball point pen or pencil will easily puncture the kraft paper (the interior bubbles do not lend themselves to a flat writing surface).  Better yet, use a label - they stick very well to the exterior of these mailers.This mailer is a decent buy if it is offered the price range of less than $.20 per mailer delivered (or picked up) and your demand/need for mailers of this size is only occasional.

Post- It Durable Filing Tabs are an effective means to improved organization of planners, folders, filing systems, etc. These small extenders attach themselves to cardboard, paper, or other material where they help to identify a specific place.Many filing and organizational systems have gone the way of high tech, but I still use cardboard folders and other, similar storage devices for various documents and forms. Many of my folders do not offer sufficient space on their tab areas to write a label, so extenders are helpful. Tabs such as these help to solve the problem by offering a place to write a label of some sort- a label that extends out from the folder, making it easier to find what you're looking for.Some of the positive aspects of these labels are the thickness and the easy removability. They are plastic in construction and are thick enough that they should last a very long time, even with frequent handling. I also like that they are so easy to remove and transfer to another place. They pull off easily without doing damage to most surfaces (paper would be the exception) and can be used again. The different colors are nice, too, because they offer another way to sort and organize.As for the negatives, a few things come to mind. One is that the area on which to write a title is not very big. The white space is about two inches wide, but only about three- eighths of an inch thick so there is very little space to write. Another potential problem is the weak adhesive. I realize that I just mentioned the ease of removal and transfer as a positive quality, but this could also be a problem because, with the adhesive being so light, it is very easy to bump the taps and cause them to shift. Another potential problem is possible smearing- the ink from some pens does not adhere very well to the area where you write and it will smear with the slightest touch.Still, when all things are considered, I like this product and consider it a nice aid in the organizational process. Organization is important and Post- It Durable Filing Tabs help make the organization process easier for those who have traditional files or filing methods and need a way to stay organized. They aren't perfect, but the low cost and other advantages make these filing tabs a product to consider.

When I get a new piece of equipment, I always evaluate it according to multiple criteria. The primary one is how well it fulfills its promised functionality. The second is ease of use/set-up. The third is value (price comparison to similar products). Finally, there are issues with design, footprint, and, if it is a portable product, portability.On the primary point of functionality, this worked very well in my experience. I tested it with Bluetooth and a cell phone as well as USB. For USB, Skype auto-detected it and I tested it by calling the Skype test call and recording my own voice from multiple positions in the room - close (leaning in unnaturally), mid-range (sitting at a table with the device about two feet away), and far away (across the room - about two and a half meters away). I wanted to test the sound because some of the lower-rated reviews said that they heard the other party clearly, but that the person on the other end couldn't hear them well because of echos. By recording myself and playing it back, I could get objective information on what the other party would be hearing. I also tested this by making a call to a live person.The results of my testing showed that it picks up voices well from all points, though it works better if you are closer and it will pick up more ambient noise in the room if you are further away. When I made a call to a live person, she told me that there was some distortion/echo at first, but I was able to fix this problem entirely by altering the microphone input levels (turning down the mic sensitivity made echos vanish). So, if you have this problem, alter your mic settings and it may be fine.In terms of ease of use, I was able to quickly and effortlessly connect and set this up. It really was a dream in this regard (especially for USB). Of course, your mileage may vary as some phones or bluetooth can be fussier than others. However, I can only speak to my experience and it was quite good.The current price for this conference speaker is $136.15. This puts it in the mid range of prices. It is neither cheap nor expensive and represents, at least in my opinion, adequate value for quality.Finally, in terms of design, this is really a nice piece of equipment. It's a little bigger than the palm of my hand, light, and comes with a carrying case made of thick felt that stores both the speaker and the USB cable. It's unobtrusive so you could fit it on a crowded table with laptops all around it and it's certainly compact and light enough to carry around without being of significant weight.Once I adjusted the mic levels, this performed perfectly for me. I can't see how it could be any better (well, it could always be cheaper, but the price is on par with similar devices).

Rather, the tape is simply communicating a public service message to check the seal before accepting the package.The tape has a double whammy. It is too thin to safely use for shipping, so it is not the best choice for packing tape, and further, it does not do the job suggested by its stated message. *EDITED AFTER MUCH RESEARCH!*You know, sometimes it really stinks to be a serious photographer on a budget. I am a wedding photographer by trade, but film photography is more my passion. The problem is that most of my budget is dedicated to digital gear with little left over for analog photography equipment. I decided that I might as well give this budget scanner a try, seeing as my local lab was charging $20 per roll scanned and my local one-hour photo (CVS) seemed to be scanning things with a potato (no really). This review is mainly going to cover the 35mm aspect of this scanner, but I will briefly touch on the other qualities.PROS- Able to scan 35mm film and slides with the built-in adapter- Scans 35mm adequately for this price range- Almost no warm-up time- Controls are easy to use- Accompanying software is pretty decent for photos and documents- VERY easy to create PDF's, OCR is really good- Scanning is relatively fast, although my last scanner was bought in 2004 so my reference point is old...- OSX Lion 10.7 Compatibility (download from Epson website)CONS- Has difficulty reproducing color from scans- Lacks sharpness on some images- Negative holder is a little flimsyI really think the output of this scanner depends on your expectations. I have seen serious photographers love and hate it online...I am somewhere in the middle. For the price of the scanner, it puts out decent images that I would gladly put up on the web. As far as printing out  'up to 13"x19" ', I'm not so sure. If I had the funds, I would have gone with the V700 in a heartbeat, but seeing as I didn't I really can't complain too much. The only REAL issue was the reproduction of colors when it came to scanning slide film. Right off of the scanner they were VERY muted, even Kodachrome which is notoriously saturated. The negative carrier is a little flimsy, but with some care you shouldn't have any problems. As I mentioned above, there are some issues with sharpness, but an unsharp mask takes care of all but the harshest issues.I would highly recommend purchasing Silverfast if you are going to be seriously scanning 35mm. The tools that come with this scanner are just not enough to provide you with GREAT scans. If you are just looking to archive some old family pictures, this will definitely do the trick and you will have some pleasing results, but if you take pride in image quality Silverfast is a must. Dust-removal, color restoration and professional sharpening are all possible with it, and it has saved me hours of hassle. No I do not work for them, and no I don't get a cut. I really can just appreciate software that works well!RECOMMENDATIONS AND SETTINGS:1) I would highly recommend flattening out your negatives before scanning. Scans with a slight curvature will leave you with some scans being out of focus in certain areas. Flattening out my negatives greatly improved my scans.2) Wear anti-static gloves at all times while handling negatives. This will greatly reduce imperfections. If you have compressed air, clean your negatives with short bursts at 12" or more away from the negatives. Hold upright so as to not damage the negatives from the cold.3)  If you have Photoshop (as I do) I would recommend skipping the unsharp mask and dust deletion, and instead use the Smart Sharpen filter in CS3+ and removing dust and speckles with the healing tool!4) Patience. Scanning at low DPI will give you poor results. Bump up the resolution - you may wait longer but I guarantee you will be happier! Speaking of which, here are my recommended settings for scanning:Epson Black and white settings (ideal for web):- Professional Mode- Doc Type: Film- Film Type: B&W; Negative- Image Type: 16bit Grayscale- Resolution 2400DPI- Target Size: 100%- Unsharp Mask ON, Medium- Dust Removal ON, Medium-High (if needed)- Save as TIFF or JPEGEpson Color Settings (ideal for web):- Professional Mode- Doc Type: Film- Film Type: Color Negative- Image Type: 48bit Color- Resolution 2400DPI- Target Size: 100%- Unsharp Mask ON, Medium- Dust Removal ON, Medium-High (if needed)- Color Restoration ON (if needed - try both)- Save as TIFF or JPEGOVERALLObviously I wasn't expecting this to be anywhere near what my lab puts out, but I was pleasantly surprised to see that it surpassed what CVS could do with higher resolution and truer colors (in most cases). While this isn't a permanent solution for me, I am relatively pleased and would recommend it to those that don't mind putting in the post work to make their images really stand out. This scanner really shines with black and white scans - I haven't scanned a color image that I was TOTALLY satisfied with yet.As far as an office scanner, this is an excellent choice and will provide you with better scans than most all-in-one office solutions on the market!

This is a "value" priced home office "all-in-one" machine. It is nicer than some, but is missing features to make it past home use. The wireless features work well and it is a compact unit for what it does. It works with Macintosh, which is a plus for me. That said, there are some compromises when you get to this level of machine, vs what you might get if you move up one level. Some specific details are presented below.Details:* Nice size. The unit does not take up a lot of extra space on the desk or table top as the paper tray does not stick out as long as you are using US letter sized (8.5"x11") paper. If you put legal sized (8.5"x14") paper in the paper drawer, you have to pull out an extender on the drawer to fit the longer paper. This will add another few inches to the front of the unit as shown in the photo I uploaded. Not a super huge issue, but something to be aware of.* touch screen works with just a normal touch. This seems obvious, but I've used other printer touch screens that required a fair amount of pressure and that had poor image quality. this one is nice.* Double sided printing. This works very well. It is NOT double sided for copying or scanning, however. This is typical in this price range, but there are other under $200 machines that can copy and scan double sided. The Epson workforce is one.* The print speed is fast enough for me that I didn't time it to check out the specs. It* The plain paper print quality is good for blacks (Brother uses pigment ink for black) and decent for the color, which are dye based inks. Business graphics (charts, etc.) are fine. Photos tend to come out washed out a bit. In fact, the photos on plain paper look a bit like my Canon MX300 all in one, which is an older, lower end machine than this one.* Photo quality on photo paper (4"x6") is acceptable. This is not what I would normally use this machine for, but it does have a 4"x6" photo paper compartment in the paper tray, so it is clearly intended to be able to print photos. I would call the results good enough to share casual photos. The colors are not as vivid and the image is not as sharp as a true photo printer.* Envelope printing. You can print envelopes, but it is a minor pain to do so. This is one of the issues that prevents this from being a "small office" printer in my opinion. In order to print an envelope, you must first remove the paper tray, remove all the paper other than the 4x6 photo paper, and then re-adjust the tray pieces to accept your envelope. Then re-install the tray. So, you probably won't do this much. What I would have rather seen is a manual insertion bypass slot that can by used for individual envelopes or paper, at a minimum. Better, since this is not a photo printer, get rid of the 4x6 area in the tray and use this for number 10 envelopes. This is part of my one star downgrade.* No manual bypass paper feed. See above. This also makes it difficult to mix logo and non-log stationery in which typically only the first page has a logo on it. This is the other half star downgrade. I would rather have had this than the less than useful CD/DVD printing feature.* There are special orange plastic pieces that are used to cover the place that the ink tanks plug into and for each of the ink tanks as well. These are necessary if you transport the machine or remove the ink tanks. Don't lose these - I have included a photo.* The system comes with "starter" ink tanks. This is the kind of thing that makes you believe the system has low capacity when it is not as bad if we had the  standard tanks. Needless to say, these go faster than hoped for. I would recommend that they ship with standard tanks so we all don't become frustrated with seemingly poor capacity.* The system can print on "printable" CD and DVD medial. It comes with a special carrier tray to put the CD or DVD on. This requires that you use the USB connection to print from. This seems like a poor choice for a wireless printer.* The iPhone printing works fine.* Set up on my home network (all Apple stuff) was super simple.Conclusion:If you can get this at a good price, go for it. If you want to go back and forth between envelopes and standard paper, this is an awkward system.

Here's the Pros and Cons:Pro:- The texture is nice - kind of like a very firm Temperpedic memory foam type mattress. I have had this printer for seven months.  I had to reinstall the printer software on my wireless laptop, which is running OSX 10.8.5.Surprise #1:  The installation CD would not longer run. I got an error message saying that the disc was incompatible with my system software. Overall, I would consider these an okay purchase.  I love the different colors so that I can code and organize with these folders. The design of these pencils is unique in my experience. This little puppy holds up under massive use and strain! Heavy duty binder material with an extra pouch in the front to hold tabs, pens, or whatever you need. This large cork board came flat packed in a pretty big flat cardboard box with room to spare inside so there was no damage to it.I have an old cork board that's about 30 years old and I can say that they don't make them like they used to. My old board is thick and has a real oak frame. The downside to that is that it's pretty heavy and you need to really attach it to the wall securely.This new board, even though it's twice as big weighs a lot less. That's because the cork is thinner and the frame (not plastic) is made of some kind of compressed board with an oak veneer finish. The pro of that is that it's very light. If it was made like my old cork board it'd probably weigh a ton.The board comes with instructions on the back and mounting hardware. The mounting hardware consists of screws, wall anchors and two flat metal plates that you insert under the frame edge.The cork itself is not very thick and has a cardboard backing. The construction materials is why this board is so inexpensive. If you push a pushpin completely in, it will come out the other side. But as the frame holds the cork a little bit away from the wall, the wall won't be marked. Once the pins are pushed in fully, they are held pretty tight, probably a combination of the cork and the cardboard.So what you have here is a budget version of a real cork board. But at this price, I won't complain. It's big, it works and it's cheap.

I have lots of staplers, but I tend to be a light user of them and actually prefer the mini version to a big bulky one in my desk. This is massively strong.  It's amazing.My monitor arm arrived without assembly instructions except for the exploded pictures on the stickers closing the boxes it arrived in. Wow. I was really put through my paces trying to set up WiFi through my Verizon Router, much like everyone has reported. I have a really hard time understanding how such a process to set up a wireless document scanner could ever make it off the early-stages of planning and development. Someone must've have REALLY dropped the ball NOT making this plug-n-play. I'm also betting that particular someone is already fired.** Note directly to Epson -- You need to address this failing with your consumers who either register this device or call in ASAP.In the past, I've used NEAT Scanners, Fujitsu Document Scanners and a few other off-name brands and pretty much across the board -- they've all been a plug and play / easy install.This was anything but. I haven't seen an installation / troubleshooting process since maybe Windows 98 or even ME.1. Installation process not simple nor easy.2. I had to reconfigure my home router.3. I had research the product online for set up and better install instructions -- before using.* I usually have no problems doing research or troubleshooting a product to either make it better or preform smoother, but to make the product operate in a basic mode ... yeah, that's a problem.4. Equally difficult installing the scanner on my Mac Mini. Probably more frustrating.5. Once I got past the wireless scanning desire, the machine did work.6. I wanted to place the scanner near the counter where I come in from outside and empty my pockets, and immediately scan all my receipts from the entire day. No this couldn't be achieved without removing a limb and making a pact with Satan. No thank you.7. When I did scan documents, wired - not wireless, I was able to scan everything with no problem. Thin small receipts from the gas station, business cards, cash register receipts, everything. this process actually worked really good. I didn't experience the problems with the feeder that others did.8. I utilized Evernote as my default save point.9. I would've likely returned this scanner to the store had it been an outright purchase and not a Beta-test.10. It's a shame, because this really is a nice looking scanner that does scan documents well. Like some Sony products however, the hardware is thwarted by the software portion making the thing immediately obsolete and troublesome for the standard consumer.Final thought:Epson needs to completely redesign the software portion of this device and offer customers either an apology, a notice to all registered buyers about a discount, and possibly even a buy back if they cannot deliver a better operating piece of software before years end.Epson has made some great hardware with bundled and branded software in the past. This is far from that standard. What a shame.

Assembling this chair was an interesting experience, not least thanks to the minimalist "instructions" (just a simple diagram). It wasn't awful, but it certainly could've been easier. First, the casters. When lined up correctly, they easily slide into their sockets. However, I couldn't see any indication of how to line them up -- I just had to fiddle around with them until they went in. The other issue is with the back. If you attach the arms tightly to the seat, as the instructions imply you should, you won't be able to fit the back between them. You have to start by attaching the arms to the seat just loosely, without tightening the screws much. Then insert the back between them, and tighten things up with the back in place. The job can be completed by one person with a little gumption.Once assembled, this is a very nice-looking piece of office furniture.The seat is relatively comfortable, but as other reviewers have mentioned, the bottom cushion is not particularly thick. This may not be an all-day, 8-hour working chair. This also may not be the chair for you if your waist is much larger than about 38". As can be seen in the product image, the fronts of the arms are tight against the sides of the seat, and will be tight against the sides of your legs if you're a very large person. Note that this chair is only "warranted" for users up to 250 pounds, so if you're that big, you'll want to find a different chair anyway.The simple recline controls, a resistance knob and a lock lever, are easy to use.This is a good, not great, chair at its price point. If you shop around, you might find better. But if you like the look of this one, you could certainly do worse.

Avery has joined forces with stamps.com to offer this "starter kit" for print-at-home postage, and while the box makes big, great-sounding promises: "Four Free Weeks of Service!" and "$45 Free Postage" ... the fine print reveals some major drawbacks.First, the "free" postage. Actually, it's only $5, not $45, unless you subscribe to stamps.com $15.99/month service. And even then it's not $40, it's $10 per month via four separate coupons (my kit had only one), redeemable only via a mail and requiring an ADDITIONAL "6-8 weeks" of waiting, FOR EACH. Oh and the postcard must be mailed using an Avery stamp and stamps.com postage, notch. Oh and, that "four weeks" of free service? It's actually 14 days. When you sign up, they state clearly they'll charge your credit card for a month's service if you don't call and cancel, "within 14 days."The (ridiculously high, in my opinion) monthly service fee is prohibitive unless you're mailing upwards of $200-$400/month on a regular basis, so that leaves most home users out. Since the postage MUST be printed on stamps.com approved labels, that's another continuing and significant expense, above and beyond the $15.99 monthly fee and postage costs. I also read complaints from people online that cancellation is very difficult (you have to call and get the hard sell from operators) and can not be done online, leaving some with endless auto debits (the only method stamps.com allows for payment), even when they're not using the service.All you're actually getting with this kit is 5 pages of self-stick, printable mailing labels (10 total), 4 pages of "3-part mailing labels pages" and 5 stamp pages (20 stamps per page).In short, this is NOT something useful to most people who use USPS simply to send cards, pay bills and mail the occasional package. Unless you're currently making daily runs to the post office and sending 10-20 packages per week, stamps.com service likely won't pay off for you. And if you DO need this service--high volume eBay or Amazon Marketplace sellers, for instance--stamps.com own trial offer (which comes with the same label/stamp printing kit), postage credits, PLUS a 10 lb. USB postage scale that automatically integrates with their system and makes the whole thing MUCH easier to use, is probably a better deal.Again, and only in the fine print, Avery acknowledges a postage scale is required to fully utilize the stamps.com service. The Avery kit claims you can get a 5 lb. postage scale (that does NOT hook up to your computer or integrate with the stamps.com software) by submitting a mail-in form and, "just pay[ing] shipping and handling." My kit lacked said form but I have a sneaking suspicion that "shipping and handling" would exceed the cost of the scale in the first place. (You can buy a basic 5 lb. postage scale for >$15 at most office supply stores.)Lastly, the Avery/stamps.com system will only work with Windows PCs. Max and Linux users are out of luck. In fact, the packaging says it only works with Vista, but Windows 7 machines seem to access everything OK too. (Stamps.com entire site only works with Windows running Internet Explorer, making it a web dinosaur. Some areas won't function under Firefox or other browsers. Who under the age of 65 uses IE?)If you do use lots of postage, stamps.com might be a good deal--for instance, you get electronic rate discounts on larger mail items and extra services--but I think there are better ways to use/access the service than via this Avery starter kit. And if you're only mailing things online, there are other places to print online postage, without a monthly fee, including the U.S. Postal Service's own website.EDIT: For some reason, even though the service name and free postage amount claim are listed in the TITLE OF THIS PRODUCT, Amazon.com redacted all references in my review to the service these Avery labels require you to use for postage and the amounts of free postage promised and/or given. I don't get that at all (especially when such things NOT redacted in a previous review) and I have no idea how you're supposed to review the labels when you can't reference the service you must subscribe to use them and the claims made on the packaging.

No more hunting around in the desk drawer for something strong enough to pry open a heavy duty staple.  I have spent more time than I care to think of doing just that. Normally I buy recycled paper by Georgia-Pacific.  One of the things I find interesting is that this paper is packed much more environmentally friendly than the recycled paper! This product is simple to use, heats up quickly and operates quietly.  --This is a great little product if you need something for quick and occasional lamination jobs.I had the opportunity a while back to review the Fellowes Callisto 125 Laminator, 12.5-Inch.  When comparing the two items, I noticed a significant difference in the sound emitted from both machines. We buy them by the box! Does anyone ever remember what we did without Sharpies? I would rather use a Sharpie than a pen. We use them in several pen tip sizes and we buy them by the box of 12.
