After several months testing out this machine, I'll say that it took some warming up to, but it's been quite a workhorse. But let me back up and start at the beginning...When I first opened up the box and unpacked its contents, I was dumbstruck. It's intimidating and the instructions might well have been written in a dead foreign language for all their helpfulness. Since I do have some measure of patience and don't mind a little trial an error, it didn't take too long to figure out what went where and how. But I will say it's a good idea to have a few test booklets ready for mangling if you aren't familiar with this particular comb binder.I've done various projects ranging from 10 sheets to just under a hundred and this binder handled each of them like a champ. It should go without saying, though, that the smaller jobs (under 20 pages) were definitely the easiest. This binder can only punch about 25 sheets at a time, though I found its sweet spot to be about 20. The punch didn't feel flimsy--in fact, *nothing* about this machine feels flimsy--and punching the holes didn't require too much effort on my part.For the larger jobs, you'll need to develop a system to keep the pages aligned after they've been punched or it can become a challenge to get them all properly lined up later for the binding. However, once you find your groove, this is one sturdy and useful machine. And the results come out looking professional every time (save those first few trial and error bindings). I even did a side-by-side comparison of a booklet I had bound at a Kinko's and couldn't tell the difference.And months later, this machine is still going strong. I'll just finish up with a mention that this binder does have a large footprint and it's quite heavy, so make sure you have the proper space for it and that you don't plan to move it often.

I'm a magazine junkie and an amateur genealogist, so I pretty well always have piles of paper lying around I'm intending to digitize.  Have been looking for this particular tech for a long time without even realizing it - what this is, is a scanner that will save you a load of time if what you're trying to do is save documents rather than make hi-res copies of photographs.What slows me down in scanning most of the time is the time-consuming 'pre-scan' process.  First I have to hook my flatbed up to my computer using a USB cable, then I have to scan once to establish the edges of the document and sometimes one or two more times to get the scanner to recognize what I'm trying to input.  What a boon to be able to set a big pile of paper up on top of a scanner and have it all read through of a piece and without me having to set and re-set the configuration and the file names and resolutions for EVERY page.  This DS-560 will handle a HUGE pile of paper without jamming and will save it as one document, without your having to set up new options for each and every page.  It's a very powerful machine - unfortunately, though, most of my review is going to be about the experience of using it - setting it up and the controls are NOT among the smoothest experiences I've ever had when handling new equipment.For starters, it isn't the world's easiest thing to configure - it ships with four or five pieces of software, and half the job is figuring out which of them you're supposed to use to do what.  It has a 'direct wi-fi' mode that it took me a couple of times to get right, and its 'Epson config' app flatly didn't recognize the scanner the first few times I tried to set it up.  Long story short I had to download some updated scanners and drivers from Epson's website (search for "DS 560 drivers" to get your own) and install the needed programs separately.  Once I did that, I had to go into 'Epson scan setup' and change the connection from 'local' to 'network' to get it to recognize the scanner on the network, which wasn't in the directions.  Long story short, you may need someone who's familiar with the IP addresses on your network to put this thing online for you, although the capability to put it online from a utility that will 'read' the local Wifi connection and configure it automatically made it relatively easy for someone like me (not particularly techie.)  You may wish to set up what's called a 'static IP' for this if you don't plan on leaving it turned on all the time - which is another reason you may need the person who set up your network to config it for you.The user manual is online, which I kind of like since it doesn't waste paper, but it's a little difficult to find what you need.  The pages don't always expand and the dialog box sometimes doesn't appear.  I had to dig around a bit to figure out what certain terms meant and some of the 'troubleshooting' was things like 'make sure your computer is turned on' - maybe some people need this but I expect a little more out of a user manual for complicated equipment.  The manual is a PDF file but it forces you to open in a Web browser - the navigation is clumsy and it isn't easy to scroll from one page or article to the next.  (I tried to save it as a PDF file I could read in Adobe Reader and AR wouldn't open it.  'Corrupted file' said the error message.  Sigh.)You also have to be fairly 'techie' I think to understand what the default applications are trying to get you to do.  Maybe this is the function of my using a Mac, but I was trying to set the 'Start' button to a default action and it wasn't at all obvious - had to click several dialogues and at one point had to select from a pull down that did not have arrows indicating what it was.  You have to just keep fooling with the software - it's not what I would call user-friendly.  Might be good to take notes for whatever you want it to do.I finally figured out how to get the DS-560 to connect to my Evernote account (though the word "Evernote" is not present in the 'Help' file for the program you must use to interface with it, of course. )  Evernote has optical character recognition (OCR) available for premium subscribers and would be a real plus to use with this scanner.  Unfortunately though Evernote sync is just another clumsily-applied interface - you scan first, pick Evernote after, and while it does default to your correct notebook if you're logged into the program, it doesn't offer predictive text for your tags, so you just have to "know" what you're going to use.  Also you can't type more than one word as a tag - any spacebar converts to a carriage return.  Gee, good for me (eyeroll) since mine are called things like "Kentucky county evolution" and "household item directions."  I foresee a lot of cleanup work in my future on this.You can also initiate the scan either from the software or the dedicated 'start' button on the machine, which is a little more complicated to set up using a Mac, but which seems to work fine.  However, though, the Start button WILL NOT WORK using Wifi without a particular piece of software.  Just one more fussy detail.In a nutshell, this is a very powerful scanner once you have it configured to do what you need.  On the downside, the software that ships with it is simply not ready for prime time.  If I had to guess it's probably a series of programs that Epson simply added to and mildly changed over time to use with different items - it really needs a top down rewrite.  Until they can create easy to use help dialogues and intuitive software, this gets three stars.  The hardware itself is impressive - it operates smoothly, it's fast, it doesn't jam.  Hopefully Epson will get it together and write a program that makes it easier to use.

I really like this stapler because it does what it's designed to do: secures important papers and documents and keeps them together in a professional manner. Since I've had Stanley, as my grand-kids nicknamed this tool, I get to see them more often because they're always seeking help with various school projects. It's fun showing them how to maneuver this very large stapler into "firing" position to staple different textures together; from construction paper to cardboard and foils, my Stanly handles it all with safety and ease.The only thing that bothers me--since I'm fussy about aesthetics--is thatStanley Bostitch EZ Squeeze 130 Flat Clinch Reduced Effort Stapler (B8130)spoils the looks of my desk. Just picture this large, black, metal thing, sitting there with it's long lever sticking up in an ungainly manner--looking for all the world like a missile launcher--and you'll know what I mean. This thing is a beast!! Two huge paper cartridges and another feeder for envelopes and such. It has a huge scanner/copier bed as well. It will scan and print up to 11 x 17 inches!!!!! Printed test page no problem then set up Epson Connect functions.Epson connect lets you print from mobile apps. It also lets you scan to the cloud. I set mine up for Dropbox. It also assigns your printer an email address so you can print things by emailing them. I emailed a picture and it printed in less than 5 minutes. Scanning to dropbox is done entirely from the touchscreen.  You don't need to use a PC at all.I really like the automatic 2 sided printing. I printed some web pages and just had to select Eco 2 Sided mode from the printer properties box within the print options of internet explorer. The large scanning bed is really nice for scanning my daughters large artwork. Before we had to do it in two parts and put them back together. The scanner is a lot faster than on my old printer. The Epson Scan program has been updated as well with more options and controls.Packaging: I'm not sure if mine was standard or not. The printer did not come in an Epson printed box. It came in just a plain brown cardboard box with some Styrofoam. The box was huge and broke open. I was surprised that the accessories where still in the box. No damage to the printer. It would have been nicer had it been double boxed like the smaller printers.Notes:- This thing is huge and heavy but prints and scans up to 11x17 inches!- Large touchscreen is awesome and makes it easy to use- Software setup is quick and easy.- Wi-Fi setup is a breeze- Can set up Epson Connect so you can email things to print to your printer- Can set up a mobile app to print to your printer- Can set up scanner to scan to the could. I scan to dropbox.- Software allows multiple printers to be setup and used- Software checks for update and can update the printer firmware- The scanner is a lot faster than my Epson 630 from a couple of years ago.- Double sided printing is smooth and easy. Just select it from the printer properties inside whatever program you are printing from.

I use this binder in my career as a teacher, so its gets almost daily use. For three hole punches, I have two simple criteria I look out for. (1) It punches decently and (2) It contains the loose punched out paper. This PaperPro 12 sheet punch satisfies me on the first, but fails for me on the second.The way the bottom of this punch is built, the bottom has a sort of mini door in the middle of one of the long sides of the puncher that swings open and closed to allow you to empty the paper holes. The door is shut by a lip of plastic on the main structure of the puncher catching and clicking into a cut out hole on the swinging "door" piece. Problem is, though it catches and closes, the hole in the door where the lip catches is still large enough when closed to allow the punched out paper to fall out should it happen to be passing around the hole area. I often use this puncher by holding it in my hand instead of leaving it on a flat surface, so the puncher is often tilting around. Pretty much every time when punching paper with this, I find a few loose paper holes that have fallen out of the puncher this way and onto the floor or other areas. People who leave this puncher on a flat surface instead of picking it up often to use will likely not have a problem with this as I do. I also didn't like the way the emptying door was situated in the middle of the side of the puncher because to empty it, you have to tilt it back and forth until the paper holes from all sides find that opening in the middle to exit. Hole punchers I've had in the past have had the emptying door either at the end so you could simply hold the puncher in one direction and easily wait for all the trash to dump out, or have had the bottoms completely removeable so aiming the holes for the exit space was a non-issue.I had no problem with the punching ability. My hand never felt strained punching several piles of about 8 sheets at a time. It even easily handled punching a hole through a plastic card so I could pin up a gift card on the wall over a thumb tack. Before this, I had a cheap puncher from an office store. The holes punched with the PaperPro were bigger, which I prefer. The old office store puncher's holes were approximately 5 mm, while the PaperPro holes are about 7 mm diameter.This puncher works, but is not my ideal design. I would prefer to look elsewhere for one that contained the punched holes better.

I've run my own business for years and tried my fair share of printer labels.  I've tried many styles and brands and Avery brand labels continue to be my favorites.  Avery seems to have done everything right with their new Easy Peel labels.  The paper is just the right thickness - blocks out any print underneath without creating a raised edge that gets caught easily.  The glue doesn't lose adhesion over time.  The paper is bright white with a smooth finish and the edges are cut smooth and clean.  Perfect!Plus the new Easy Peel feature makes peeling off a label nearly effortless.  The page is creased under the edge of the label sticker.  Just bend the page and the edge of the label pops up for easy grabbing.  Ingenious design!Number two runner up is 3M brand.  Their paper has a slightly rougher face, but their glue is just as strong.  No Easy Peel technology with 3M labels however.I've learned to stay away from Staples brand labels and the other generic brands.  The glue is worthless and the paper is too thin to cover over any old print.So if you're looking for a great printer label and don't mind spending a little more for quality, Avery brand Easy Peel labels are the way to go.  I've tried 5 different Avery Easy Peel styles and all are top notch.

This awesome stapler for booklets would be a five-star stapler if the markings were easier to read; as it is, while I love it, I'm always second-guessing myself when it comes time to staple my booklets.Pros:  Works really well on booklets up to 20-ish pagesCons: Hard to read markings make me feel like it's a toss up as to whether I'm stapling in the right place

The Epson WF-7620 is a remarkably full-featured workgroup scanner/copier/fax/printer with performance that rivals big-iron printers costing thousands of dollars.Being targeted at mid-sized offices, it is no surprise that the WF-7620 is a lot bigger than what you'd put on your desk.  A multi-function unit like this belongs in the mail room or in an open space for everyone to access and the larger size is perfectly reasonable for this usage.Before I go into details, here are a few features that I love about the WF-7620:+Double-sided scan of a document directly to a USB thumb drive.+Double-sided photo copying.+Double-sided printing.+Fast printing with laser-printer quality.+Large, helpful touch screen and plenty of physical buttons.+AirPrint from iPhones and iPads.SETUP---------------Setup was quite easy and only took me about 15 minutes.  It involved unboxing , removing a large number of tape fasteners used during shipping, installing the four ink cartridges, adding it to my wireless network (they provide several easy ways to do this), and adding paper.  Once operational, I let the Epson utility on my Windows 7 laptop download new firmware to the printer.  All-in-all, it was very easy to get this thing on the network for all to use.PRINTING---------------This printer is competing with entry-level laser printers and it does a fine job at that.  I printed a document with text and images and then compared a printout of the same document that was performed on a $3000 HP LaserJet.  Even under a magnifying glass, the Epson's print quality was identical.  The printouts were quite fast, even when printing double sided.  The ink is smudge proof and even a wet finger couldn't smear the text.I tried to print Avery labels but that did not work for me.  I was using the rear feeder and each time I would insert the blank sheet of labels, only to have the printer tell me that it was "ejecting" them.  I tried four times and gave up.  This was disappointing and I took away a star for this.  Unless something changes, I don't think you can use this printer for envelopes or labels.There are two paper trays and either can hold longer paper such as legal.A 14 page document with color images printed double sided in 2 minutes.  It would be much faster if printed single-sided because flipping the paper over seems to take extra time.Overall though, the print functionality is great and the print speed is commendable.  Having only four colors, its color printouts compete well with laser printers but I wouldn't advise using this as a photo printer due the limited color palette.COPYING & SCANNING--------------------------------------The WF-7620 is a competent photo copier and scanner.  I love being able to scan directly to a thumb drive.  You simply insert a thumb drive, choose your scan target as "memory device", and click "start".  It writes a JPG or PDF file .  The scanner has a sheet feeder and can do a stack of pages, even double sided.  When photo copying, you have options to go from2 sided -> 2 sided1 sided -> 2 sided2 sided -> 1 sided1 sided -> 1 sidedYou can also zoom and shrink, for example, copying a page of legal and printing it to letter size.Photo copying is also quite fast.  Copying a two page document and converting it to a single double-sided document took less than 30 seconds.  The scanner has a feature that digitally removes any folds or hole punches from your printouts.  It works perfectly, but does also remove any feint horizontal lines that might be printed on the original.  It's easy to disable this feature.MISCELLANEOUS--------------------------------------Setup was very easy on my mac, it didn't even need the installation disk and all of the drivers downloaded directly in the OS without going to any websites.The SD/MS card can be used to print photos, but having only four colors, I think this is a poor photo printer.  Color printouts are decent and compete well with the $3000 laser printer in my main office.  But for photos, they look bad compared to dedicated photo printers with 6 or more ink cartridges.The printer says it can handle triple sized ink cartridges (labeled "XL") but at the time of this review, Amazon did not sell them.  This printer seems pretty new, that should change.

The set of six 12" ECR4Kids chairs, geared for children aged 3-7, are well-constructed, well-designed and comfortable. What I particularly liked about these resin chairs is that they are easy to clean and won't chip or crack, despite kids tendency to bang their feet against them. Further, their one-piece design with rounded, smooth edges makes these chairs above average in terms of being safe. I guess some might consider the fact that the chairs can't be folded for easy storage when not being used to be negative, although I don't see it that way as they are easily stackable.Be aware that if you have some children older than 7 years of age, they might be too big to be very comfortable in these chairs. As mentioned above, the recommended age group for these chairs is 3-7 (maximum). The dimensions for these chairs are as follows: 12.8" wide, 14.8" deep and 21.6" high, with a seat height of 12"; so you might want to first check out if these dimensions would be good for your children. The desert sand color in my set is very attractive-looking but if sand doesn't work for you, the set also is available in  cornflower blue, spring green, candy red and canary yellow.While Amazon doesn't state the price for the set of six 12" ECR4Kids chairs, the price for the set of 14" chairs is $131.99 and $143.99 for the 16" set -- so I assume the price for the set of six 12" chairs is in the neighborhood of $120. You'll have to decide if this price is too high for a set of six chairs (and if you really need six chairs) that only have a recommended "age window" of five years.

We needed a specific size cork board and couldn't seem to find it in a regular cork board.  At least not a reasonably priced one anyway.  So we got the the idea to buy these square cork tiles and just make our own custom cork board.  The mounting tape included with these tiles isn't that great -- and they don't give you anywhere near enough of it to stick these tiles down securely.  So we just staple gunned them to the wall.  Problem is, they're not very thick at all -- maybe an eighth of an inch at best -- so push pins and thumbtacks quickly bottom out and hit the wall behind the cork tile.  It doesn't make for a great cork board if you can't really stick the pushpins in far enough to hold anything securely.  So we decided to make a smaller cork board and double layered the tiles.  This makes the cork board plenty thick, but it doesn't lay as nicely flat against the wall; the tiles bow out in the middle, even with extra long staples holding them in.  It works well enough, but it's not as good as we hoped it would be.  The idea doesn't translate well, so these tiles are just mediocre at best.

The printer I previously used (HP PhotoSmart 2575 All-in-One Printer / Copier / Scanner) was working perfectly well for me but lacked FAX functionality so given the chance to snag one of these All-in-Ones, I did just that.The Epson WorkForce 635 is a nice printer but compared to the 2575 from HP I was immediately struck by just how much bigger and bulkier this printer is.  Actually, even compared to an older HP OfficeJet All-in-One (HP Officejet 5610 All-in-One Printer/Fax/Scanner/Copier (Q7311A#ABA)) that I also have and use in my household (it was the primary FAX machine in the house for years) this unit is bigger and bulkier.  For me the size and bulk makes this All-in-One a bit more difficult to find a good place to station it within my somewhat limited desk space.On the plus side, this printer has bult-in Wi-Fi networking that does help to lessen the issues with where the printer can be placed, though you'd still have to find a place to plug the printer in so depending on where your electrical outlets are it may not be as convenient as that sounds.I guess I should back up a bit here too and note that one frustration I was immediately struck with upon opening the box that the printer comes in is that it ships with two large styrofoam pieces wrapped completely around either end of the printer.  Unlike other companies (for example TV manufacturers) that use the styrofoam around only the corners of the devices they are packaging, Epson (or their suppliers/shippers) uses full-sized pieces of styrofoam that make the printer a chore to remove from the packaging.  Once you flip the box over and "dump" the contents out things are fine, but you'll likely curse whomever choose the foam material specs for not going with something that would have been easier to remove the device from.Once the printer has been removed from the box the setup is fairly simple.  Remove the tape that was applied and securing the various items during the shipping process then open up the lid to gain access to the area where the ink trays/cartridges will be installed.  The ink trays/cartridges are simple enough to install as well.  Again remove the protective tape from each and snap them in matching the arrangement shown in pictures in the quick install/setup documentation.Software installation was also simple though time consuming, and additional updates should be planned for as the software on the supplied discs may be (and was for me) old relative to what is available from the manufacturer's website.  During the software install process you should also plan to be monitoring your screen as you'll be prompted about allowing access through firewalls as necessary.  If you miss the prompts and/or answer NO you will find that you won't get the latest software updates until running the updater software again (and answering correctly) later.In terms of printing, copying, and the other functions I have no issue with this printer.  It is reasonably speedy though it is hard to say it is really that much faster than other competitors (despite marketing jargon that may be applied).If space is not an issue in your home office then I don't think I'd really have any issues with this device, and even then comparitively speaking this device isn't really that different than others in its same category.

And, so when I found the Paper Mate Mates Mechanical Pencils on Amazon, I was willing to give them a shot. First, they are as fat as a first grade pencil -- they certainly takes some getting used to there! The barrel, however is triangular in shape and rests easily in the hand in spite of its girth. Would be a plus to those with arthritic hands. The 1.3mm lead is a bit thicker than I care for, leaning more toward the .5 or .7 ordinarily, but for taking notes, scrawling grocery lists and that sort of writing, it is fine. If you use a stylus much on a tablet or your phone, then you will be right at home with the thicker line. The crowning glory, literally, of these pencils though is the eraser -- it resides on top as it does on every pencil, but it is LONG and it is hearty. There is a lot of eraser there. The lead, of course advances when you push down briskly on the eraser, but it requires enough force that it doesn't advance the lead when you don't want it to happen.  I like the muted colors; I like the pencils.Paper Mate Mates 1.3mm Mechanical Pencils, 5 Yellow Barrel Mechanical Pencils (1862167)

We used this at my husband's desk.  He is an artist who spends long hours working at his computer.  The ergonomic design of this has helped him a great deal with tiredness in his arms and hand and with alleviating the pain in his lower back, as he is now sitting properly in his seat while using his keyboard.  This is an amazing product.The instruction sheet for assembly and installation is entirely visual, consisting of line drawings, directional indicators, and exploded views for each of the 12 steps.  There are no verbal instructions or clarifications.  Initially, this looked dangerous but each step was adequately explained and each of the steps was logical and clear.There are still ways to get hurt.  Care should be given when removing the cardboard piece that separates the moving parts of the arm mechanism.  The spring in this device is very powerful and can cause the arm parts to snap together, becoming an effective "mouse trap" for fingers.The adhesive strip on the top side of the attachment rail is strong enough to hold the rail in position under the table/desk top while screws are being attached.  This was greatly helpful although it was important to position the rail in the correct position the first time.  It was also helpful to have a carpenter's square to assure that the rail was perpendicular to the front edge of the table/desk.All of the other parts were also easy to install.  Attachment of the front bumper bar that keeps the arm mechanism on the rail was straightforward.  Be sure that the bracket overlaps the end of the rails, and that the flat vertical side faces the front of the table/desk.  The guides for positioning keyboard and mouse cables are of two types.  One is a clip that slides onto the adjustable arm that supports the keyboard.  The other two have adhesive backing and may be positioned in any convenient location depending upon desk configuration.  Step 8 illustrates suggested location on the arm mechanism, but these might also attach to the under side of the table/desk.  The mouse pad may be attached on either right or left side of the keyboard platform, depending on preference and or "handedness."My husband measured all of these parts for me because this item does put you back away from your desk a distance and you need to have the space for it.  The keyboard platform may be adjusted for height, for distance from table/desk edge, and for rotation in relation to the edge of the table/desk.  In the "closed" position, the platform stows completely beneath the front edge of the table/desk with the bottom of the platform approximately 3.5" lower than desk top.  When positioned in its highest position,  the platform for keyboard is 2.5" below the desk top and the mouse caddy is 1.5" below desk top.  This makes the entire device much lower than you would think, but somehow this causes less strain on the lower back after hours at the computer.  When it is in this position, the keyboard platform extends 12.5" in front of the desk edge.  The greatest extension in the upper position places the front edge of the keyboard platform 16.5" in front of the desk edge.  In lowest position, the keyboard extends only 10" in front of the desk edge.  The mouse caddy may be adjusted in relation to the keyboard by positioning the sliding attachment and also by rotating the caddy.  The 8.75" diameter of the caddy seems adequate for the majority of mouse movements.The keyboard platform is sturdy, and the wrist support padding at the forward edge allows for good support.  Non-skid pads keep the keyboard in position, even when the platform is tilted away from level.  The angle of the platform may be adjusted to elevate the wrist pad above the normal position, but not lower than normal.  The Keyboard manager is versatile and allows for a good range of user adjustment.  It supports the keyboard securely and affords excellent wrist and arm support.  The mouse caddy is conveniently located, and also feels very secure in use.Overall, this product is well engineered, and installs in a straightforward process.  The design and the quality of materials suggest that this device will provide good service over time with minimal maintenance.

**First Impressions:**This thing is HUGE, easily bigger than a carryon bag, it looks like it ate 3 regular sized printers.  I had to clear everything off of my dresser so that I had a place to put it.  If you have a small apartment make sure you can actually dedicate the space.  (Also 13x19 paper looks like a gag gift the first time you see it.) If you do have the space though... the Pro-10 is worth it.I know the exact dimensions are already on the web site but keep in mind when choosing a location that (ideally) you want 10 inches behind the printer and 17 inches in front of the printer so that you can fully extend the trays (these can be over open air).Other initial notes:1. There is a handy slot underneath to keep the tray for printing on DVD-Rs.2. This thing ways almost 50 pounds and has to be attached to the computer via USB for setup, so if you plan to keep it somewhere far away from your computer bring it to the computer first and then move it to its final destination, you don't want to have to lug it back and forth any more than you have to.**Now on to the printing:**Many people have mentioned that this printer provides either near lab level prints or lab level prints.  I would argue that this printer, if used correctly is capable of producing prints that are better than you could get from most labs.Why?Complete control over all aspects of the print.What do I mean by "if used correctly?"Ultimately a great print will have both great print quality (something labs and this printer have in common) and will perfectly match your intentions for color, contrast, and brightness.  Even if you use a calibration tool (I use aDatacolor Spyder4Pro S4P100 Colorimeter for Display Calibration) keep everything in the same color space, and use proof previews in either Lightroom or Photoshop, you will often discover that what you see on the screen doesn't quite match what you get in prints.  If you are printing from a lab this usually means you are stuck with what the results (hey they're "pretty close" right?).If however, you to have a printer like this one, you can completely eliminate this problem.  As the title says, practice makes perfect.  Print the picture as a smaller analogue on a piece of 8.5x11 paper, adjust the printer settings to correct for any differences between the print and the screen and then try again.  When you feel you are getting perfect prints, save the settings as a preset (I use lightroom for this but the canon plugin allows for essentially the same thing) and use it as a starting point the next time.  Assuming you are using the same type of paper you should get near perfect results every time once this process is complete.Yah I know this seems like a waste of ink and paper, but most people aren't considering this printer because they want to print more 4x6s of their family.  They are looking to make high quality prints to either sell or frame and hang on their walls, and in either of those instances the Canon Pro-10 will allow you to get not just lab quality prints, but perfect prints.I highly recommend this printer.

Features, it's got features:  You already know that this printer has the ability to produce large format prints (13" X 19", +.).  Actually, all the features are listed and I would just be wasting your time to reiterate.  I'm just going to tell what the printer is made for, how it accomplishes this, and my impressions of its performance.The Epson  WF-7620 is manufactured to meet the requirements of the business community.  Most ink jet printers are made to excel in either photo printing or text and graphics, not in both.  This may have been the driving force that created a need for color laser printers.  Laser printers are fine, except that they are expensive, both with the hardware and the cost per page to print.  Laser printers use quite a bit of electricity.  The WF-7620 is rated as an Energy Star device.With improvements in printer technology (They call it PRECISIONCORE) the WF-7620 prints text, graphics and photographs really fast and really sharp,  With only a tiny bit of  hype, really sharp..  (The speed of this printer is demonstrated on YouTube.  Just key in the name and model.)  The sharpness of text and graphics may be a tiny bit overstated, but most people probably won't be able to see the difference.The manufacturer also makes the claim that the cost of printing per page is 40% lower than laser printers.  They won't like me saying this, but as far as that goes, the cost p page can be further reduced by using other brands of ink cartridges.  I've had very good luck with these.  But if I had needed any service, my warrantee from Canon would have be void for m using them.Some minor criticisms come to mind:  It's big and heavy.  Not everyone will have enough space for it.  And it makes noise.  But that is all the small stuff I can think of.  Oh yea, their is some very important big stuff: OEM ink cartridges are not yet available.  Epson's ink cartridges, and photo paper, cost per color print is way too high.  It may be cheaper than color laser photo prints by 40%, but it's still way to high.  I'll have to use OEM photo paper and ink.  Also, I have had some paper jams using 4" X 6" photo paper. Maybe the Polaroid paper is too thin but their is no problem running through one at a time.I'm still glad to get the WF-7620.  It prints fast except when printing photo's at maximum resolution.  But I've shown both standard printing and High resolution. and most people I've shown the prints to, see little or no difference. But I can see the difference.  Standard definition is more like that from a retail store.I have the printer wired straight to my desktop computer, so I can't talk about wireless use, sorry.  To install, I just ran the included CD and installed it to my computer running Windows 8.1, and without any problems.  Minutes later they updated the software.  I had a chance to print a favorite picture before update and afterwards.  The update improved contrast and solved the slightly garish appearance of the earlier color print.  For me, the really greatest thing about the WF-7620 is that it actually beats out my expensive Canon 9000 Mark II.  It's faster and prints photographs better..  The prints are an improvement in accurate color rendering, contrast, and sharpness.  I have had the Canon  Pro 9000 for a couple years, and I have always been proud of the photographs printed on it.  I still like my old Canon printer better than most others I've seen.  But viewing prints side by side, on high definition, the W-7620 easily wins.  But standard definition is still slightly better than my Canon Pro 9000.  Epson seems to have taken the high ground in printer technology.  I will certainly recommend this printer to my photo hobbyist friends.

From the moment I opened up my Canon image FORMULA P-215 I was in absolute awe. Before going on, let me just state for the record that I am a "gadget guy" all the way and have an entire office full of sweet equipment, but as far as scanners go, this one really takes the cake.Here's my breakdown:Size:This thing is tiny! It sits about a little over an inch tall, three inches deep, and 11 inches wide. This can easily be plopped right into an attaché without adding any more bulk than a 300 page book. Miraculously, even though it is so small, it feels really well built and sturdy.  And while we're talking about looks, even though I am a function over form guy, this think is darn right sexy. Can a scanner be sexy? If you see this thing in person, you'll see what I mean.Installation:This scanner does not even need to have any software installed to run on PC or Mac. I don't own a Mac, but on the PC I just plugged it in to my USB 3.0 port and a pop-up came, I clicked the scanner file (which is located WITHIN the scanner), and the software was up on my screen in less than half a minute. Next, I walked over to my wife's computer and plugged it in there with the dual USB 2.0 connection and it was up and running in the same amount of time. Although not necessary, this dual connection will allow you to scan at high-speed (like USB 3.0) on a USB 2.0 computer. In either configuration, there are NO POWER CORDS! This means that when you want to use it at work or at a client's location, you don't have to get on your knees to plug it in. Also note: this thing doesn't even have a power button! It just turns on when you open it up to scan! Brilliant!Software:When running the software built into the scanner, you can have it run in full-auto mode, or change all the settings to your liking. Settings include color mode, page size, DPI, skip blank pages, straighten skewed images, rotate to match text orientation, and even more if you want to use the advanced settings.  You can also save the file in the following types:  PDF, TIFF, JPG,  PPTX (Powerpoint), or BMP. Also note that this scanner automatically uses OCR (optical character recognition) so that your PDFs are immediately searchable from within. ( In fact, in Windows you can download a small patch from Microsoft and make all your PDFs content searchable right from Windows Expolorer.)Performance:I scanned things like crazy to put this thing through the paces. The claim that it can scan a 20-page stack is indeed accurate. The scans look fantastic and the OCR was accurate as well.Comparison to my Fujitsu ScanSnap s1500This unit, which is approximately half the price of my Fujitsu, compares favorably to it in terms of ease of use and output. The only differences (for me) are that the Canon scanner is a tad slower and doesn't hold enough sheets. If I wasn't such a heavy scanner-user then I would definitely switch over to the Canon because of its small footprint, but as it stands, I will definitely be using this as my go-to travel scanner.Additional Software:This scanner also comes with CaptureOnTouch software, which is a more permanent solution for using this scanner as a desk scanner (as opposed to a portable on-location scanner). Also note that you can download the latest software/drivers from the Canon website including: ScanToEvernote, ScanToGoogle, and ScanToSharePoint.Final thought:All in all, this scanner gets my HIGHEST RECOMMENDATION. It is a 5-star product in every way.

I'll go into more detail about what's superior about Avery below, but first, regarding this size --These will fit three lines of 10 point Arial, or one line of something bigger. I use them regularly at work for their intended purpose, and I also use them at home to label stuff going into the freezer. They do stay on even when frozen, but are easiest to remove while still frozen. If they get wet before I try to remove the label, some adhesive has to be scrubbed off.I doubt Avery matters for the freezer application, but if you want a professional result for more traditional uses, Avery and name brand printer toner are a must.I've tried several different generic brands -- from all three big office retailers -- and the letters get smeared or flake off when applying the labels. Add generic toner, and the problem gets so bad that the printing becomes almost illegible. With generic toner these smear a little bit, but with the name brand toner (I've used these in both HPs and Canons), there's no problem. The generic labels might seem a lot cheaper, but these are well worth the extra dough.As far as True Block goes, well, I don't really care, but it does work. The labels have an opaque backing between the paper and adhesive, which doesn't allow anything below it to show through. I usually just remove the label if I'm going to re-use a file folder, because I'm just going to covering up the damaged area with another label anyway. True Block seems more useful for shipping applications than for file folders. I don't know whether or not Avery is selling these labels in a non-True Block form, but if so, it may be worth looking closely at price.

I usually dread laminating objects at the office. I regularly use a GBC Brand laminator to mint items like parking, media and access passes that need waterproofing. There's nothing more aggravating than having a laminator: a)take 20 minutes to heat up, b)not work well on the first try, and c)having to process a job twice. This Fellowes brand laminator actually works well.For me, the Fellowes' Mars 125 model is a breeze to use compared to the GBC. It is a 12.5 inch laminator, which is easy to pick up and handle.(There are inner handles on the sides of the laminator).This laminator heated up faster than the GBC one! It took about 5 minutes for it to warm up (although the directions indicates it could take as long as 8 minutes for the laminator to heat up). An indicator light turns from red to green when its ready to work. Once heated up, the laminator stayed hot.I was pleased -- the initial go around -- that it laminated documents well the first time with the Fellowes machine. I used 8 x 12" sheets of paper (and 3 mil pouches) similar to materials that I laminate at the office.The machine was much quieter than the GBC model too (although there is a slight whirring buzz as its heating up). Once laminated, the documents (at the far end) were cool to the touch. Another surprise. I'm not sure if this is the case with all models, but for me, my processed documents remained cool.Documents also laminated much quicker with the Fellowes brand (the speed is around 11" per minute.)  I had no problem laminating smaller objects (like a several paper id cards) .Those looking to laminate items that are 8 x 12 (with 5 mil) pouches should probably seek a different model better suited to your needs. This Fellowes model does laminate 5 mil pouches, but only for documents that are index-card size or smaller. They make special pouches they make for this, so if you're seeking to laminate say a social security card with thicker lamination, then you can use the small, pouch-sized ones they sell.My only critique is that I wish there was a feeder area (similar to ones found on printers where paper can lay) to place the laminated item on while laminating (instead of hand feeding the objects. Another note, laminator pouches are not included with the laminator, so you'll have to purchase separately. Other than that I recommend this product.

Who does not get the mailing tape all tangled up and rolled on itself, or pick it up only to find it completely sealed upon itself?  Oh, I love Scotch clear mailing tape, but it is really such a royal pain.  I always turn down a corner (just a little, teeny bit) when I finish using it so I can get it started next time.  But my husband can't stand the turned-down corner.  He gets frustrated every time he sees it, and every time he uses the mailing tape, he makes sure it's sealed tightly back onto the roll.  Grr!  And it will not stay on the dispenser, so we've had a mailing tape standoff for years.With the old stuff, if you don't turn down a corner, or if the tape slaps back down before you can turn it down, you're going to spend some time trying to get it started.  You have to find the edge, which you can't see if you're over 40, and peel with your fingernails (or some kind of tool if you're smart enough to think of it ahead of time) to start it.  Then, half the time, once you do get some peeled up, it splits and you wind up with a little hunk of tape in one hand and a roll of completely sealed-on-itself tape in the other.  This cycle repeats until the gods decide to have mercy on you.  Eventually you get the job done, and well.  But it's a hassle.I pulled and teared piece after piece off this tape.  Yes, you do have to find the edge.  But it isn't as hard to pry up.  The tape tears easily, unlike, say, a bag of Fritos!  I tried it with both hands.  This tape is ambidextrous!  It's so easy!  Now, if you have any kind of "-itis," you may need to use scissors still, but I was prepared to do battle and this tape COOPERATED.  I don't see how this tape can be as strong as the old stuff, but I don't have a test lab.  It seems plenty strong, and I don't notice a significant difference in stickiness, either.It's a miracle!  The standoff is over.  Henceforth, we'll buy this instead of the dispenser tape, and life will be a little more peaceful for both of us.  And we won't be cussing at the mailing tape any more.

NO MORE SEWINGBeacon Fabri-Tak does an excellent job of bonding fabrics, without soaking through.  For guys, its a Godsend---no more stapling torn pants pockets or hemming pant-legs with duck-tape.  I've used Fabri-Tak to hem pants, to apply patches to holes in work-clothes, to apply uniform patches, even to make up straps and belts with webbing and plastic buckles.  For repair patches, it works better than iron-on patches.  The only real major limit is seams which come under alot of stress, such as pants inseams (i.e., crotches) (including zippers), or children's play clothes.TACKINGAnother use is to make difficult sewing jobs easier.  For example, you can "tack" material together for a rough fitting, adjust to a tighter fit, and then sew the seams.  Or you can assemble a garment with Fabri-Tac, and then sew it easier (i.e., with simple stitches rather than multiple rows or complicated stitches).FOR COSTUMESAlthough no other reviewers mention it, Fabri-Tac is ideal for assembling costumes which will only be worn a few hours and probably never be washed.FOR UNIFORM OR DECORATIVE PATCHES1) Mark the target area.  I suggest using a soft pencil (or water soluble felt-tip marker) to mark underneath the edges of the patches (where the marks won't show) For round patches, mark the orientation, i.e., the exact top and/or exact bottom.  Do NOT wash the garment immediately after applying patches.2) Apply a light bead of glue 3/16 to 1/4" from the edge around the circumference, and then thin parallel lines about 3/8" apart across the interior which corresponding to embroidered parts of the patch.  Some patches are virtually completely filled with embroidery, some aren't---do NOT apply Fabri-Tak to large (> 3/8" in diameter)unbroidered areas, or the patch may "pucker".3) Align and press hard enough to spread out the glue.  Place a heavy object (such as a brick or several thick books) on top of the patch (and underneath if you need to make a flat surface), and leave it for an hour.  If you do this alot, then squares of thin plywood the size of the patches (on the top and bottom) and spring clamps will do the trick and allow you to apply several patches at a time.WARNING--patches applied this way may be impossible to remove after a week---if the patches are temporary, don't be so diligent, a light bead around the circumference is enough, or better yet, sew temporary patches on.TIP ON USEIt REALLY dries fast.  Maybe after a minute you can still tack things together temporarily, but you won't have a permanent bond.  If you want a permanent bond, apply to a small section and quickly press the fabric pieces together, and hold for at least 5 seconds, before moving on to the next section.  If you can, clamp the section behind you as you go--clothespins will usually do,  but spring clamps with flat pivitong jaws are better--Denali 14-Piece Spring Clamp Assortment.  Press the fabric pretty hard--that gets the glue into the fibers.  When you are done, go back and press the fabric together again.GENERAL PRINCIPALS OF GLUING ANYTHING WITH ANY GLUE1) The strength of the bond is proportional to the area.  That means, spread the glue uniformly over the whole surface.2) Although counter-intuitive, the THINNER the layer of glue the stronger the bond.  Especially with other types of glues, it often helps to use a spatula (such as an old plastic credit card) or popsicle stick to spread a then uniform layer of glue.  With Fabri-Tac and some other glues/situations, you can apply a thin bead, and then squeeze it out into a thin uniform layer by pressing or clamping the peices together.  Light clamping, or using weights for the same purpose, until the glue sets improves any gluing job.3) Regardless of the instructions, all glues take days, even weeks, to reach full strength.  So, it is best to set aside garments repaired with Fabri-Tac in a warm ventilated place for a couple of days before use---and NEVER wash garments immediately after repairing them.THIN ON THINApplying thin fabric (such as ribbon, or a large area of thin felt), especially on thin fabric is a challenge.  Mark the target (see above).  Cut the ribbon to its final length.  Then work fast.  Apply the glue to the full length of the ribbon.  Apply the ribbon to the target.  Place a thick piece of paper over the ribbon and burnish.  That means to rub hard. It is best to burnish in two or more stages, 1) quickly to get the whole ribbon burnished down, 2) repeat slower, and 3) repeat even slower.  A small pastry roller is good for the first stage--but you can use your fingers or a spatula (don't forget the paper).  For the last stage, an old thick credit card works well---push hard with the edge, bending the card, but keep it moving, in multiple short strokes(don't forget the paper).  For items which will not be washed glue sticks will probably work betterAvery Glue Stic, 0.26 oz, Pack of 6, (98095).  For the most difficult projects, use spray glue.PREVENTING LEAKING AND THICKENINGMy experience is that the bottle inevitably falls over on its side, and leaks.  Tightening the cap doesn't seem to help.  The same problem causes the glue to thicken over time.  The simple solution to this to store the bottle in a tall glass bottle.  A 6 1/2" tall olive jar is perfect.

First of all, I like the packaging of this item.  The individual plastic sheets are all separated by a very thin piece of tissue paper.  If you've ever had to deal with these plastic covers sticking together due to static cling, you can really appreciate this. I bought this to replace a 10 year old shredder that broke. Overall I like it. My old shredder had a pull out bin that inevitably left a mess of shredded paper on the floor. With this one, it's fairly easy to keep the mess contained. My only wish is that the base were on wheels. Also, it's pretty loud. Not a big deal for occasional shredding, but I think this would drive you nuts if you used it all the time in an office setting.

This is a paper cutter suitable for small projects. While it works as intended, I found some limitations that detract from its usefulness. As such, there are a few things to keep in mind when using it that will make it a less frustrating device.First off, this is a small and portable paper slicer, and this is good for my needs as it can be moved all over the house. It can be used on most flat surfaces so moving from a work table to the kitchen counter is not a problem. It is lightweight and easy to move. Now, because it's a lightweight and light-duty paper slicer, it should be used with care - I don't think it will be hard to break if used like a heavy-duty gadget.It slices paper by use of a sliding blade that works very well, though I have found that it works best for single sheets of standard weight (20-24 lb.) paper. When I fed a light envelope through it and tried to cut it, it did cut but it required much more effort and it had a tendency to stop the blade from moving without applying some extra force. It was also difficult to hold it straight. For very lightweight paper such as some photo papers, it helps a lot to have some way to hold the edge outside of the slider because the paper tends to bunch and wrinkle instead of slicing properly. It can be worked around but it requires thinking about it BEFORE trying to cut.This is not a bad paper cutter. It works well and it is priced right. It is a light-duty device, though, and some projects require a little extra effort and thought beforehand, but used properly it should last for a long time and serve well.

The Scotch Pop-Up Tape Refillable Deskgrip Dispenser is a good product I will continue to use.  The dispenser is easy to load and the tape is truly invisible when applied.  The way it "grips" to the desk without a suction cup or adhesive, is pretty cool.  With no resistance at all, you can slide the dispenser across the desk to wherever you need it without breaking contact with the desk.  The down-side of the sliding feature is if you don't hold on to the dispenser or pull the tape straight up it slides away from you in the direction you are pulling.  Also, the purple/pink color is pretty bright and may be a little too eye-catching/youthful for certain work environments.

This is pretty much as you would expect, three fairly tall stacks of post-it notes in a fruit motif, the paper on top is colored in a solid hue, the fruit pattern only appears on the side. Like others, I've tried those carpet pads that are supposed to keep rugs from slipping but was never satisfied. This stuff is great! I don't like hunting for pens, either, but solve that problem by gluing strips of flat magnets to the back of a few ballpoint pens so they stay put on my refrigerator doors. My medicine cabinet door is made of metal, so I stuck this inside and now use it to hold my tweezers, eyelash curler, nail file and my contact lens case (when not in use).It dawned on me there are some other great uses for it, too:- Attach it to the front of your washer to hold collar stays and clothing embellishments that need to be removed before laundering. These storage boxes are very functional.  They easily hold stacks of papers, documents, photos, etc.  The handles make them easy to carry.  And they don't look bad.  I recommend them over the metal file cabinets, especially if the documents to be stored are not sensitive.

This product is very easy to use. You can set up and start using even without looking at the directions. I did have to read the directions for the meaning of some of the buttons. You can adjust height, width and add symbols, etc. I have been wanting a labeler for awhile and read that this one was easy, cheap and recommended. That did it for me.I have to say as some others have, it does go through batteries. It takes four AAA batteries and after 15 labels that I printed all at one time, it needed new batteries. I'm going to invest in some rechargable ones for this since I already have a charger for them anyway.This is perfect to label DVDs, file folders and we are building a new house and for awhile at least I'm going to label the light switches so I will know what turns what on. I already knew I loved these pens, but these cases make them even better.  I have the cascading 100-pen set which collapses into a carrying case; however that case requires some room to open as it's more of an artistic display (and the lid can be a pain to put on and take off).  The cases in this set are much more convenient and compact, though also displaying the pens so the user can easily pick the one he or she wants.  The cases fold closed and lock shut so they can be easily carried by the handle on top of each case.The pens themselves write smoothly.  The set contains a mix of colors and styles, including glitter ink and fluorescent ink.  There are many different colors, some of which are duplicated.  I do love the pens; I wish my set didn't include duplicates of certain colors, such as the brownish-orange colors (I have maybe 6 overall of the one shade between this set and the 100 set, yet only 4 of each blue, green, purple, and others).  There are already several shades of these weird colors--they just aren't that great colors.  I also wish they had a glitter version of the gold-ish colored pen.  I have noticed the ink seems to go down rather quickly (compared to normal pens), though I have yet to use up an entire pen.Nevertheless, the pens are still awesome and I highly recommend them.  They write smoothly and do not smear easily (the ink dries quickly, though not instantly), and the color variety is the best I've seen in a pen set.  It sort of reminds me of years ago when Crayola came out with the box of 64 crayons--you just couldn't pick which color to start with!

This is a good scanner for the price and much better than any all in one scanner/printer can offer.  Sadly I was looking for a photo scanner and this didn't quite cut the performance I had envisioned.  After giving away my Officejet 6110 that did a horrible scan job on photo, magazine, I got another all-in-oneCanon PIXMA MP560 Wireless Inkjet All-In-One Photo Printer (3747B002).  The spec of scanner for the MP 560 is basically theCanon LiDE100 Color Image Scanner (2923B002).  I got the V30 base on the high review, but I guess no one was very picky about photo scan or compared different scanner models or brands.Performance:For the price, this maybe one of the best overall scanner out there.  Scanning document, PDF, magazine there isn't much diffidence to the Canon MP560, where I do see quite an improvement is the photo scan.  Scanning at 600dpi on the V30 and MP560 or Lide100 spec there is a notable different in image qualities.  Epson photo scan was not as washout as the Canon just like how the advertisement of the V30 sensor 2 pictures appear.  I also noticed the V30 image was a tad sharper.  I saw very little different between V30 600 and 1200 dpi, there is a quite a different in color depth when bumping 8, 16,24 and 48 bits.  The dust removing feature is worth it and this is a must feature when scanning at high dpi, which pick up more detail.  If it is turn-off it makes the picture look very cheap.  The color restoration is nice, but has some side effects.  The overall image is more balance and a tad sharper, but what it does is it bleach everything to be more white, so skin tone looks more pale then before.  Now I am going to compare the V30 to my standard scan in photo with a HP 3010 I did at Kits Camera.  HP 6-color scan is way more vibrant in color range or color saturation, making the photo scan seem to pop out more.  The image looks more like the original photo taken.  Skin tone is almost perfect and I get less grainy image in the face on the HP 3010.  The only thing that V30 does better it produces sharper detail or deep of field, my eyes prefer HP much more.Design/ Feature.I did like the built design of the V30.  It is compact and very sturdy.  Modern looking with easy to access buttons.  The USB and power outlet is oddly place (front right side) but wasn't a big deal for me.  The LED scan was fast.  It is a little noisier then the quite Canon MP560.  Software isn't bad either.  I found the scanning option on the Epson to be much more then the Canon, but liked the Canon interface more.  I own Corel Draw, Photoshop and got paint.net (free download) so I didn't don't care much for photo-editing software that comes with these scanners.  The ABBYY Fine reader is an interesting OCE scan where it can pull texts from a scanning document.Overall I am impressed with the V30, but decide to returned it since I didn't get the photo scan I wanted base on my experience with the HP3010, so I will be looking into the new HP 4010 orHP Scanjet G4050 Photo Scanner (L1957A#B1H)with 6-colors.  The Epson V500 doesn't seem to have much of an improvement over the V30 or V300, and the V700 is out of my price range.  I have avoided HP scanner base on the bad result of the Officejet 6110 and decided to try out other brands like Epson and Canon.  For now the Canon MP560 can do all the documents and lower quality scans fine till I find the perfect photo scanner.

There's a reason 3M's Scotch tape sells so well--it does the job perfectly with no muss and no fuss (and the price is reasonable). If you're doing any kind of painting project, home improvement task, or crafty thing, then spend a little more to buy Scotch High Performance Masking Tape. It has the perfect amount of tack to stick to most surfaces without damaging them, and the backing is strong enough to allow you to remove it in one piece. If your time is worth anything, then those two simple features--never a given with other masking tape brands--are worth the slight extra cost. There's a reason this is an iconic product, folks--it just works so darned well!

I ship out a lot of books and I'm usually cutting up sheets of paper, trying hard to keep it neat.  NOW, I don't have to worry with all of that.  Makes packages look just that much better.  I've also found other uses such as labeling bags I stick in the freezer, and putting the kids names on their plastic cups and water bottles when we're on the go.  It's so much better than just using a sharpie which sometimes isn't as permanent or dark enough for me.
What can you say about index cards? Index cards are index cards, but these are usually a lot cheaper than what you will find in an office supply store. They get the job done!

We needed a corded phone to use during winter power outages here in rural northern Vermont.  I tried a couple of the cheapo Radio Shack specials and they were absolutely unsatisfactory with small cramped buttons, unlit keypads, and poor volume.  I went through the reviews and settled on this AT&T; handset and it's worked out very, very well.PROS:- The handset is sizeable and you can actually get a decent grip on it.- The ear receiver is larger than other handsets and actually fits right on the ear. This doesn't sound like much, but it makes a difference in a noisy atmosphere.- The buttons are good sized and light well enough to see in dim lighting.- The volume is adjustable and even though I am slightly hard of hearing, it is more than adequate without turning it all the way up.- The price! The price! The price!  It's a bargain!CONS:- The base is light for a desk-top type phone. Got to be careful when you yank it around - it will fly off the counter. (Alternately, it does mount on the wall.)- The handset cord is too short. I read this in the other reviews so I did order a 12-foot stretchable replacement handset cord with the phone and I'm glad I did.  If you buy this phone, you should too.All in all, it's a very, very good phone.  Good quality at a great price.

The first time I plugged this, I thought it was a broken one.  The green LED that supposed to light up when it is ready took a long time to come on.  Then it started smoking and a burning rubber smell emanates from the top loader.  If it has been plugged for some time and you have not feed anything to it, the machine may be too hot.  The manual suggest to feed a bond paper to cool it off, and so I did that.  Right after the green LED lights up.  I fed the 3mil 8 x 10 with some business cards and photos.  Came up perfect.  Ever since, we never have any problem using it although we never used it for more than 30 minutes at a time.  The machine gets hot and if left on for a long time might not be good as most of the parts are made of plastic.There are only 2 parts.  The machine itself and the top loader tray.  They can make it shipped in one piece except they will need a bigger box.I bought a box of 100 pcs 4" x 6" 5 mil pouches from a less known brand.  We are happy that the result is fantastic as well.  No edges come out undone - completely sealed.Great laminator for kids projects and more.  We are having fun with this one.

I touched Setup and selected “8 X 10 on 8.5 X 11.”  I set this as my default.  When I printed a photo, it came out with a border that made sizing and cutting for a frame extremely easy.The easiest, most entertaining method for printing photographs was from my new HP Pavilion TouchSmart 14-inch Sleekbook. I am very familiar with all types of packing and mailing tapes from working in factories for decades. The last factory I worked in produced cosmetics and we shipped packages to retailers all over the world. We always used Scotch brand tapes, as we couldn't risk a cheaper tape that couldn't hold the weight of dozens of heavy fragile glass perfume bottles.  Scotch tapes are extremely dependable with their durable plastic, strong adhesive and waterproof quality.When it comes to boxes that weighed over 150 pounds, we always used Scotch filament tape, as it is the only tape strong enough to keep such a heavy box from splitting open. The filament is made from fiberglass and it is really indestructible, as far as keeping the box sealed in transport. You need a really sharp blade cutter to open the box, cutting through the fiberglass filament, as it is so strong. The only thing stronger than filament tape, is Bi-directional filament tape, as now the fiberglass is running in two directions. We used this Scotch Bi-Directional Filament tape not only to seal our heaviest packages, but to actually tape the heavy glass filled boxes to the wood pallets. Nothing moved an inch with this tape!For repairing wood pallets, we actually used this tape to clamp two pieces of wood together to drill a new screw in place. I don't know of any tape strong enough that can do that. The tape was also used to keep pipes from banging- the pipe was wrapped in this tape and then fastened  to the wall. This lasted for months, showing it's total waterproof capability. I didn't realize that I would ever need a tape this heavy for my own personal use, until one day when I took some boxes of books to sell at a local used book store. I had 4 boxes- all heavy and 3 of the four boxes bottomed out with my regular packing tape. Of course, the books all got their corners crushed falling to the floor, leaving me with way less value than if the books hadn't been damaged.That's when I decided to invest the higher price just to keep a roll of this heavy duty bi-directional filament tape around the house. I found out that it sticks to not only cardboard, but plastic, metal and wood with it's strong adhesive. For shipping or packing heavy items, it's a must have and it's waterproof design comes in handy for so many things.  Having a tape around the house that can hold a box together that contains super heavy weight,  that can clamp wood together just like a vice grip and keep pipes from banging is much more than just a super strong tape, this tape can actually be used as a tool.  I'll never carry heavy boxes of books again without this tape. Scotch Bi-Directional Filament Tape is just as wonderful at home as it is in the factory where I worked.
I think this is the best tape for your money and it's the kind I always buy.  It's virtually invisible upon use and it's not too expensive.  I won't use any other tape for gift wrapping.

I am extremely pleased with the HP Officejet 8500 Wireless All-In-One Printer. It is a full-featured and very capable ink-jet printer that should fulfill most office printing, faxing, scanning and copying chores with ease. Of particular note is its wireless and duplex capability.Setup of the printer was fairly straightforward with one exception. I have a home network of mixed computers; desktops, laptops, Apple and PC. HP software installation went off without a hitch on all the computers except the older G4 iMac. This particular computer did not have an Apple Airport Extreme card installed. Instead, it had a USB wireless card. The HP installer software was not able to "see" the printer over the network and therefore was not able to complete the software installation rendering the printer useless with the iMac. By using a USB cable, I was able to complete the software installation on the iMac, but once the USB cable was disconnected, all advanced functions of the printer were not useable since the computer was not "seen" over the network by the HP software on the iMac. A call to HP did not resolve this issue. My solution was to get rid of the USB wireless card and purchase an Apple Airport Extreme card. Once I did that, I was able to run the HP installer again and complete the installation. All is well with the iMac and wireless functions now.The printer has a touchscreen screen that is very easy to use generally, but the menus can be a bit confusing at first. The various memory card slots that are on the front of the printer make printing photos from memory cards a breeze. The duplex feature is awesome and saves paper. I have not had any problems with paper jams so far and think that duplex is one of the features that really makes this a great office printer. I also own a Brother MFC-490CW, Brother MFC-490CW Color Inkjet Multifunction Printer which is also a wireless all-in-one printer (and is a very good value for the money, but the Brother printer does not have duplex). The HP prints faster than the Brother and is a more substantial printer as concerns build quality.Another feature of this printer that is simply outstanding is the OCR capabilities. I have, up until now, never had much success with OCR software. The Brother printer also has OCR, but the software is so error prone, it makes it mostly useless and an exercise in futility. The OCR included with the HP, on the other hand, just works. It actually works for me and has been astoundingly accurate for me so far.I think this is a great printer and would buy it again based on what I've experienced so far. I'm not yet convinced that I'll save up to 50% off printing costs (as per their advertising) compared to laser printing because I have not owned the printer long enough to make that determination. My previous experience with various ink-jets over the years is that they are quite expensive to operate... the consumable costs are quite high. So if there is a cost savings with this printer, I will be extremely pleased.I have to give this a 5 star rating. It does what it's supposed to do and quite well.

The pendaflex project management kit is a binder with a unique "channel lock" system for inserting/ holding additional pages.The basic kit comes with a large (3 inch thick) binder which is made of hard plastic (with a stamped pattern on the outside and small pockets inside) and a toggle lock closure.  This binder can hold up to 8 organizational tools, and came with 5:1) a 4 pocket media file (sized for cd storage and transportation)2) an envelope (8.5 x 11)with a secure toggle closure3 &4) 2 secure file folders (folders which can be kept closed with an elastic loop)5) a removable hard plastic clip boardIn addition to the included items, Pendaflex offers traditional twin pocket dividers, a "display book" (removable album), a "project pocket," an envelope which opens lengthwise, and single pocket dividers.The binder itself is sturdy, and th4 insert system innovative, but I am not sure I like it as well as traditional 3 ring binders. This system limits the number of organizational tools you can add by the number of available slot which means you have to know exactly what you want from the get-go. Because they are pre-spaced, you are limited in the amount you can add to each pocket or envelope (without putting stress on the system or pushing the adjacent tool out of place).  Finally, while the binding system is innovative, I think it serves the company better than the consumer to the extent that you are limited to using proprietary products.  My children would not be able to easily use this system as it does not allow them to add their notebooks, looseleaf paper, or the binder which they occasionally are given (and expected to use; turn their work in with).  While the binder itself is sturdy, it is not terribly flexible.  It is hard plastic with creases (to delineate the cover, binding and back) and keeps springing open.  This is fine if you are using it as a file folder but would work less well on a day to day basis as a school binder, or primary work organizational system.What I like about the Pendaflex system is the variety of options it provides for organization and storage, and that most of them are secure (your paperwork will not be falling out or getting lost).  I do not like that I am limited in the number of things I can add and forced to use only those which lock in to the proprietary binding. Another plus is that each of the envelopes, folders, etc. lay flat when removed and do not rely on the binding system to keep them together.i have been looking for tools which would help me get my taxes organized and this system might suit that purpose well because it can hold a variety of items of different sizes, the secure closures keep things in place (so they can be removed and placed in file folders or cabinets), and the binder itself can be held closed.  Beyond that, because it is something I pretty much do once a year, it will not be handled much or carried around, and is somewhat self-limited in scope.  That is, by the end of the fiscal year you more or less know what it is you have to organize and store.I would say that the best use of this system is for discrete projects which are limited in scope.  I believe this is an organizational system for people who are already pretty well organized to the extent that you have to know how many tools and of what sort you need when you set out.  There is a bit of flexibility in that the system comes with extra slots, and a nice variety of organizational tools are available which fit.  You just need to be sure that your project will fit in 8 pockets or envelopes or be prepared to use several binders.it is a nice system, but not likely to become my personal favorite.

Now that many, if not all, of the TI/HP graphing calculators are banned from standardized exams, scientific calculators are generally approved for use. The HP 33/35 are overpriced calculators, and the TI-30XS MultiView is too basic of a calculator. The FX-115ES includes many features like differentials, integration, matrices (albeit only up to 3x3 matrices), "pretty print" or math print (where fractions are displayed like fractions in a textbook, and has a dual power system (solar power and batteries). The instruction pamphlet is large and unwieldy. TI at least includes a "booklet", while the Casio instructions are printed on a huge foldout sheet that is easily torn or lost. The ON/OFF controls for the FX-115ES are unintuitive. To turn ON the calculator, you must press a special ON button. To turn it off, you press SHIFT + AC. I instinctively hit AC to try to turn on the calculator since my old Casio scientifics all turned on in this manner. Why did they change this? The Casio also takes getting used to for TI graphing calculator users. I've used my TI-86 and TI-89 for nearly a decade and now I am forced to get acquainted with the Casio. It's not difficult but it is almost like learning a new keyboard layout. The screen text/font is also too large. While it offers a 2-line display, it really is useless for scrolling back. I am more used to the multi-line display of a TI-86/TI-89 where you can see 3-4 previous problems at a single time. They could have tried and squeezed more lines of text, but this is just a minor inconvenience. The protective cover also requires extra care to slide into place. It is not as positive or easy to use as a TI graphing calculator cover. They should have extended the tracks instead of making a curved design.Pros: Lot of calculator for the money. Beats out the TI-30XS for power, and beats out the HP 33/35 for value.Cons: Unwieldy instruction foldout, quirky on/off buttons (not intuitive), slightly more difficult to get used to for the TI user.Overall: Simply one of the top choices for modern standardized exams if graphing calculators are banned.
