I use these Sharpie markers to color in the alopecia areata spots on my brunette head. Just move the long hair out of the way, and smear this on the fleshy spots. Works well for spots up to 3/4 inch; I have found that spots larger than that size tend to color in poorly and appear like somebody used magic marker on my head.I find the King Size markers to be far too large for effective dobbing of my spots.  One would think this would be idea, and that the smaller, finer pointed ones would be too pointed and make unsightly lines.  Well, the smallers ones are better; the thick King sized ones do not permit the finesse necessary for cosmetic perfection.I have tried eyebrow pencils and Marks-A-Lot brand, but both of those run in rainstorms. I have streaks of black like ruined mascara down my neck when I have hit a downpour with those products. The Sharpie, conversely, stays in place and doesn't ruin my neck or my clothes.When you first put this on, smudge it around with a paper towel; it has a working time of approximately thirty seconds, after which it cannot be blended on your skin. If I have a particularly nasty outbreak of "pecia", as we call it, I will have my wife apply to the back of my squash because there are so many spots that I cannot see them well by holding a mirror to the back of my head.I will note that there is a faint odor of magic marker from this product for about the first hour or so after one applies it to their head skin. If there are plans for a dinner party, unless you want the hosts to think that you were wearing an advertising sandwich board all day, you might want to apply the Sharpie long before you leave the house.When I sweat, the marker does get slightly mobile. What do I mean? If I lay back on a pillow, it will stain the pillow. This is particularly important, once again, at the dinner party. You will want to avoid high backed, upholstered chairs.Finally, I have never had a lack of hair re-growth from the toxicity of this product on my head. Seems as though the nascent hairs, typically white in color, do not mind the daily bath of Sharpie. I have not experienced yet any ill effects such as loss of memory or dulled ability for computations, but I will update this review should that occur (if I remember to update it).

The PIXMA PRO-1 Professional Inkjet Printer is an amazing piece of equipment for the professional photographer or for the amateur who wants professional quality prints. I recently reviewed the Canon PIXMA PRO-100 and was delighted with the prints, however, comparing the same prints done on the PIXMA PRO-1, there was a definition and depth of color that exceeded the PIXMA PRO-100. My husband does wild bird photography and the results were nothing short of amazing. While the PIXMA PRO-100 has eight cartridges, the PIXMA PRO-1 comes with a full set of  12 LUCIA pigment ink system cartridges to ensure higher levels of color accuracy and stunning detail. While I have tested this unit only on color prints, there are as well five monochrome inks to raise your level of professional print quality when creating the dramatic expression of grayscale photography.Other features include built-in Ethernet connection (cable not supplied) allows multiple users to seamlessly print from several networked computers in any environment.The PIXMA PRO-1 also offers two-way paper feeding and professional photo printing on a variety of Fine Art and Glossy Photo Papers.  That said, there are a few considerations that should be mentioned before you spring for this printer.Even thought the cartridges are stated to be 2  times larger than conventional cartridges, they use an incredible amount of ink, approximately 25% of each cartridge just to prime the printer head. Other reviewers write of getting 30 13 x 19 prints out of the cartridges before they go empty, and a full set of replacements with shipping and tax can run $430. So as amazing as this printer is, it can be very pricy to operate if printing photographs and selling them is not your business.The printer is huge (27" x 9.5" x 18.5" and weighs about 75 pounds) and requires a table to set it on. Also, you need to leave some access in the rear of the printer. I have mine sitting on half of a six-foot table in my office.The printer can be set up to use USB or Ethernet connected to a switch/router. (Note: I needed to use both USB and Ethernet to configure the software). Since the laptop this printer is connected to has no unused USB ports and since I wanted to connect to a home network, I opted for the Ethernet hookup. You choose your desired connection during the set-up process, however, you'll need to have both cables on hand since they aren't supplied.Installation took approximately 40 minutes plus additional time to install the ink cartridges and print head, which took 20 minutes to prime. I had trouble getting my system to recognize the additional printer, but after connecting both USB and Ethernet cables, I was able to complete the task. The included quick start and User's Manual detailed each operation so the setup is simple, even for a beginner. There's  a toll-free live technical support number (1-800-OK-CANON) in case you need additional help.In conclusion, I certainly recommend this printer, but be aware that it is expensive to maintain. Others have suggested that you should run a print at least every week or so to keep the print head from requiring additional priming. This will save on the amount of ink used as well as help preventing clogging and the need to clean the head.WHAT'S IN THE BOXPIXMA PRO-1 Professional Inkjet PrinterCD/DVD Printing TrayDocument Kit: Cross Sell Sheet, Getting Started, Important Information Sheet, Safety Environment Information, Setup Software & User's Guide CD-ROM, Warranty CardInk Tanks: PGI-29 Matte Black, PGI-29 Photo Black, PGI-29 Cyan, PGI-29 Magenta, PGI-29 Yellow, PGI-29 Photo Cyan, PGI-29 Photo Magenta, PGI-29 Red, PGI-29 Dark Gray, PGI-29 Light Gray, PGI-29 Gray, PGI-29 Chroma OptimizerPower CordPrint Head

Overall, these whisper-thin transparent plastic sticky notes are awesome! You can use them to mark up a passage (or recipe, or knitting pattern) right over the printed text, without damaging your book. They're excellent for books with detail photos--you can add notes when there's not enough white space, but still leave the photos visible. I'm a book abuser and tend to mark up my cookbooks from the get-go--but I also tend to give a lot of my old cookbooks away, so I like the idea of being able to make my notes but not make the book a ratty mess for people who are more delicate with their libraries.They're also great for marking up knitting patterns--they're particularly handy for 1) making your own notes for converting a flat lace pattern to round; 2) marking personal pattern adjustments right over the text; or 3) marking your place in a lace or colorwork chart, so you can see what's next but also clearly keep your place.They're so very thin that I don't think loading a book with a ton of them would at all compromise the binding, either, which is nice if you're a careful book owner--or borrowing a book from someone else. The pad of 50 was about half the thickness of a pad of 40 regular postits I had on hand.I was able to use pencils, sharpies and some pens successfully. That's my one warning: not all ballpoint pens seem to write well on this surface (though some did), particularly if it's been handled much. If you use hand lotion or if your hands get oil on them cooking, even the slightest residue prevented some ballpoints from marking (though other ballpoints had no problem in the same spots, so go figure). Didn't seem to have an effect on sharpie or pencil, though. A pretty minor thing. If I could knock off half a star, I would; but since I can't, it's not worth a whole star.(I also might have qualms about the plastic, except that I think these are best for permanent notes (vs. regular paper postits, more for throwaway notes); the higher cost also dictates a less frivolous use.

It's hard to tell from the picture just how nice this chair looks. Even if this particular style isn't to your liking, the company makes this chair with a variety of other fabrics.From a functional standpoint, this chair has it all. Many years ago, my company brought in ergonomic experts as a proactive measure, and this chair will allow employees to adjust it in myriad ways that the experts recommended to me. As with most good office chairs, adjusting the height is easy. The chair also allows you to adjust the resistance for the tilt of the seat, as well as allowing you to lock the seat at a certain inclination. The arm rests adjust in height and also have the unique feature of adjusting in width.In the past, I've used more ornate, expensive leather chairs that are designed for comfort. A more pragmatic solution would have been to get a chair such as this one with a back that provides plenty of support and comfort, and enough ventilation to be comfortable both when wearing a suit and when wearing more casual attire. Overall, this chair will be a better fit.As a man who is above average in height, I had no problems adjusting this chair quickly and easily to suit my frame. I also had a woman who is under five feet tall use the chair for several days. She was very pleased with it and felt as if it had been designed with her in mind.  For those who have more girth, the fact that the arms can be moved outward by several inches on each side may be a welcome feature.My experience was not problem free, however, as the chair arrived with some damage. Although I'm not sure if the damage occurred in shipping, whether the box had been opened by somebody else and repacked, or whether there was some other issue, the company didn't care what caused the problems and saw it as theirs to fix. They stood by their product and sent me replacement arms using two day FedEx service. They recognize the needs of businesses both big and small and want to assure a good long term relationship.I pressed the issue in order to assure that my experience was an anomaly, and the company was able to quickly trace every place the chair had been since it left the factory until it got to Amazon's location that shipped it to me. While I still can't be sure where the damage occurred, I appreciate the extent to which they cared about my problem.Although my experience was less than perfect, I now have a chair that lives up to the standard that warrants a five star review. The sixty five pound package is shipped for free by Amazon, who will also handle any problems with its condition. In the unlikely event of a problem, it's good to be able to rely on Amazon's customer service, but even better when you can also deal directly with the manufacturer without the slightest hassle.

These markers are for hobbyists. They have a place in every scrapbooker's, rubber stamper's, and card maker's tool box and a unique niche in the creative workflow. They don't do everything, but what they do, they do well.They are very good for outlining, crosshatching, handwriting and even sketching. For any function in which it is important the ink not smudge, flow smoothly, dry fast, and be acid-free. You could color small areas with them but they are fine point and it could get tedious to try to use them for coloring.If you were to compare them to ballpoint pens, these are what would be called medium point. Usually, coloring markers are a bit thicker.The best comparison to make is to the Marvy markers that hobbyists are so familiar with. Marvy markers can be watered down, they can blend into each other, they have two points so you can easily color larger areas, and it is possible to achieve a watercolor-like appearance with Marvy markers.  But if you try to use them on a non-paper surface, they will wash off. If you use them for outlining, they will run, and it's easy to over saturate the paper to the point of curling or breaking. They drag on the paper more than ballpoints so your handwriting won't be the best.These markers will create indelible outlines that can be filled in with water-based colors and will not run. They are instant drying even on glossy paper, so they cannot be blended together to form a new color unless you crosshatch. They are comfortable to hold and smooth flowing without pressure. The points are firm and will hold their shape better than the Marvys which tend to get mushy with use. They are as easy to write with as ballpoints and don't have a strong smell (like other quick-drying markers such dry erase markers). I strongly suspect that stains will not be easy to remove and that, like all other markers, they need to be kept covered to not dry out.They are not competitors for the Marvy Markers, they are compliments to them. Having both is the perfect combination since one can fill in where the other leaves off and you probably already have a Marvy that will match every color in this assortment.The Bic Mark It marker is usable on non-paper surfaces (similar to Sharpies) but there is no reason to need this large an assortment just for marking. This is more of an art assortment. I just used them to write names on Christmas balls and draw shapes for my nieces to fill in with glitter glue and they worked perfectly. This is something I would have normally used Sharpies for.They come in a plastic case that opens into three parts. The right flap holds the pastel colors. The other two flaps are arranged in a color-wheel like progression that begins and ends with green. Ideally, this would be the way to store them.In general, I'm delighted with the assortment. But the only problem I've found is a bit bothersome: the ink color defined by the various identifiers (top/bottom dot, barrel strip, and cap clip) that are supposed to indicate color is not always representative of the actual color of the ink. The pastels, for example, while lighter than their regular counterparts, aren't as light as you would suppose. The final three greens in the center flap have almost identical identifiers, but they are three distinctly different greens. This results in a lot of opening, testing, and closing. I imagine I'll get it figured out eventually, but I would have rated this set five stars if they'd gotten this right.

One day while strolling through Office Max on Michigan Avenue in Chicago, I stumbled across what I thought was an exceptional deal - a 1200 DPI laser printer under $200! It almost seemed too good to be true.  After some initial skepticism and subsequent analysis, I realized that it was, in fact, an excellent deal - for a niche low volume user who needs fast printing.As a frequent author of reviews, I would typically check Amazon before buying such an item.  So after returning to my office, printer in hand, my enthusiasm was somewhat dampened by the negative reviews on the HL-1440.  I almost returned it before seeing the print quality and performing some basic calculations.  In the end, I am glad I kept it as it serves my need for having a fast, high quality, low volume printer in my one-man office.Currently I own a [large] microwave-sized multifunction HP inkjet (d155xi), which is at my home office.  I decided that if I needed another printer in a second location, it should be a inexpensive laser printer.  Initially, I thought I would purchase a $300 HP.  My concern with such printers and the other sub-$500 printers was the cost of the consumables. Experience with ink-jets (such as my HP-d155xi) demonstrated that the ink expenditures are a real killer. This, of course, is a ploy by the manufacturers to recoup equipment costs via pricy consumables.The sales associate at Office Max suggested that the replacement toner cartridges last 6000 sheets for around $60. After some mental calculations, I figured that it would be a good deal.  Only when I returned to read the Amazon customer reviews did I learn that there was a second consumable - the drum - that lasts, at best, 20,000 sheets.  This is something I did not anticipate.  While I have no way of determining if this second consumable was created for purely technical reasons or merely as a financial/marketing strategy, I would guess that it is a bit of both.  Moreover, at a cost of $115 w/tax, the drum costs about 65% of the cost of a HL-1440, making a second drum purchase a psychological obstacle.To determine if the Brother HL-1440 was a good value, I opened Excel and performed some basic calculations, which you can see below.Assumptions - Drum replaced at 15,000 sheets first time; 18,000 additional sheets second time.  High capacity toner lasts stated 6000 sheets, original yields 3000 sheets.  Note that it doesn't come with a USB cable ($20) but I had a surplus one.$w_tax  total$  total sheets  _sheetprinter  $176 $176 3k  5.9HC toner 1 $57 $232 9k  2.6HC toner 2 $57 $289 15k  1.9New Drum  $115 $404 15kHC toner 3 $57 $461 21k  2.2HC toner 4 $57 $518 27k  1.9HC toner 5 $57 $574 33k  1.7As you can see, if you chose to toss the printer at 15,000 sheets, the average price per sheet is 1.9 cents. This is far below the cost of printing at Kinko's - excluding transportation costs and convenience value.  The tricky part comes from the decision to purchase a new drum.  It takes a while to recoup the cost of the drum, making it a very tough decision for some. Moreover, one has to guess  how long the other components will last. Given my level of use, I would probably not purchase the drum. In the three years that it would take to wear out the first drum, another, more cost effective solution would become available.Like expectancy issues aside, there are some nice features to this printer.  Print quality is excellent (as least after the first 500 pages). While somewhat lightweight compared to workgroup printers, it is built better than most inkjets I have used.  Nice touches include the paper level meter where a mechanical needle on the front indicates the height of the paper reserves in the tray.Some strange problems include mirror printing from certain applications, such as MS Streets and Trips 2004. This is corrected by a patch.  There is also a recurring "Found New Hardware" problem where it creates a new printer icon (Copy 1, 2, etc).  It usually stops at copy 2.  Brother suggests that this is a Windows XP problem. As I have used multiple USB printers on this and similar computers, I doubt that it is just an XP problem.  In the end, it appears that a full drive uninstall may have solved this minor annoyance.In the end, I would suggest this printer is a good choice for low volume home offices or single person companies. If you are like me, someone who prints around a 100 pages per week and needs a fast printer when on deadline, the HL-1440 is a good choice. I would not recommend this for any moderate volume or workgroup environment.Pro'sExcellent print qualityVery inexpensiveLow total cost of ownership/price per pageNice paper level meterCon'sPoor front interfaceShort lifePossible driver problemsStrange printing anomalies (corrected by patches)Only 2MB memoryNo USB cabled included

These push pin type magnets are very easy to use and YES, they are powerful. I notice that it mentions it will hold (under ideal circumstances) 16 sheets of 20lb weight paper. Convenient is the right word to describe this printer. I say convenient because it automates most things that cheaper all-in-ones require you to do manually.  This is exactly like the Workforce 635 but add the option to print from the internet.You can use either Epson Email, Epson iPrint app for Android or iPhone, or Google Cloud Print. Setting Google Cloud Print is a little ackward, since you can't set the printer up online. You need to download Epson Downloader, install that, and then run it. It will then list another download for your printer that must be installed for Cloud Print to be enabled. Epson Email Print on the other hand supplies you with an email address for your printer, and you can email any documents you want to print to that address (as attachments).That's all the differences between Workforce 645 and Workforce 635.The following was taken from my review of Workforce 635, since scanning functionality is the same:Duplex scanning with automatic sheet feeder is a godsend. I really like the scanning capabilities of this thing. You have the option to use either the flatbed scanner or the sheet feeder.I recently opened a bank account with a local institution, and they gave me 32 sheets of documents with terms and conditions (with text on both sides). As soon as I came home I placed the entire stack of papers in the automatic sheet feeder of this device, opened Adobe Acrobat X Pro, and told it to scan whatever is in the sheet feeder and create a PDF document. Workforce 635 scanned the entire stack (both sides of each page), and Acrobat automatically created a single PDF document of every page in that stack while I was occupying my time with other things. Saved me 10-15 minutes of manual work. I really liked that. :)To be honest my excitement comes from the fact that this is my first duplex scanner, so I'm not sure how it compares with other duplex scanners. I also used the regular flatbed scanner to digitize pages of a book, and was impressed with its scanning speed (about 2-3 seconds for grayscale scans at 300dpi).Print quality is fine. I had to clean the print heads a couple of times at first (lots of ink wasted), but now it's fine.Buyer beware: there are no cheap 3rd party ink cartridges for this printer. Epson has apparently declared war 3rd party suppliers, and currently Epson is the ONLY supplier of Epson ink here in the US. It would be a good idea to avoid Epson printers if you want the option of paying for cheaper 3rd party ink. Otherwise, this is a great all-in-one printer for the money.

Label makers are one of the most useful devices you can own.  Some label makers are great for labeling manila folders, wires, your toolbox, and anything else that you plan on keeping for a long time.  Some label makers can print graphics and have many options for boxes.  Many label makers can make bar codes, which seem to be ubiquitous in offices, factories and even homes.Electronic label makers have come along since the first label makers were produced.  Considering the premium price of this label maker, I assumed (incorrectly) that it would have as many features as, if not more than, a comparably priced handheld label maker.  After all, this label maker plugs into a computer and has a neat screen for setting up your label.  Then I started running into limitations.The first annoyance I had was in designing the label.  I wanted to try boxes around my labels.  Admittedly, the boxes are for esthetic reasons, but I use boxes a lot.  Your choice seems to be box or no box, though you have a choice of five line types.  In comparison, the lower priced Epson LW-400 has at least 75 frames or boxes you can select and the Brother PT1290 has seven frames, all of which I have used.  While I personally have only used a few of the Epson's frames, 75 or more frames will please nearly anyone making labels.I thought having a label maker on my desk would be a cool thing, and it is, until I want to move the label maker to the garage, or the kitchen, or anywhere else in the house.  Suddenly, a label maker that sits on my desk is not such a good idea any more.  Sure, I could carry my laptop with the label maker, along with a USB cord, but it is easier just to grab a handheld label maker.This label maker has a few other limitations that several lower-priced label makers do not seem to have.  This label will not print out cable flags, which the Epson LW-400 will do.  This label maker will handle tape up to a half inch, which is useful for many things, but it would have been nice to have the option for three quarter inch.This label maker does some things really well.  On two-line labels, the label centers both lines, which I really like.  The number of fonts available with this label maker is huge.  I am not sure how many fonts are available, but the number is somewhere around 90.  Perhaps one of the biggest advantages of this label maker is that it can store labels.  If you tend to make the same labels, like an address label, often, then this feature is extremely valuable.  Of course, some other label makers, such as the Epson LW-400, can save a limited number of labels.Potentially one of the most interesting features of this label maker is its graphics capability.  You can print pictures, though the quality is low.  The software includes a number of clip art and other symbols, which print reasonably well.Dymo advertises that this label maker is "plug and play."  That claim is true, with a caveat.  The software included with the label maker is somewhat limited.  You can download a fancier version to your computer that includes more features than the light version included with your label maker.  All my comments in this review relate to Dymo Label v.8 software rather than the Dymo Label Light version.  One of the biggest advantages to this label maker is that you use your keyboard and mouse to design the labels rather than the itty-bitty keyboard that comes with most handheld label makers.The cost of the Dymo D1 tape is quite reasonable and even inexpensive compared to some competitors.  There seems to be a reasonable variety of D1 tapes available as well.  I have seen several complaints regarding defective cartridges.  One complaint might be expected.  Two complaints from two individuals is a caution.  Three complaints from three different individuals I find disturbing.  I have a Brother P-Touch label maker and have yet to see anyone complain about a defective P-Touch cartridge, and Brother has sold millions of those cartridges.  I have also seen complaints about poor adhesion with the Dymo tape cartridge.  My experience with the Brother P-Touch is almost exactly the opposite.  Once the P-Touch tape sticks, it can be difficult to get it back off again.In summary:Pro:- The cost of the tape is competitive or less expensive than the tape of many competitors.- Lots of memory for commonly used labels.- Lines can be centered on the label easily.- Uses a relatively small amount of tape on print out.- Plug and play device; just connect to your computer.- Great graphics capability.- Huge array of fonts.- Labels are set up from your computer keyboard versus the small keyboard of handheld devices.Con:- Limited label features, e.g., limited box options.- Complaints about the quality of the tape and tape cartridges.- Portability is relatively limited since it requires a computer.- Limited print configurations, e.g., will not print cable flags.- To access all the features of the label maker you need to download Dymo's proprietary software.- Limited to half-inch tape.As you can see, this label maker has many nice features.  However, it also has some limitations.  Perhaps the most troubling concern about this label maker is the complaints about the tape.  Some of the complaints relate to the tape not feeding.  Other complaints relate to the tape losing adhesion in a relatively short period.  Personally, this label maker is not my favorite.  I prefer both my Brother P-Touch and my Epson LW-400.Good Luck!

I've owned several Brother PC-based label printers. I'd first bought one for my SOHO which eventually folded, but that's a different story.  I then bought a couple more later for other purposes.  I've always enjoyed printing labels from my laptops.The DYMO D1 label printer is a small-footprint, attractive-looking device out of the box. It has the light-weight version of DYMO's label manager in memory, so it's truly pure plug-n-play, especially on Windows computers (Macintosh users need one extra step in running the software and also one extra step when unpluggying it from the computer). But, to my disappointment, it uses a proprietary LiIon rechargable battery, which seems odd since, when connected to a USB port, it gets power directly from the port, so why including a battery? And why not allowing us to use the common AA or AAA batteries? (One possible reason is that apparently a lot of Mac computers do not have adequately powered USB ports, so maybe for these users, they're to charge the battery by connecting the D1 to a PC, and then once the battery is recharged, they can use it with a Mac computer.) Note to self: I should try using the machine without the battery and see if it works...You can download a free, full version of DYMO's label management software, which works seamlessly with Microsoft Word.What really disappoints me is the print quality. My Brother label printers printed high-quality text, but the D1's print quality seems low-quality. It's passable, but came as quite a shock to me. Also, whereas Brother models can often print on 1" or wider tapes (and not being much bigger than the D1), the D1 can use 1/4", 3/8" or 1/2" label tapes, and it's not pleasant to try to print two lines on the included 1/2" tape. Forget about printing mailing addresses. On the Brothers, I could easily print three or even four lines of clear text.In short, while I find the D1 physically attractive and the concept a very good one, the implementation leaves much to be desired. It sure is fast and easy, but the print quality should have been better.

Let's start with the "elephant in the room", "the moose head on the table", the "fly in the ointment"... the labels are expensive.  They certainly aren't cheap.  A 26' cartridge of 2" TZ labels costs about $11.  That would allow you to print a one 26' label or, more likely a whole bunch of shorter ones.  It's when you print shorter ones that this gets even more expensive.  The problem is the printer needs to "waste" about 1" of label material each time it starts printing.  So, if you print out a lot of 3" labels individually (that's the typical size for file folders), each one will take 4" of label stock.  I'll do the arithmetic so you don't have to, worst case is each file folder label costs about $0.14.By contrast, using myBrother QL-570 Professional Label Printerand 2.4" continuous stock gets me file folder labels for about $0.03 each.  (Even less when I use third party label stock.)  However, with the PT-P750W I do get a wider range of label stock and can opt for more durable materials.  Also, the laminated TZ series labels look better and last a heck of a lot longer.OK, with that done, let's talk about other good and bad points with *this* printer.I had it out of the box and printing labels from my iPhone without ever connecting it to a computer.  It's easy and quick.  First I needed to do a one-time download of the free label printing iPhone app.  Then I dropped the label cartridge in the printer, plugged in it, turned it on, and pressed the "WiFi" button.  Since my iPhone is "challenged" and doesn't do the NFC tap-to-set wireless configuration thing I needed to open my phone's network settings and select the dedicated wireless network that is broadcast by the printer.  The first time I did this, and only the first time, I needed to enter the "super secret network key", 00000000.  (more on that in a bit)  That was it.  From there I went to the app and printed some labels.  When I turned the label printer off my phone automatically reverted to my home network.Even  if this seems like a lot, after the first time, after that it takes about 10 seconds to switch over to the printer's network and start printing labels.  Also, with the latest version of iOS my iPhone can access the Internet (over the 4G network) while it remains connected to the printer's WiFi.  I can surf and print without having to jump back and forth.Another great feature of this printer is that it is portable.  I have the option to use either six AA batteries (either regular or rechargeable) or Brother's special lithium-ion rechargeable battery.  Two things to note, if you are using rechargeable AA batteries, they won't recharge when they're in the printer and the included adapter is connected.  (The Brother Li-ion battery will.)  Also, this printer is new and Amazon still doesn't have the Brother battery listed.  Still, with 10 hours of life from a single set of AA batteries, you'll be printing a lot of labels before you'll need to replace them.About the super-secret network key...  Keeping it is a bad idea.  That's because if someone sees you're using this printer and does a bit of research they'll be able to print.  If they have a sense of humor you could see the results of someone trying to print that 26' label I mentioned a while back.  The good news is that it's easy to change the network key.  The bad news is you have to download software to do it and need to know to look for it on the brother-usa (dot) com site.  The good news is that now you know to do that.On balance, this is a nifty printer that can sit anywhere and is great for printing folder labels or other "signage" that needs to last.

I use these as labels for bottles. It is the perfect size for labeling 12.7 ounce bottles. The positive points are:1 - They do not jam, bend or otherwise get messed up during the printing cycle.2 - They peel easily from the sheet, but stick VERY firmly to glass.3 - They are thick enough so that they can be applied to bottles smoothly with no wrinkles. This is a HUGE advantage over some other types of labels we have tried.4 - The 5264 template is built in to most major software packages. Setting up the labels for printing was a breeze.The negatives are: Haven't found any yet!One reviewer mentioned that he had problems removing labels once they were applied to bottles. First, that's generally a good thing. The last thing I would want to happen is to have the labels just slide off after getting wet or being subjected to temperature changes. However I tried removing labels for the first time last week and didn't really find it all that hard. What I did was rinse the bottles with hot running water for a couple of minutes. I then places the bottles in a boiling water bath for 5 minutes. The labels peeled right off for the most part. In a couple of cases there was a bit of adhesive left on bottles, but that rubbed off easily enough while the bottle was still hot.My wife actually then used a bit of an environmentally friendly degreaser on a bottle that was not boiled, and that seemed to remove the adhesive easily enough as well.I highly recommend this product.

The labels are lightly textured to help hold the graphite (as others have said - use pencil) and come with a hole so that you can tie them onto your plants if you prefer. They are quite strong, although when my soil is dry (heavy clay), I have to make a hole with a sharp stick first before the tag can penetrate. Because they're bright white, they're easy to see in the garden, which is a positive and a negative. Yes, they're easy to find, but they're visually rather jarring. That's just the nature of the plant tag, though. If I were crazy wealthy, I might have lovely, subtle tags printed, like you see at an arboretum. But since I'm not, these are a heck of an inexpensive alternative.

The board is a very good size for the fridge, and the quality is very good. It has a metallic surface that makes wiping easy, and magnets stick to it well. My only complaint about the product is the very cheap marker that comes with the board. It was already dried up or it didn't work well to begin with. I ended up using another dry erase marker I already had. The board sticks to your refrigerator with sticky pads, so it's pretty much permanent once you put it up. Make sure you place it where you won't have to move it.

I used to use two-sided tape for gift wrapping, but it tends to be a pain. This is the ideal solution.  It lays down a strip of adhesive made up of tightly packed tiny dots. I've used similar products that would lay down a narrow strip of adhesive. The problem was that the strip would not always stick, or would pull up, or wind back into the dispenser. Since this uses a whole lot of tiny dots, that's not an issue.Looking for a great way to perfectly wrap your next gift?  Here it is!

Like all Canon products I've used over the last 20 years, this printer is easy to use and reliable. I don't know why they didn't include a retractable printing tray though. I thought that was pretty standard. I bought this knowing that it lacked the tray, but potential buyers should be aware of this in case you want to use it on a shelf instead of a desk top.

I think the Heart Shaped Post It dispenser is a nice addition to my desktop.  It is attractive and heavy enough to serve as a paper weight.  Actually the weight is what makes it wonderful.  I have had problems in the past with the dispenser either coming apart or dispensing too many Post It Notes.  This dispenser is attractive and it works.  I'm lovin' it.

This is a handy little pop-up dispenser for your desk.  It has a very grippy suction cup on the bottom that works well on any smooth surface.  The suction cup does prevent the holder from lifting up as you pull out a tape.  However, it does not prevent it from sliding around on the surface.  You may consider this a plus or a minus.  To load tape you have to slide part of the cover open.  You have to press pretty hard to get it to release and slide, but once you get the hang of it, it's pretty easy to open.  Overall I'm pleased with this holder and it is a nice handy way to keep these tapes accessible

I think Canon is the best printer maker period. I hate all the printers that make it so difficult to setup the wireless and the other funtions. Most of the HP and Lexmark printers requrie you to install the software before making it wireless. This is very easy to setup and printing quality is great as always. I have been using canon printers for over 5 years and they are durable and the ink seems to last much longer than the other brands that I have tried. As for the bad reviews for this product, people expect too much for a simple all in one printer and some people just have bad luck with electronics.For me this is how I set it up and I had no issues with it for the past 6 months of usage.-It was delivered withing two days and I unpacked everything-Put the ink in and plug in the power cable and turn it on-Go to settings and connect to wireless network-Go to PC and "Add a Printer" under "Devices & Printers"-The printer showed up, I select it and clicked next and followed two more steps and it installed automatically from windows update (If it doesn't auto install, simply put the disk in and when prompted to select a location, select the disk)- Start enjoying printing wirelessly and scanning wirelessly.You can also plug it in directly to your computer and it should install by itself. You don't need the cannon software. I think printer all softwares are useless. The ink lasts as long as most inject printers.Overall, Im happy with a printer that is easy to setup and simply works.
I have an HP Pavilion Notebook that is almost 9 years old.  I love my new printer, even tho I don't print much, when I do print, it's reliable and does the job well.

If you're into mechanical pencils, you might like this. The lead is strong and the loading mechanism reliable. Granted it's difficult to wax lyrical about packing tape. I like writing with ball point pens and like this pen.  If you are not into ball point pens I don't think this will really change your mind.  The pen does write neatly and has a comfortable grip. It is a pretty good pen for the price.

I ordered these pens as part of the Vine program since, as an English professor, I go through a lot of pens each semester, and am always on the hunt for colored pens to use for grading.  My absolute favorite pens (which I've been using for at least twelve years) are the Pilot Precise V5 pens (such as these in the multi-pack:Pilot Precise V5 Stick Rolling Ball Pens, Extra Fine Point, 7-Pack Pouch, Assorted Color Inks (26015)), which don't bleed through, and yet still leave a nice, vibrant mark. I have aScotch Thermal Laminator 2 Roller System (TL901)that I use to protect important documents in my office and less-than-important documents that are going to get a bit exposed to the world's harshness.The laminator came with 2 Scotch brand pouches, but before buying more of those I wanted to compare other brands.I like the Fellowes. The lamination turns out good, no waves, no problems.  The 3mm is what I got, and works well for the copy paper (or equivalent) that I tend to be trying to protect.  Two differences I noticed right away. The Fellowes is a bit more clingy than the Scotch, making it harder to open the pouch and harder to position the paper just right. This isn't necessarily a bad thing as it also means it may hold in in place a bit better in the process. Just adds a few extra seconds of very mild frustration.It's also a bit cloudier than the Scotch, not quite as transparent. It's by no means opaque or even close, it is very clear for typed pages and such. But if you're concerned about specific colors, this might wash those out a bit, taking a bit away from brightness or clarity.

This is a good, heavy-duty stapler.  It can staple up to 75 sheets together at one time.  I've tried about 50 sheets, and it does a good job.  Nothing special, but it works well and staples through a large stack of papers without a ton of effort and without jamming.I also like the fact that you load the staples by pushing a button on the stapler which pushes the front out and you can just drop the staples in.  This is an easy, convenient way to load the stapler.The drawback?  There were no staples included with the stapler, and standard size staples don't fit.  My husband's office has an assortment of heavy-duty staplers, and I finally found a few staples that fit this stapler.  This would get a 5 star review if it took more standard size staples.

If you are older and remember back to college when no nails or damaging adhesives were allowed in the dorm rooms to mount posters--you had an option of sticky tabs. Unfortunately the weight of the posters often found them, along with the tabs on the floor come morning!These Scotch reusable sticky tabs are a great improvement over the older models by companies I can't remember! These are great for mounting pictures, labels etc. on posterboard for presentations. You can move things around easily, yet the tabs stick well and you don't find yourself fumbling and grabbing for the pictures, labels or charts midway through your presentation.I do some scrapbooking and found them to work well for the uses I needed them for which included temporary page positioning as well as holding pictures, labels, and things in place while trying to visualize alternate placements. They do, however, rip off a layer of the more porous papers which then renders them unusable as well as destroying the portion of the paper you had them positioned on.The sticky tabs also hold posters on the walls much better than their predecessors from the 70's! However, they don't work as well on rough walls which unfortunately I mostly have. The lighter the poster, the more success I had with it staying up on my porous walls. I have several laminated posters that were too heavy on these walls, but they stuck fine on the newer, flatter walls in the rooms that had been redone.All in all a wonderful addition to your adhesive collection whether it is for poster presentations, scrapbooking, or just hanging posters on walls!

I'm pretty impressed by this gadget and it's shortcomings are fairly minor. The Nyrius Translator can be used for 7 languages including English, French, German, Spanish, Italian, Japanese, and Mandarin Chinese. I'd say this selection covers a very broad spectrum of the most popular travel destinations. It's use is pretty basic and the directions for it consist of only 2 pages, to give you an idea.  After you set it up you use it by selecting one of 8 categories, General, Emergency, Entertainment, Sightseeing, Direction, Restaurant, Transport, or Hotel.  Once you've selected a category you browse through the preset phrases within that category until you find what you want.  You can view the phrase in your home or target language (e.g. home is English, target is Spanish) and speak it yourself. If you don't want to do this, you can press the speaker button and the Nyrius will speak it for you.  The volume and annunciation of the speaker are loud and clear. Volume is adjustable and the LCD screen can be back lit. You can also tag most used phrases as Favorites so that you can access them quicker than scrolling through the category. Additionally, there is a headphone jack so you can practice your pronunciation if desired.On the whole I really like this tool and I have only 2 reservations about it.  I was hoping there would be a speech recognition capability that would allow me to speak in an English phrase and get the corresponding phrase in the target language.  Speech recognition software is pretty common and at this point, very effective.  My second nit is the printing on the front of the tool is minuscule.  This thing is about the size of a folded cell phone, maybe a little bigger.  The print, white on black, is VERY tiny, even if your vision is 20/20, which mine is not. Beyond those reservations, I recommend this as a very useful tool for traveling to a country that speaks one of the 7 languages.

The Epson WorkForce WF-7010 printer is a beast of a printer both in size and quality.  It prints large (up to 13x9) prints, as well as regular 8x11 prints,  which at its price makes it an affordable wide-format printer that is of course fast since its an Epson.  My favorite feature is probably that it hold up to 500 sheets, which is pretty much a ream of paper.  I feel like I am constantly adding paper so it would be nice to not have to do that so often.  I haven't tried out the two-sided printing yet, but I am excited about that since there has been times when that would have been handy for both display purposes and to save on paper.  It also uses Epson ink (multi-cartridges) which lasts longer and is smudge, fade and water resistant.While this printer is great for everyday uses, due to its large size (not many people would have room for this beast of a printer) it is probably not a good purchase for the everyday person.  Since it has such heavy-duty features I'd say this would be a perfect printer for a small-business or office who is looking for an affordable printer that can handle heavy loads and produce good quality prints.  At less than $250 it also makes it a very affordable business printer.

Ordinarily one of my least favorite things to do is to set up office equipment like printers or fax machines.  I was prepared to hunker down for the evening and install this multi function printer on a wireless network with three PC's and two Mac's.  Four of the computers are connected toLinksys WRT54G2 Wireless-G Broadband Routerby ethernet and the other wireless. The set-up of the printer was a snap.  It probably took about 40 minutes from taking the printer out of the box to printing a test picture on the last computer and most of that time was taking the plastic packing material off the printer and waiting while the software and drivers installed on the computers.  It was painless.  No foul words, no bad temper or snarling.After plugging in the printer and connecting the phone line for the fax, I installed the ink cartridges and set up the fax info on the little LED screen.  It was simple, just followed the directions in the quick start guide.  (They even supplied pictures)  Then I followed the prompts on that little LCD screen to connect to my wireless network.  It saw it right away, asked for passwords, etc. and, POOF! the printer was connected to my network.  Then I just put the CD that came with the printer into each of the computers, one at a time (They have installers for both the Mac and PC on the same CD) and POOF! again.  They were all hooked up and I could print pictures.  It was that easy. I don't know why, but when I compared one of these sticky notes to one of my regulars, the stick-factor was much less. I used to be a firm fan of genuine manufacturer cartridges as I'd had bad experiences years ago with generics and as the reviews of generics always seem to be so variable. As we have other printers it was not critical for us if the printer cartridge died or did not work properly. I used a company called Supplies_Outlet - really for no good reason except that they were the headline supplier that day but now I always buy from the same company and the toner seems identical each time.Anyway the cartridge arrived and was packed well - it had a label on it saying Brother TN45O for what its worth. It worked fine in a Brother MFC 7860 producing streak-free copies with no issues whatsoever. I've now used four from the same supplier with no problems. We've not kept page counts but they seem to last almost as long as a genuine Brother. I'm going to keep better records of page counts for this printer from now on.I'm just guessing here but I wonder if the reason that there are so many diametrically opposed views about the quality of the cartridges is dependent on whatever is supplied by a particular vendor? The featured supplier seems to change every day and for each generic cartridge listing so there seems to be a wide range of re-manufactured cartridges out there. I believe some of them are really bad and some are good but reviewers do not usually mention from whom the toner was supplied or any identifying marks on the cartridge - unless it is a branded re-manufactured one that has a company label on it. So I think this is why you get some people saying the toner is great whilst others say it is lousy. I don't know how many factories remanufacture cartridges but if there is a lot I'd say quality control varies enormously. If you have a bad experience from one supplier maybe change to another?Sorry for the long review that is not really a review.

Additional information after using them for some time. They do contain a lot less ink. They are still a lot less expensive though. There have been no clogs or problems. For everyday printing there is no real difference. I will change back to the good ones when printing high quality photos though. The leaking problem others have mentioned is there. Hold them in a rag when opening them and no problem. Just make sure that when switching back to the "good stuff for pictures that your first couple of pics will still have the cheap stuff on them and plan accordingly.Although the picture shows Cannon Genuine Inks they are, as stated, aftermarket replacements. This is deceptive and not legal.That having been said they are good inks though not as good as the genuine ones. I plan to use them or some like them in most of my printing where perfection is not critical. Since they are cheaper by a factor of 10 I can overlook a small difference. In use printing graphics or pictures on plain paper they are mainly fine. Their single fault is that they have a longer dry time than the Cannon inks. This results in loss of sharpness that is noticeable  side by side if you are comparing.When printing large photos on glossy paper the difference is more noticeable. I am an amateur photographer. When printing large photos taken on a good camera this ink will usually not be good enough. The green comes out greener, the blue less intense. Overall sharpness is reduced because the longer drying time allows the droplets to mix. The print is subtly not quite right. This is the result of blind tests with pictures printed with both inks.If you are printing your vacation snaps on 4x6 however you might not notice at all. This goes double if you have a small point and shoot or a phone camera. These inks might just be good enough.Something to remember- These inks feed a separate print head so there will be some old ink left in the system when you switch over. You can't just slap the good ones in when you want to print photos and then put these back. The first few you print will still be using the old ink.Rob Sez- They are downright cheap and will work fine for all the times when pretty good is good enough. Don't expect them to produce lab quality color glossies though.

Imagine my surprise when I opened the front door to find a box that could have held a small refrigerator. Make sure you check out the dimensions prior to ordering this printer, or you could be in for a surprise, or find that your desk just isn't big enough. I've attached some photos to show the size difference between my Epson 340 and this printer. The product's photo shows a photo in the tray -- it's probably a 13x19" sheet coming out in portrait mode. The printer's heavy, too, and the interior bag shows two people lifting it. I did it myself -- and I'm a girl -- but it wasn't easy. It's in its permanent spot -- it will not be moved again. It didn't fit on my desk so it now lives in a spare bedroom. None of this is a complaint; it's purely informational. Once I've mastered the printer, I look forward to making some larger prints.The instructions are extremely easy to follow, and I think my 80-year-old neighbor could follow them. The only point I missed -- and had to Google -- was why the printer wasn't connected to the network when I first tried to print. When setting up, the printer needs to be listed twice, once for USB and once for wireless, and you need to choose the right one.I first loaded this on my old MacBook Pro running OS 10.5.8, since the specs indicated the printer is not compatible with anything above 10.7. Everything worked well from the onset. Then, on a lark, I tried to load the software in my new retina MacBook Pro. I got a compatibility warning, continued, and the software loaded easily and, again, printing went off without a hitch.Now about those prints. They're beautiful and I didn't have to do any tweaking. They're very true to my monitor's images. Side-by-side comparisons with photos printed on my Epson showed the Canon has a clear advantage.I printed eight 8.5x11" photos on the five sheets of Canon Pro Luster paper provided with the printer and some Epson Ultra Premium Photo Paper Luster. They were comparable and gorgeous. After printing the eight photos, all ten ink tanks showed 100% full.Ink is expensive, so there's little (financial) room for experimentation.My old CD print program doesn't work with my Mac, but when I've printed my first CD/DVD, I'll update.All-in-all a great printer if you're really serious about your photography. Since many of my photos hang in my home, it's important to me that my prints look professional. After spending a large amount on cameras and lenses, why scrimp on the printer?

This is the best thing since sliced bread - seriously.  It is fast, feeds well generally, and doesn't require annoying cropping, etc., like so many scanners/scanning programs.  My former scanners all required that - selecting the "area" of what the scanner "saw."  Who wants to do that for a ton of pages?LOVE the auto feed feature.  LOVE the way you can put multiple, disparate types of paper into the feed tray at once, and voila - a document with all your little "bits," each one on it's own page.I did not give it five stars because it misfeeds just a *tad* too often to deserve that, IMO.  Removing misfeeds is a breeze, however - the lever is right in the front, presto - but it is supposed to be able to handle varying thicknesses, so in my experience, this could be improved upon.  Overall, it is amazing.  Compared to anything else out there, the misfeeds are a very small issue.  But for the record, they're a bit more frequent than they should be, at least with disparate paper thicknesses, as compared to a straight sheaf of 8.5" x 11" paper.  Those scanning the latter should experience fewer problems.The value is terrific, as you not only get a fabulous machine, but also the full Adobe Acrobat software...which means you can create and modify PDFs.  It is stand-alone, so you can use it apart from the ScanSnap, printing to a PDF from any application from which you can print (fabulous).  In addition, the OCR software really works!  My husband is an editor, and uses it regularly to pull book text into Word so he can make edits without retyping everything.  Works almost flawlessly, with any issues showing up more with margins and pagination than with content error.Usage tip:  If you are scanning multiple pages removed at one time from a magazine, make sure there isn't any glue left at the margin from the binding.  Sounds dumb, but sometimes it is almost invisible, and this will create a torn document and a jam (i.e., you'll not likely have anything scannable left from the page that jammed).Wish list:  The ability to scan long (longer than legal paper) pieces of paper.  Currently, this results in what the machine believes is a misfeed:  two pages being accidentally fed at once.  It would be nice if it could recognize a contiguous piece, and keep scanning it onto  separate PDF page(s), with a page break or something within the PDF.Overall a huge time saver and vastly superior to a flatbed.  Pop 40 pages in there and walk away...come back and save the document.  Then the best part?  Shred that 40 pages of paper!  ;-)

I have owned laser printers of all brands over the years -- HP, Brother, Samsung, and now Panasonic -- and this one offers many home-office functions in the lower end price range with decent speed.  If you print professional documents in black-and-white, a laser printer is a must for its crisp look and  permanent ink.Installation was a breeze on my IMac running the latest/last version of Snow Leopard; I'm certain it will install just as easily on Lion since the device is new enough to contain the appropriate drivers.  All you have to do is remove the tape, insert the toner cartridge, insert paper, and follow the directions on the CD.  (As with many printers today, this one requires you to start the Set-Up Wizard process before you connect it via USB to your computer.)  I printed my first page in ten minutes from opening the box.Copies and scans show slight degradation, particularly with handwriting, but no more than I expected.  The scan feature has several modes, depending on your computer software and purposes.  I especially like the ability to scan a document and create an email with the file automatically added as an attachment -- very cool.  The fax feature allows you to fax documents directly from your computer or from the flatbed on top of the printer.Pros: high-quality printing; decent speed; scans in several modes; copies; faxes from flatbed or computer; caller id ready; easy-to-use controls; includes a starter toner cartridge (see cons); phone cable for fax set-up included.Cons: not wireless/network-ready; noisy; includes only a starter toner cartridge for 500 pages; small paper tray (150 pages); no duplex printing; the screen is difficult to see without excellent lighting.  Because I placed this in a corner of my home office, I had to use a flashlight to read the display.If you buy this, make sure you have a printer-end to USB cable like this:Belkin Hi-Speed USB 2.0 Cable (10 Feet).  You will also want to buy a full toner cartridge to have on hand when the starter one runs dry: Panasonic Toner Cartridge - Black,Laser - 2500 Page.This printer performs well, but buyers should consider whether they want to have more features -- Wi-Fi capable, duplex printing, bigger paper tray -- or fewer.  If you are looking for a budget laser printer and don't need a scanner and fax, look at the currently less expensiveBrother HL-2270DW Compact Laser Printer with Wireless Networking and Duplex; it has networking and duplex printing, but is a printer only.  The Panasonic is perfect for those who want an "all-in-one" laser printer.-- Debbie Lee Wesselmann

This is a Vine review of the "Fellowes Heat and Slide Footrest, Black/Grey" that we were provided with to test out.This was a team effort: I assembled it and my better (and chillier) half tested it out.My rating on the assembly and integrity of the unit: 3 stars. In her words:"This works nicely to warm the bottoms of your feet if you are wearing socks but I couldn't really feel the heat through shoes or even my slippers. I've never used a heated footrest before and I do think I'll get some use of this as it gets colder this winter, but I don't see how it would provide enough heat in a really chilly space.So there you have it. An average rating for an average performer. For what it is, I don't think I'd buy one at this price point...$15-$20 seems more reasonable. If it had a fan to circulate the heat, then their price range might make sense.

Let's face it.  The ubiquitous office stapler gets little, if any, respect.  It's a utilitarian tool that nevertheless is a necessary office implement.  Staples are the best way to semi-permanently attach papers to one another.You'd think in this 'paperless' office of the future, we would have little need for a stapler.  Not so!  We use more paper now than ever before, not in small part because of the ready availability of home printers and copiers.  The humble stapler is thus squeezed and squeezed, and hit and punched and pushed and slammed all too often, even at home.  It serves its purpose, if it is well-made and can stand a lot of abuse (I've been known to use my old school Swingline stapler to smash nuts, pound a nail into the wall, and as a paperweight.Sometimes the good old stapler just isn't up to the task, if you ask too much of your old friend.  Let's say you have a thick stack of papers you need to assemble and keep, or maybe pass around at meetings.  The standard stapler isn't going to go through that thick sheaf of paper.  You could staple through one side, then the back, and that would sort of hold, until it came apart in the middle.  Or, you could break down and buy this Swingline heavy-duty stapler.I was like you, limping by on that decades-old stapler, perhaps lugging that thick stack of papers to the office, where I could borrow the office heavy-duty stapler.  Finally, I broke down and bought this stapler.  I'm glad I did, and I know you will be too.OK, I don't use it as often as I use the other stapler.  But, it's a perfect tool when you have that 100 page document you don't want flying all over the place, when you it's a professional-looking document that's called for.And this stapler performs!  It will take several lengths of staples, from a 1/8 inch to a 3/4 inch, the latter being capable of affixing staples to 160 sheets of paper.  And that's a lot of paper.  Maybe if you're writing the sequel to 'War and Peace' it won't be enough, but for most of us, that's a lot of paper!I love this stapler!  It works when you need it to work, and it does its job with aplomb. It doesn't take a lot of force to use it (surprisingly).  If you have a lot of paper (maybe that 160 page autobiography), just use gravity to help get through that much.Highly recommended.  No home office should be without one!

Back in the 1970's when I was in elementary school, by dad bought a hand-cranked pencil sharpener like the ones hanging from the wall in every classroom I ever was in and bolted it down to a table in his work shop beside the house. My dad is gone, now, but that pencil sharpener is still there, doing its thing like it did all those years ago. What I want to know is, where can I buy one of  those? I work in a private school where we live out the saga of the crappy pencil sharpener on a daily basis. The ubiquitous electric ones are constantly conking out or whirring away noisily without ever actually putting a decent point on a pencil. I sound like my own grandma, but those really were the days if you actually wanted to get a pencil sharp. I got this one, the highest end electric pencil sharpener I've ever used, from the Amazon Vine program, and it seems to work okay. It takes different sized pencils, including some larger ones, and so far has put a decent point on every one I've tried in it and has done so in a reasonable amount of time. It also makes less noise than the two less-expensive X-ACTO sharpeners I've tested it against. So  far it's the best electric sharpener I've used in years. But it still doesn't hold a candle to those indestructible buggers from my childhood, and I honestly think the best pencil sharpener I own is the tiny metal handheld one that I bought at the art supply store. When my kids need a pencil sharpened, that's the one they always get. So much for modern technology.

I have used document scanners since before they were common place.  The key to purchasing a product like this is understanding the application and then meeting that application need with the right product.  For example, I would never purchase a $6,500 Kyocera network stand alone scanner for a home based business, even if I got a great deal.  Simply put, the TCO (Total Cost of Ownership) would be way too high. Then again, I would not purchase a Neato Desktop scanner for a Small or Medium Sized business, especially if the businesses were document centric or heavy.  It simply would not last (a few of my friends can attest to that). The Epson Workforce DS-510 is a fantastic product for home based or small to medium sized businesses, even if they are document intensive.  It would also serve a small work-group within a larger organization very well.The Epson comes perfectly packaged with very clear instructions.  Removing and setting up the scanner is easy.  I installed this system (and software) on a 4 year old Dell Inspiron Windows 7 system with 12gb of RAM with no glitches, even setting up my Evernote ([...] account as a destination using my desktop as a client relay (which is typical anyway as the desktop synchronizes with Evernote the same way Google Drive synchronizes with your desktop).  Total install time was about 8 minutes once out of the box.  You will need an available USB 2.0 port of course (cable included).  The DS-510 has a solid build quality and feels very reliable and will easily take any abuse a workgroup might throw at it.  The footprint of the scanner is small enough that space will not be an issue for most environments. Of course the scanner is TWAIN compliant and ISIS available via download. Another reviewer noted the "15 page document feeder" was too small.  However, my DS-510 came with a 50 page document tray that I found more than sufficient (even getting 61 pages in the tray). This tray capacity is likely more than sufficient for most small/medium businesses unless they are something like a law firm or medical billing company.  In those cases, these businesses are likely opting for large scale Kyocera's or Ricoh's anyway. Also, I confirmed the tray capacity with the Epson website and product specs ([...]Operation of the scanner was flawless in my two weeks of regular use.  Though rated at 3,000 sheets per day, I never hit that of course. In my use, the scanner easily handled folded paper, torn paper, old paper, new paper, receipts, photographs (though I do not recommend this scanner for quality image scanning), even a few missed staples, etc.  If you never had duplex scanning capability (scans both sides at once), you will never go back once you do.  If you think you can save a few dollars by avoiding it, I would recommend you just shell out the few extra dollars and get the Duplex.  First time you need it, you will be thankful.  Although one reviewer complained about the blank page detection, I experienced no issues and the software eliminated all blank pages with a single exception in which there was doodling on the back of the page.  More than reasonable in my opinion.  Both duplex (double side) and simplex (single side) scanning was more than fast enough to meet my needs. Time to first scan completion was less than 2 seconds from initiation.  The software was very reliable and the TWAIN driver allowed me to interface with all my TWAIN compliant software. Creating Adobe .pdf documents is easy and the scanner will take paper sizes up to 8.5 X 36.What This Scanner is NOT:☞In my opinion (as a photographer), this scanner is not designed nor intended for quality photograph reproduction. A flatbed scanner is needed for that application despite the scanner specs of 600dpi and 48 bit color bit depth.  However, this scanner will reproduce quality images for business purposes.☞This is not a true network scanner. For true network scanning capability, you will need the optional Epson Network Interface Unit (RJ-45, 10BaseT/100Base TX).  However, to avoid the need for this option, you can simply make the destination folder a shared resource on your network- which allows to create an instant archive anyway.  You can also scan to any cloud service such as Google Drive, Evernote, etc...; making the optional network need a thing of the past unless you are dealing with very confidential documents.As I said earlier, understanding your application is critical.  In my opinion, this is a perfect device for a home based business or small to even medium sized business.  Total Cost of ownership is minimal and the price point is exactly where it should be for my needs. In the end, I could find very little to fault with this scanner except, perhaps, I would have liked a 100 sheet capacity document feeder. By the way, the Amazon price seems to be the least expensive I have found so far on this product.

UPDATE after a couple of months: I have updated this printer from 2 to 4 stars, though the stars are dependent on the price. What has changed since below? I always thought it odd the way you have to set up profiles to do scanning - it just seemed to hard to be the way it was. But the user guide is really horrible.So.... about 2 weeks ago the printer stopped printing and I wound up reinstalling the software suite. I know it was the same version as I used the install program I'd downloaded before. But this time a desktop shortcut appeared that hadn't been there before, which opens a page that enables a few things, including easy scanning, and it has an "Advanced" button on scanning that lets you do what you should be able to.Also, I found that going to the printer's web page and setting up 'network scanning' to be a great help. You have to have a folder that is a network shared folder on your PC (I'm using Win 7) and you tell the printer to put the docs if creates in that folder.There is one thing that I don't like: Several times a day, but at no set times, the printer wakes up, sort of 'looks around', as it were, and then goes back to sleep. In a regular office I doubt anyone would notice but I use this in my home office and it's right next to my desk, and it's annoying.These are early impressions as I've been using the printer for about 3 days, so I can't say anything about toner usage and the like. However, there are certain pros and cons that are obvious from the beginning that aren't going to change, I think. I should point out that I think printers have to be evaluated based on their price and right now amazon is selling this for about $250.PROS:1) it's a fast printer for it's price, and the time-to-first-page is quick (from sleep, not from power up - it's slow to reach ready if it's been turned off.2) Power draw: I have yet to have this draw more than 600 watts. I have a Brother that I like that is about the same speed but the power draw is much much higher. At 600 watts, this one shouldn't cause problems. (I'm using a simple KillAWatt to determine this.) When it's resting but still awake it draws 12 watts and when sleeping about 6.3) About as noisy as expected for this speed printing. However, if you don't need speed that high there is a 'quiet mode' that slows down the printing but draws less power and is genuinely pretty quiet.4) At $250, if you really just need a group printer with minimal faxing and scanning, this might be a good deal.CONS:Some of these don't much matter, like the really bad unpacking, setup guide, as if you're careful it'll be fine. But I've set up a lot of printers and this seems very clumsy. But as this is a one time thing I'm not listing it other than as an aside.1) Network setup (and this is the only way I use these kinds of printers, I don't do USB) is clumsy. The install finds the printer easily enough and though the printer doesn't seem to lose connectivity, the danged monitor program often thinks the printer is off-line, but then changes it's mind a moment later.2) The interface is wretched. You can use a web browser, which is probably the best way. There is also a little program but it seems cumbersome and lacks access to all of the options. But even the web browser interface seems crude and poorly designed, especially compared to an HP or Brother interface.3) Print quality is OK, but even on the highest setting it doesn't handle small fonts well. For instance, I printed out the front page of the NY Times website, and I have a little Brother laser that prints the small text perfectly fine using 600 DPI. On this machine, even using 1200 DPI and setting the toner to the darkest setting, the text is poor.4) Scanning seems so convoluted that I find myself thinking "oh, c'mon, Dave, you're just not paying attention." I can make it work, but it means starting a fax on the computer, then walking over to the printer and pushing buttons and then going back to the computer and waiting... and waiting... It's incredibly slow, and I don't mean the mechanical process of scanning, I mean how long it takes for the image to be available on the computer. At first I thought something wasn't working (and this is doing a 1-page scan either to PDF or to JPG) so I'd cancel. Eventually I just waited and sure enough, it's just that slow.5) Scan quality is OK for utility/general purposes, but it's not good for photos. And it lacks some of the obvious things: If you're scanning a photo (and you tell it you're scanning a photo) I can find no way to get it to show a preview so that I can create a border around the photo: It scans the entire platen and then you have to crop the photo. This is the kind of feature that was on the first scanner I bought in the late 90's.6) The control panel on the printer is crude and minimal. I don't usually have it connected to a phone line, but during first-power-on allowed fax and now I can't get rid of constant error messages complaining that it's not connected to a phone line, nor does there seem to be a way to disable faxing, having once OK'ed it. Also, you can't initiate scanning from the printer, which is unusual.Some of these issues might seem less problematic if the user guide weren't so minimal. I kid you not: The instructions for scanning to a computer fit on one page, and if you single-spaced them would take about half a page. There's no discussion of all of the options at all.I'm a vine reviewer and I didn't pay for this, but if I had I'd return it. It's not a horrible printer, and I suspect that most of the issues are software-related. But I downloaded the latest drivers and made sure my device had the latest firmware.  But it's not acceptable to me with the software as it is. Are there ways around some of the problems I mentioned above? Perhaps. But the documentation is very poor and it's just not worth my time to try to figure it out when other brands make is so easy.

I have used Uniden phones for a while.  I find they typically have good features, good quality and a nice price.  I was offered the opportunity to review this phone and, frankly,  this is a most impressive phone system.1.  What is in the box?  You receive, in a surprisingly small box, two headsets, with separated batteries and back covers, along with a answering machine base for one headset and a second small base with a charger unit attached (you, of course, also receive the two phone lines.  Also included is a decent (but not comprehensive) list of instructions.2. Set-up: Easy.  Frankly, very easy.  Without looking at the instructions, I simply placed the batteries in the headsets, and the phone had some power and was ready to go.  After placing the phone in the cradle, and placing the wires for power and the phone-line, I was ready to go.  Phone: I was immediately able to use the phone immediately.3. Features: The most impressive aspect of this phone is the Bluetooth connect feature.  I cannot state how awesome a tool this is.  Using the Bluetooth feature on my cellphone, I simply uploaded the PIN and this phone and my cellphone connected.  I was able to actually upload my phone book from my cell to this headset as well.  By selecting either the phone button or cell button I can use either to dial or answer either phone using just this headset.  Wow.The other cool feature is that you can set-up two cell phones for interaction with this system and assign distinctive ring-tones.  Thus, you can answer this phone or two cell-phones no matter where you are in the house (it gives a 33 foot range, but in practice I have achieved 40-50 feet in many areas of my home without an issue).I love this feature.  I have no idea if it is proprietary to Uniden, but it is easy to set-up and use and makes things very easy.4. Aesthetic: The headsets are silver in color, with the inner phone parts being black.  The buttons are lit during use and are fairly large and easy to see.  The buttons signifying Home and Cell are green and purple, respectively, and are easily found.  The Home base with answering machine is also silver with black features.  It is not the most stylish phone system I have seen, but it is nice looking and certainly not something to be embarrassed about in the slightest.Positives:1.  There are a number of positives with this phone.  First, the phone is nice looking and easy to hold.  The buttons are easily read and to use.  The display is a nice feature as well with caller ID showing and possible messages displayed along with date and time.The Bluetooth connection makes this phone a winner.  Love this feature (see above).  The phone also has a speaker on each headset (can use this as an intercom).  Another interesting thing is that the phone has the correct date and time displayed without my entering it because I think it uploaded the information from my cellphone.  Cool.2. Neutral:  Nothing stands out in my mind after use as being mediocre.3. Negatives:  Not many negatives at all with this phone. In fact, I have none. The only quibble is I think the "End" button is too small and poorly placed, resulting in some thought about where my fat finger has to go to terminate the call.  I think this irritation will go away with more use, but it is the only (little) negative I have about this phone.Conclusions:In short, I am very impressed with this phone system.  In my mind, the over the top feature is the Bluetooth connection, which really expands the range and use of this phone (and justifies the landline, which becomes an afterthought in my household because of the use of a cellphone). The price currently on Amazon is around 50 to 60ish and this is an excellent price point for the features available.  I wouldn't hesitate with purchasing this item.I reserve judgment for battery life and use, but for the few days I have had it, the system seems to conserve battery power off the chargers quite well.  A winning system that is worth an upgrade for the Bluetooth features alone.  A winner.  I am very happy with this item, and I think a potential buyer would be as well.
