When purchasing binders, one needs to consider the use you have intended for them.  There are two things I look at,  the cover and the rings.  As a teacher and a mom, I have a lot of experience with binders.The cover:If I am simply going to put papers in them and store them on the shelf, I like the hard binders.  I use this type for filing recipes and documents I need to access.  Since they are stiff they are easy to shove back onto the shelf.  In the classroom these also work better, as they are less likely to slip off the shelf than the flexible cover binders.However, I find that buying hard binders for my kids leads to problems.  The kids like to stuff these into their backpacks, and the edges where the plastic is sealed quickly start to peel off, and the covers get folded over.  For them, I have found that a flexible binder in general will make it farther though the school year.  They will sometimes crack along the spine, but usually not enough to make the binder unusable, and a little duct tape will fix it.The rings:The second thing to look at is the rings.  The best ones (in my opinion) are the D shaped, as they hold more, with the little dimple on one side that fits into a depression on the other side.  This prevents papers from getting caught as you flip through.  They also hurt less if you snap them onto your fingers! It's hard to know exactly what to think of these folders.  For a product such as this, my judgment critera are utility and durability. How easy are the folders to use, how well do they suit my intended purpose, and how will they stand up to sometimes rigorous office use?Taking the second criterion first, the folders are very sturdy and very well made. The outsides are made of tough cardboard-like material that is unlikely to wear significantly even under heavy use. The inside dividers are naturally somewhat less heavy, but more than adequate for the simple duty of separating papers. The prongs used to hold papers punched with two holes at the top are often the weak point; if they are opened and closed constantly to remove and insert papers, they might be subject to failure from metal fatigue. While I haven't used the folders for a long enough period of time to see if this will indeed happen, it looks unlikely. The prongs seem strong enough to last, although pliable enough (just about) to not be difficult to use. Overall, then, I'd have to say that the folders rate right at the top for durability.Unfortunately, I can't say the same for utility. The design of these folders seems a little strange. There are the aforementioned metal prongs; there's nothing really new here. There are two dividers, allowing papers to be stored in three groups or sections. Again, nothing really new.What is unusual is the combination of interior dividers and prongs. How is this supposed to work? It would seem, offhand, that you can only use the prongs to hold  papers in the third, backmost section of the folder. However, the dividers are cut so that you can slip them between pages that are held by the prongs. But would you really want to do that? It would make access to interior pages quite difficult. Or, perhaps the idea is to use the folders one way or another: Use dividers to separate sections of pages, or ignore the dividers and secure punched sheets with the prongs. But that leads to the next problem.There are no side walls on these folders, and there can't be any, because then using prongs to secure pages would be difficult, perhaps impossible, and pointless. But if you store a lot of pages--- enough to justify sectioning--- wouldn't you rather have side walls so that the pages don't potentiallly spill out when the folders are carried, or while being removed from often-jammed filing cabinets?In short ,the folders seem like a compromise design, attempting to combine two different usage styles, and ultimately falling short at both. I think you'd be better off buying separate, single-purpose folders. I'm not going to be using these except for casual purposes. For general office usage, I'll turn to other options.

I wanted to scan old negatives and slides.  This scanner does a very nice job.  It wanted something faster but could not afford it.  So I scan while doing other things.  I am very happy with the result.  I am saving money and getting results much more to my liking than by having my slides and negatives scanned by a service.  I am a power-user who is knowledgeable about photography, so this choice will not suit everyone.Scanning of negatives and slides in high resolution (4800 dpi and higher) is slow, but you can't get faster without spending a lot more money.  The Digital Ice technology is a must for scanning slides and negatives and works VERY well.  I removes the appearance of dust without a negative impact on quality.  Don't scan slide or negatives without it.I usually scan slides and negatives at 4800 DPI and that gives quite detailed images.  I scan to TIF format and then use a good photo editor to do corrections (exposure, cropping, color balance, resize) and export JPG format final versions in the 3-5 MP size range (but you can resize and compress to get smaller sizes if you want).  Then I delete the TIF files.I have some 25 ISO Kodachrome slides which have a lot of fine detail, so I scan them at 6400 DPI which gives a very nice result, but it is slow and results in very large file sizes.  I crop or resize the 6400 DPI scans of 25 ISO Kodachrome slides to 30 MP images (6300 x 4725) or smaller.  I have not tried higher than that.  The detail in the scans at this high resolution is higher than I expected.I would buy this scanner again.  I think that Epson makes the best scanners for my use.  I would not buy a less expensive Epson scanner than the v500 for my use.  If my pockets were deeper I would opt for something a little faster.

Why "again"? Because I'm leaving this review on every set of Prismas Amazon has. Why? Because I want anyone buying any quantity of these pencils to know how lovely they are.When I started developing a more serious interest in drawing and art in general I immediately began researching tools and techniques. If you've read any other reviews I've left on products you'll notice that that's a recurring theme! I was fortunate enough have been born in an era where I've had internet access since I was pretty young so it's never been very hard for me to find information.In my research I noticed that a lot of the people I admired on various forums and art websites liked Prismacolor. I loved the way their pieces looked and I wanted the same smooth, deep, well-blended coloring effects that they were able to achieve. We all know that typical children's colored pencils don't do that job very well, so I set out to get myself this small set of Prismas.That experience was quite a few years ago now (where does the time go??) and I've been hooked ever since. I was later gifted the 60 set, and I've continued to build my collection up since then. Just this week I purchased the remaining few pencils I didn't have so now I have all 150!These pencils are incredibly soft, vibrant and they blend beautifully. I've tried Derwent Coloursoft, Derwent Studio, and Faber-Castell Polychromos and they're also lovely pencils -- I even gave them glowing reviews here on Amazon -- but Prismacolor continues to be my favorite. I think that anyone of any skill level should have access to these pencils. Since Amazon sells them so much cheaper than anywhere else I would even recommend buying a smaller set for the young children in your life because everyone deserves to work with such brilliant colors!Pros:Soft, creamy, blendableExtremely pigmentedInexpensive compared to other artist-grade brandsCan give you a painterly effect that other brands can'tCons:Since the leads are super soft and aren't bound to the wood casing, they're prone to breakage. I don't seem to have as much of an issue with it as other people do. I've dropped pencils several times and they've been fine. However, I gifted a friend the 24 set a couple Christmases ago and she had some issues with breakage.These pencils are wax-based so you might encounter some bloom, but that is true of any wax-based pencil, not just PrismaThey don't score as high in the lightfastness department as other brands do :( (biggest bummer)If you're unsure, but the 12 color set first. I've seen it as low as ten bucks and rarely higher than 15 on Amazon, and even if you decide to buy a larger set you'll have backups of your primaries/secondaries + black, white and brown which definitely isn't a bad thing.

I don't know how well it combats wrist pain; I'm not used to using a cushion, and it seemed like elevating my wrist was more uncomfortable than leaving it flat.  Plus, this item is bulky & claims more desk space than a traditional mouse pad.The soft cushion comes off with a good tug.  I tried using the pad without the pillow, but now neither way feels right.  I put the pillow back on, and I'm using it now, but I feel ambivalent.  The mere presence of this big white rubbery lump is beginning to bug me.  I think I will eventually end up taking it off.The mouse pad surface, however, is excellent.

UpdateI've been using this for a couple months and other than the slowness of the scanning, have really come to appreciate this machine more and more. I'm beginning to think this is an isolated problem on this machine since none of the others have experienced similiar issues. The quality of the scan is superb (just slow) but aside from that...this machine really grows on you the more it is used. Print is nice speed, paper tray very sufficient, VERY nice sized ink catridges that seem to be lasting a suprisingly long time.I've upped my original review based upon more use and the suspicion the scan related issues could be an isolated problem.Original ReviewI've been a Brother user for many years but needed a quick solution for an inexpensive printer/scanner and opted for an Epson last year. I was quite satisfied with the price to quality ratio so when this came up for review I jumped at the opportunity as I routinely have a minimum of three printers (two home offices and one off-site home office).Now, this is a bit better model than the prior Epson so I was expecting more out of it. In some aspects it is better but in others...actually performs worse than the 840 model.Pro's:It holds a nice amount of paper, provides an above average print at a very respectable speed and the ink cartridges are much larger...a distinct advantage for serious home office users.Netural Notables:Set-up seemed a bit slow (but intuitive). Software installed without a glitch but took over ten minutes. Re-booted and computer recognized everything. Test print looked good.Con's:Scanning is SLOWWWWWWWWWW. The image actually looks substantially better in terms of quality but the process is unacceptably slow. Worse, it's glitchy so won't fully "import" when using other software to perform the scan. I suspect a glitch somewhere but the prior Epson (lower model) worked flawlessly with both Google Picasso, Lightroom and Adobe products. I expected this to perform Better NOT worse. Now, despite how slow the scan is, the result looks very nice even on the lower settings. Colors are very true, details look surprisingly nice. Everything is clear. However, for a small office use...this won't work. Unless I can find the glitch, this will be banished to the side office for only sporadic use.Next Glitch - it decides not to print now and then for absolutely no apparent reason. Yes, settings are all good. It will print one time and then simply want to spool the next. We're talking one page prints so it's not related to memory etc...I have had to cancel a print on several sessions then start over. VERY irritating.Bottom line - This would be a good option for someone that needs quality over quantity. It's not fast enough for a serious home office user and small glitches get old VERY fast. I will update if I find out what the glitches are but to date, all tests and settings show up as being fine...it's just "finicky".

When it comes down to everyday uses, we all need a little helo now and then. For Scotch, they know how to make clever things come around, and that is there with this Handband Dispenser. It is simple and easy to use, by just wrapping it around your hand. The strips are also pre-cut and come out of the dispenser with a simple touch. I really am surprised at how easy it is to use, and no mess or clutter. I absolutely suggest you get this if you want to find a easier way to tape up all your projects, letters to mail, or anything else. Scotch does it right, with a taped message.Price: A-Convience: B+Overall: B+

Everyone loves Post-Its, but these labels are only marginally adequate.PROS:- You can print on them and they will stick to some things, like paper.CONS:- They are 3 7/16" long, which is too large for many folders.- The Post-It template for the labels is poor, though an Avery equivalent is available.- If you use the labels on anything but a folder-like surface, the adhesive is weak and the labels tend to curl.If you have a specific need for labels this size and plan to use them only as intended, on folders, then they're fine. Otherwise there are many superior options.

These Fellowes Hot Laminating Pouches, are letter size and slightly heavier than your basic laminating pouch. They ran right through my Fellows Cosmic 95 laminator without any problems. The laminated sheets are not stiff like the more heavier weight pouches but are a good step up from your standard 3 mil laminating pouches that come with the laminating machine. There is a slight ripple to the finished piece but all in all I like the weight of the laminated sheet. Packaged with 100 pouches per pack the cost savings are excellent.

While the glossy tape that I use at the office is good for keeping things together, it shows up very easily on gift wrap, being all shiny.  The matte or satin finsh on this is perfect for gifts..  doesnt attract or reflect light, so that you see the wrapping paper and not the tape. Very simple and it works.Con:  this type of tape is really for gift wrapping and isnt as attractive for normal everyday use, but it can be used as such.  Get both scotch gift tape and scotch regualr tape and you will have the right tape for the right occasion.

When I got tired of all the loose papers on my desk, I shopped around for some clever organization products. These pockets are very useful. They stick to all kinds of surfaces. I use them to organize bills that need to be paid, outgoing mail, and stuff that needs to be followed up on. My desk looks so much cleaner, and I feel so much more organized. Nice.

These fun fruit-designed Post-It Notes were just exactly what I expect from Post-It Products... colorful designs on quality paper.  My family broke the stack into three sections, with each of my kids claiming a fruit section as their own.  I wound up with the green limes, and I'm using them here on the computer desk.  It's a nice change of pace from my usual yellow or pink notes.

My personal scanning needs are simple but even if yours are more complex, the Canon image FORMULA P-150 should be able to satisfy you. Here's why I think that is: it's fast (15 max. ppm; 30 max ipm), quiet, easy to use and set up,  compact, TWAIN compliant, produces high quality scans in both b&w; and color, batches up to 20 sheets, has 1 pass duplex scanning (i.e., two-sided scanning), and scans a variety of different size documents and images virtually effortlessly.The one factor that causes me to deduct 1/2 star from my rating is that while it is compact, it, at a little over two lbs, is not as lightweight as I expected it to be (given that Canon refers to it as the Scan-tini).Despite this one very minor con, the Canon image FORMULA P-150 is a scanner I'd recommend you consider very seriously.

I'm notorious for using things for purposes they were not intended for, and these labels are no exception. I don't use them as mailing labels.When this big box of 3,000 labels arrived, I immediately pulled off a few of the labels and stuck them to the top and smooth side (vertically) of a half-pint canning jar and onto a ziplock bag and put them in the freezer. A day later, the labels were still adhering well, and yet they were not a complete pain to get off. (Try pulling the label off dry, and if it doesn't come right off, it will come off after a soak in dishwater.) So now I can print out sheets of labels like "08/2010 Tomato Sauce" or "2010 Okra Seeds" and have them handy for when I'm canning, freezing, and dehydrating all my garden produce and saving seeds for next season. I put up a LOT of food. Also, I can quickly write and stick eat-by dates on anything in the fridge.Labels for canning jars cost a lot of money. These are just the ticket, and I can print whatever info onto them that I need. They will work at room temperature, in the fridge, or in the freezer, and there are lots and lots of them. Just what I needed!

This is a review for a wide ruled filler paper. It's 3 hole punched with blue lines and a red margin. The paper is light yet strong. I tested it with a gel pen and a regular #2 pencil. The paper withstood the gel well and did not bleed through. It also withstood the #2 pencil well and did not imprint through. Overall a nice light filler paper that is also pretty sturdy. Overall, very pleased with the quality. A sample was provided for review purposes.

It's tape, so it's not going to change your life or anything.  But Scotch brand tape is vastly superior to the generic crap my wife usually buys, because:  (1) it tears cleanly so you can apply it, (2) it doesn't split along its length and cause you to lose your sanity trying to get back to a single strip the entire width of the roll, and (3) it doesn't have gobs of adhesive that come off the sticky side and stick to the side that's not supposed to be sticky.I'm not sure I see the advantage of the three small rolls in this pack; I prefer larger single rolls myself.  But, as I said, it's good stuff.

The only advantage is that it can staple about 60 pages (claim is 75) with ease because it has more leverage due to its big size. But it is heavy, bulky, takes a lot of room on the desk and uses properieteryStanley Bostitch B8 Xtra High Carbon PowerCrown Staples (STCR75XHC)that are more than double the price of  Swingline staples. The stapler itself does not come with any staples at all and standard staples -Swingline S.F. 3 Premium Chisel Point Staples, 0.25 Inch Leg Length, 105 Count Half Strips, Silver, 5000 Staples per Box (S7035440)- do not fit in this stapler. The basis for antibacterial claim is hard to figure out. The stapler comes with no instructions or staples and you have to figure out to press the button and then pull staple housing forward to load the staples.There is a reason it probably does not come with any staples: when you order the staples, you are going to feel ripped off! Most expensive staples out there.Even if you need to staple multiple pages (>50), I feel thatSwingline Deluxe Heavy Duty Stapler (S7039005R), which, as of now is a few cents more expensive, is better constructed and more ergonomic stapler. In the long run you will save a lot in the cost of staples with Swingline stapler because the staples for this Stanley stapler are exorbitantly expensive.

I purchased these to use for shipping out my customer orders.  Each label is exactly half the sheet of paper (making each label 8.5" tall x 5.5" wide).  They print well, and the adhesive is great.  Simply trim off the excess white paper after you print, peel it off, and stick it on your package.  Can't get much easier than that!

This is a functional, inexpensive binder that is not really intended to stand up to a lot of wear and tear.  The materials are inexpensive, although sturdy enough to see the average kid through a school year.  The kind of binder that can be bought in September and tossed in June when it's been used up and looks dilapidated.  A good product for the price.

The Brother PT-2430PC label printer is an extremely nice PC-connected unit.  When I received the unit I followed the directions for preparing the printer to be attached to my PC...OK, here's all there was to it:1) Unpack the label printer, and power and USB cords2) Open the label printer and insert the label tape cartridge3) Close the unit and connect the label printer to the power cord4) Connect the USB cord to the unit and to the PC5) The PC (mine runs Windows XP) finds the hardware (this took 2-3 minutes at the most)6) The directions state that you will then be ready to use the label printer, but I received a prompt that I needed to restart my computer to complete the installation process.  I turned off the label printer and restarted the computer7) When the computer finished rebooting and I turned the label printer back on the PC found it immediately and a pop-up window appeared that allows you to generate the text, etc., for a labelNote: a disc is included with the label printer, but you do not need to install anything before using the printer.  Software for running the label printer is housed in the printer itself.  If, however, you want to produce fancier labels than the built-in software can handle, then you can install the supplemental software onto your PC's hard drive.  The built-in software was more than adequate for my needs.Preparing to print a label...I found the built-in software to be quite intuitive.  There are default settings that allow you start typing the text for a label right off the bat.  After poking around for less than 5 minutes I was able to discover how to insert a text-box, produce multiple-line text labels, insert a photo or image from a file, and there is even a screen-capture option.  Of course the labels are B/W so any photos or figures will be pixilated - like a newspaper photo, but, of course, small.When you are ready to print your label just click on the appropriate button on the pop-up screen menu and the label printer starts right up.  First it will spit out and clip off a piece of label tape about 1.5 cm (um...3/4") long.  It then prints the label and clips it off automatically.All in all, this is an awesome unit...well, as awesome as a label printer is likely to get...I mean, it's not a big-screen LCD TV or anything, but it does its job just fine.Oh, and if you need to make labels on the run...as from a lap-top where you do not have access to a power outlet, the label printer can run on 6 AA batteries.So, all in all, I find this label printer to do a great job.  It will certainly take care of just about any labeling tasks you may have...and it can use labels of different widths, up to 1" wide.  Since the tape is installed in a cassette you can switch between sizes as needed.The only downside I see to the unit is the 1.5 cm bit of labelling tape that is snipped off every time you make a label.  That's not a major drawback, but I thought you'd want to know about it.I rate this as a 5-star product.  You'll have to check out the price and your own label-making needs to see if this is a good value for you.  If you make LOTS of labels this printer well almost certainly be worth it for you, your family, or office.5 stars!  Print-on! :-)

If you are the hunt for a small binder that you can slip in with your laptop and carry those few important notes then this is the binder for you. The extra inner pocket is a great feature and it means that you can add in everything from a calculator to a phone.  It is sturdy and appears to be built to last. I have had other binders of bigger sizes from the same people and have not had any problems with them.  The size although is a plus if that is what you are looking for does make it a little specialized and I would have loved a starter pack of paper. But alas no but still 4 stars.

I tried OBi110 Voice Service Bridge and VoIP Telephone Adapter but found that if you don't use Google Voice, its complicated to set up. I tried and tried to set it up with my subscription Skype account to no avail. I sent that back and ordered Ooma Telo. 10 minutes, up and running. Then I opted for the Premier package which comes with all the bells and whistles you could ask for. As long as Ooma don't raise their subscription prices I will be a happy camper.

We use this with a 2 inch Avery binder to keep all our finances and household affairs in order.  The tabs are great to quickly customize categories that need to be specific.  More useful than pre-printed tabs that just say BANK, HOME, AUTO, etc.  Very easy to set up, print and use.

This wrist rest is perfect for our mouse pad. It adheres really securely to the glass desk, almost as if it has adhesive, but it doesn't.  And if I want to move it, it comes right off, so it's not a problem to move it.  It's the perfect amount of cushion and makes using the mouse much more comfortable.

I have had difficulty finding these pens in my area, so I was pleased to find them on Amazon, and at a good price.  Sometimes, I can find them in black ink, but not the red ink.  I also like their extra fine point.  They are great little pens.

I had to find out for myself. It has been suggested to me that this is the best paper out there to get. I have to admit this is good paper. I don't have that many paper jams. I would recommend this to others.

Out of the box took me about 35-45 minutes to set up wirelessly and most of the time was just watching it install to my computer. Really easy setup compared to other wireless devices I have used. A novice would not have any problem setting this thing up.The wireless scanning and printing makes my life a millions times easier. Have had it a week and have not have a problem yet.Printing speed is nothing special.Scanning speed is much quicker than my old printer. Same with copying.Overall, it is a great printer for $80. It does everything and works well.

They came in three colors.  A slate grey, lime green and hot pink with detailing.  The holders are made of a slightly rigid plastic.  They have two peel off adhesive areas on the back that allow you to stick them on any smooth, clean surface.  And they seem to peel back off O.K. but I would not stick them on anything delicate.  The  zig-zag stacked post-its dispense well.

This glue is just OK and the quality is lacking. Not the same glue I used to use. I don't know if I have gotten a bad batch or the glue is just subpar. The glue doesn't stick  paper on cardboard, it just falls off.
It is good for what it does. I have another wireless phone and some other devices. I think there is a radio wave interference.

These are your basic sticky notes, but in a pastel color selection (light pink, really light blue, and yellow).  The paper is advertised as recycled, and they really feel like it.  I know I've had other "recycled" products in the past that didn't feel like they were recycled, so I was hoping these might feel better.  Rather, they feel thin, like a cheap paper.  I'm glad they are recycled, but I wish they didn't feel so "used"

My wife and teenage daughter are getting ready to thumb-wrestle over who gets which color.  I guess that means that they are good looking....  These are very bright and sticky (but they are not as sticky as the classic post-it notes).  They really do look good and 400 of them is enough to decorate a couple walls.  While I think they are brighter and more vivid than the classic post-it notes I don't know if that justifies the relatively high price.

Die-hard crossword fan; these do the job wonderfully, especially with the extended erasers (I didn't say I was excellent at crosswords or did them in ink!) 0.7 mm is just the right thickness, too - you can write dark enough and thick enough to see easily. Highly recommend!

I tested this model at a local Staples against a slightly lower priced Canon all-in-one.  Did a color copy on each to compare output, and I was surprised / disappointed to see that the HP copy had shifted the red in the original to orange, and navy blue was being printed as black.  Since I plan to use my next all-in-one to print 4x6 and 8x10 photos, this is a fatal flaw for me.Perhaps it was an issue with this unit only, or perhaps photo printing will be better than color copying - but I can't highly reccommend based on my testing above.  Shame too, because the HP scored points with me initially due to the larger-than-average ink cartridges and smart design.

The Epson Workforce 645 Wireless Printer, Scanner Copier and Fax is a great choice  for anyone who is looking for a good, moderately priced unit of this type.  Setting it up on my Vista desktop was almost as easy as my other Epson printers.  It did present a little bit of a challenge as in following the enclosed directions. It says not to use the plug-and-play features that most Windows OS's have. However, if you do follow the directions, it wants to make it primarily a fax.  That was a bit frustrating at first!  Take it for gratned that everyone's computer system is going to be a bit different, give yourself time to walk through it. Other than that it really is very simple compated to early models of all in one units.All of the necessary printer ink is included within the box.  It takes approximately 7 - 10 minutes to initialize before you can actually end up using it for the first time.  This printer also scans beautifully and makes a quick and quiet print that has really good overall quality.  Like the Epson Artisoan 730 that I have on another computer in our home office, this printer is also very easy to set up.This unit is standard size. It is fairly compact, you can fit it into a space that I was not able to put my other Epson printer into simply because of the footprint being so very large.  Instead of having to make sure that I had enough room, this one fit on.  In short, it won't overhwelm most homes or offices.Like anything that Epson makes, the printer ink cartridges are proprietary.  You won't very likely find after market brands to avoid paying Epson's higher price model. No surprise there. Printer ink always seems to require a bit of cash outlay.  This unit, more than the Epson Artisan 730 eats ink. Make sure you really need to print. I don't use a FAX much anymore except to send things. I would imagine that recieving faxes on a more frequent basis would make those ink purchases a bit more frequent.Overall print quality is excellent. I think that Epson does a superior job compared to HP's printers of the same type and price range. Images are crisp, the printing process is quiet and very fast.All in all, I would recommend it to anyone who needs a FAX, otherwise there are other printer, scanner copiers that have a bit better performance, even within the Epson line that might be a bit better choice.

I already had the Brother 7840W at my other office, and bought the 7860DW for my home office. I have two Macbook Pros, and a wireless network.I pulled this out of the box and set it in the place of my old copier that recently was giving me problems. I pulled off all the shipping tape, pulled out the toner cartridge and shook side to side and replaced it per the instructions, plugged her in, added 8.5 x 11 paper, and tested the copier. Works beautifully! I wanted everything to work wirelessly, so I used the menus to sync up the unit per the instructions with my wireless network. This took literally one minute. I then used the CD to load software, including the Presto PageManager scanner software. I also went online to Brother's website to load latest printer driver, scanner TWAIN driver, and PPD drivers, basically everything they offered. The install took only a few minutes.I also have an iPhone, and tested out my Brother iPrint&Scan; app. It prints directly/wirelessly from my iPhone, and also scans directly into my iPhone. What is cool about the app is if there is a document in the feeder, it scans from there. If there is no document in the feeder, it automatically scans from the glass. Yes, it scans color also!I set it up to go to sleep after 3 minutes, and it works fine. The unit is very quiet, and when it sleeps, it is perfectly silent. Some reviewers said it was loud and/or would not sleep when used wirelessly. Not with a Mac setup. It sleeps fine and is not loud when printing or scanning.I am not using the fax feature on this unit, but am using it on the sister unit at my office and it works perfectly.I tried the duplex printing option, and the n in 1 printing option, and it works fine. It sounds like a lot is going on (noise) when printing double sided to duplex the paper, so I am not sure if I will eventually get paper jams. But, so far so good. Nice to be able to save paper by automatically printing double sided.I can't speak to Windows machines, but the Mac setup on this thing required no cables, and took a total of 30 minutes counting downloading the latest drivers.It also comes with Presto! PageManager Standard version 9.0. It linked up instantly with my scanner wirelessly and it works fine. Look up what this scanning software can do by going to the NewSoft website at [...].I have set up a lot of printers, scanners, all-in-ones over the years, and by far this setup was the easiest and best. This printer/scanner/fax is perfect for a small office. The printer has a nice document feeder and the paper tray holds plenty of paper. I bought a high capacity toner cartridge for when the starter cartridge runs out.

I am usually a pen person, but when I had the chance to get the new mechanical pencil from uni-ball I decided to give it a go.  I often have used uni-ball pens for the smooth writing and the way they feel in my hand and this pen supposedly had stronger lead, which made me want to try it.  Ordinarily, I am somewhat hesitant to use a mechanical pen because I have a tendency to write rather hard and there is nothing more jarring then writing and having that nasty snap of the lead....arrrgh.  I have been writing with this on and off for a week and I have had only one incidence of breaking the lead, which is not nearly as many times as I usually experience it.  The kit comes with a little container of extra lead and a couple extra erasers.The technology of the pen turns the lead to keep it nice and sharp.  I wasn't quite sure what to expect, I mean, was I going to hear a sound when I wrote?  No, it is just like using a regular mechanical pen and the technology of it all is transparent to the user.I have already recommended this pencil to my mom who almost exclusively uses mechnanical pencils.  I felt that due to the stronger lead alone that this would be the one that I would purchase again, and I know that she will enjoy the pencil just as much when she tries hers.Overall I felt this was a nice set, good for the mechanical pencil lover and for me, the ultimate crossword puzzle pencil!

This does what its designed to do.  It is intended to be used within another binder, not as a stand alone.  It has a flimsy feel to it when attempting to use solo, however once I installed this within the 5 Star Zipper Binder, it was actually a nice addition.  Its lightweight so it didn't add much additional bulk or weight.

Note: Although Mead suggested that a reviewer examine the entire Writing Fundamentals line, only this Stage 4 item was available to me.My six year old has a lot of difficulty with her fine motor skills. She tries to cram the end of words onto the edges of the page or starts writing sideways down it. She also has trouble, as a left handed person, remembering the proper direction for words and letters. It's not uncommon for her to start writing on the wrong side of the paper or in reverse. I was very pleased with the design of RediSpace transitional notebook paper because it directly addresses this issue. By lining the page with a green 'go' stripe and a red 'stop' line she has a visual cue. With this cue she can start on the proper side and aim her letters at the red line. Mead suggests using this paper for math as well. I think this will make excellent 'scratch' paper for my older daughter. She gets sloppy when converting word problems and carries her 1's to the wrong place in the problem. The spacing bars on the page make it easier to maintain the proper numeric placing when hurrying.The pages came out easily. A bit too easily if one wanted to use this as a journal - for that it would require more careful handing than my kids give their schoolwork.  I could do without the logo branded on to every page. My daughter numbers her pages on the bottom, not the top corner, so the logo in the center of the page is annoying. Overall, that's a small complaint. Mead makes a high quality paper and this product is no exception. This is the rare educational aid that offers real value. A simple, well designed product for kids struggling with their handwriting issues.

I'm not sure if I could accurately quantify a percent reduction in effort required to use this stapler, but I can say that it is noticeably easier.  I compared it to the one that I have been using at work on a stack of papers, and I was sold.  The staples also come out straight.  One of the things that I have noticed with other staplers is that the staples tend to bend when I have to use a lot of force or slam them to get the staple to go all the way through.  I recommend it without reservation.

I gave these five stars, because they're about as good as labels could be.  Of course, at the end of the day, they're still labels.  They are nice, crisp, and sticky, and worked well with my inkjet printer.  (I have aCanon MP530).  Avery's new improvement is their "Easy Peel" technology - there's no label paper in between the columns, so you can bend the paper underneath to get a grip on your finished labels.  I have never noticed problems lifting traditional labels, but if it's a pet peeve of yours, then "Easy Peel" is something to look forward to.Where Avery really impressed me was their software.  If you go to their website, they have four free options to generate labels, including mail merges, included graphics, font formatting, etc.:1) The old standard, Microsoft Word mail merges with templates.  This is pretty much the same as I remembered - the 5160 template works perfectly, and I was able to do a test merge using my holiday list.2) An all online solution, "Avery Design and Print Online."  This is the standout for me.  Cool, fully online, capable of using my data files, with clip art and good features.  I like this a lot.  (It was a little finicky with my address file, but with a little editing, I got things running nicely).3) The "Avery Wizard" is a downloadable wizard that runs inside office products.  It basically does a mail merge, but simplifies things.4) "Avery Design Pro" - I had trouble figuring out this program.  It looks good for cards or envelopes, but for labels this small, it seems like more power than I needed.

I see a lot of negative reviews on this product and at first it confused me.  I can only guess that many if these reviews had earlier versions of the print software or drivers.  The dates on these negative reviews seem to be Summer 2013 or before.  My experience has been positive.  The setup was trouble free.  Print was easy from Windows 7 and IOS.  Network setup was easy although not nearly as speedy for features as direct USB connect.  As a printer this is a 5.  Excellent output quality and speed.  The scanner seems a bit more clugey and I give it more of a 3.  The fax I tested but don't plan on using.  Seems to work fine.  The printer management tools for a device of this class are very robust.  I would say the MFD is well worth the money.

I was hoping to use this as a dispenser of tape for those times when I just need a little piece and don't want to mess with the big, heavy desk dispenser. I initially was hoping to mount it on the door of a cabinet over my desk, but it will not stick on vertical surfaces, no matter how smooth. I suppose it would be handy for wrapping presents, but for the amount it holds and the price, I doubt it would be cost effective.  It would be a much better product if it stuck vertically and to any surface type. As it is, it is a handy gadget but not worth the money.

I've had a few of these Mead workbooks for my niece to work on and she's enjoyed them. Now that my two nephews are both kindergarten, they can enjoy doing these fun workbooks as well.The Mead workbooks work really well in not only educating your child but making it fun to do. This particular  book is based on working on kids problem solving skills. There are pages where children work on writing, rhyming, finding things that don't belong in groups, shapes, colors, counting, the five senses, etc. These activities can keep your children occupied for hours. Being a kindergarten age group, children may need some adult help in knowing what to do on each page but it's a great way for parents to be involved in helping their children learn.I would definitely recommend this workbook for teachers and parents alike.

I like that this binder is recycled and recyclable.  You can take off the rings and spine when your ready to toss it. Although it seems pretty tough so I'm sure it's going to be a long time before it goes on the trash.The brown is a nice color and doesn't look cheap.  Also the included pocket makes it nice to put a notecard, business card, coupon or whatever.Its a pretty cool idea so I can for sure recommend it.

It is alright for the price, I guess.  The blue and green are too dark to clearly see what you are highlighting, so they are useless. The orange and yellow are the best colors, and fluorescent upon drying.  The pink is dull but light enough to see the highlighted words.  They are already drying up and I haven't used them that much or had them for very long.

I was on the hunt for a couple of new all-in-one printers that could work in a mixed Mac/PC environment and wanted to get machines that were fairly well built and had relatively low print costs.  I did not plan on even considering another HP printer since the last HP I had deployed had a number of problems, most of them related to extremely bad Windows drivers and print software.I was strongly leaning towards the Epson 845 Workforce printer, but I thought it made sense to do a comparison with the HP since it also seemed to have all of the features that I needed.  After doing a head to head evaluation between the Epson and the HP 8600 I ended up going with two of the 8600 units.My criteria was that I needed well built all-in-ones that had relatively low operating costs, worked well with Macs and PCs as well as iDevices, had to have good fax and scan capabilities and, very importantly, had to be pretty well built so that in a busy dental practice the unit would not fail prematurely.I did a direct "bake off" in which I purchased an Epson Workforce 845, and an HP 8600 and ran both of them through their paces.In the end I chose the HP 8600 over the Epson Workforce printer.Why?The biggest detriment to the Epson Workforce printer is that it is relatively cheaply built.  It has flimsy paper trays that don't feel particularly solid.  The entire printer actually weighs about 50% of what the HP 8600 weighs.  While `weight' is not a direct indicator of product quality, on something like a printer, which gets a lot of mechanical use of the paper trays and ADF, a more solid feeling, heavier unit, should usually hold up a bit better to normal wear and tear.In other comparisons I observed that the Epson had better draft quality, but the HP was much faster, and seemed to use less ink when it was used in the economy/draft mode.  In Photo printing, neither printer was outstanding, but both would meet our needs for printing casual snapshots or business type photo materials on glossy 4X6 print paper.The single biggest `deal killer' for me with the Epson 845 is that Epson has very lackluster Mac drivers, and their `network scan to PC' software does not currently work with Macs newer than OS X 10.5, which is going on 3 years old.  Epson's inability to update this software (they claimed a new version was in testing) left me with an extreme lack of confidence that if we discovered problems with the Mac OS X software or drivers, that Epson would be prompt with fixing the issue.We also liked the touch-screen on the HP 8600 much better (although sometimes it's a little too sensitive) than on the Epson, as it was larger and could be angled easily.  A final advantage of the 8600 was the included e-print capabilities, such as the ability to set the printer up with its own free HP email print address, so that people can simply send an email directly to the printer with an attachment and have it print emails, pdf files, word documents, etc.  We were also able to easily set the HP up to archive faxes to a network share, as well as creating a "one touch" scan option where the office can scan documents directly to a network share, which is really handy for archiving documents as well as when a receptionist scans something in but someone else on another PC will need to look at the document later.Another plus to the 8600 that's worth mentioning is that ink tanks are loaded directly into the front of the unit.  Simply open up the front service door, and the tanks are ready to be changed.  This beats having to open up the whole printer (as is the case with the Epson and Canon units) and another, added bonus, is that the HP ink tanks are sealed until they are installed into the unit, meaning no smeared or dripped ink from popping off tabs and other parts on the cartridges when you are getting ready to put them in.What's not to like about the 8600?  Not a whole lot, but there are some nits.  If I fax directly from the machine, using my Ooma phone service, I can dial a *99- which dials *99 to disable the Ooma features, followed by a pause, and faxing works.  However, dialing the same way with the print to fax feature on my Mac, does not work, I suspect a problem with the print drivers for OS X.  Fortunately I don't do a ton of print-to-fax jobs, so it's not a deal killer.I do not like how deep the 8600 is with the output paper tray extended for regular size paper.  It's deep enough that in the office location I put it in I am nervous that one of the employees could come around the corner and smack into the paper output tray, possibly breaking it eventually.  I should also point out that the ADF slide adjusters have a little bit of a gap so if you are persistent it is possible to accidentally insert the paper UNDER the ADF feeder, I have also observed that the way this printer feeds documents in to the ADF tends to pull the paper in and crease it, resulting in crooked scans, so it's important to make sure that the ADF guides are snug against the paper you are loading for scan.  This is the first printer I have owned in years that has had this kind of a problem, but since I have two of these and they both work this way I know it's not a defect, but a design issue.Other than that, I don't have too many complaints.  The ink tanks seem to last a really really long time and they are relatively inexpensive when bought in bulk at our local warehouse store.  The costs so far appear to be roughly half of what we were spending on toner for our Brother color laser printer, so the printer will pay for itself in just a few months.All in all we are quite happy with these.  It's worth noting that I bought one HP 8600 Plus and one Premium.  I wanted to add the second paper tray to the 8600 Plus and discovered that I could actually order it from Provantage for about $59 shipped, it's too bad Amazon doesn't sell this part.

This is an excellent double sided mounting tape for small items. However, you have to make sure the surface you attach it to is absolutely clean. If there is oil, dirt, grease, etc, it is not going to stick for very long. And the surface you attach it to has to be dry and stay dry and it has to be strong enough to hold whatever you are mounting. If the surface has been waxed, it may not stick for very long. All you have to do is clean the area where you are going to use it and it will do an excellent job. This is a light to medium strength mounting tape and should not be subject to heat or vibration. If you want to mount something in your car or boat, there are other very high strength mounting tapes. If you want to mount a small picture or similar then use 4 good sized pieces, one in each corner, don't use just one in the middle. This mounting tape would be excellent for mounting poster boards.

Having suffered with many inferior binders, I was glad for the opportunity to test out this Wilson Jones version. With so many NON-durable binders touting their "Heavy Duty" titles, I tend to skeptical. You get what you pay for with binders, so if you're going to spent more than $6 on a 2-inch binder, you're hoping it will last. And I have to say, you won't be disappointed with this.It's solid, without being heavy. The D-rings glide easily open and closed and are constructed to not wear down within a short period which could cause the clips to let papers slide out. (Once a binder's rings get warped you may as well toss it to save the annoyance).There are clear sleeves allowing you to insert decorations/instructions/etc  on the front, spine and back, which is almost expected anymore. I will say that the clear sleeves are not as thick as some binders and to my dissappointment, the back sleeve is bolted down. The bolts make the D-ring bolted within the binder, but this means you can only use the portion to the left of the bolts or grab an exacto blade and gently cut the sleeve from the "bolts". By doing that you can fill the entire back with a paper insert, but you run the risk of ugly cut marks. I did this with a similar binder recently and ended up adding stickers over my poor cut-jobOne cool feature is that the inner pockets are double pockets. So you can put smaller items in the front and the full page sized docs behind them in a separate sleeve/pocket.All in all, this will well outlast its $3 cousins and save you from the frustration when that cheap version quickly flattens into an annoying and ugly waste of money.I'm shaving off a star for:1. Somewhat thin sleeve material2. Back sleeve bolted down (some binders have a hold punched in the sleeve material at that location in order for people to fill the entire back sleeve.3. It's not exactly beautiful. They have a funky angled stitching on the seams, which looks very sturdy but also looks a bit utilitarian.  But once I put some snazzy scrapbook paper inserts in the outer sleeves, no one will notice the "sensible" sleeves.Feel free to ask questions below. Thanks for any positive feedback!

It's tape! Sticky on one side, not sticky on the other. In this age of putting warning labels on hot coffee, have we not become completely immune to this sort of thing?There's not much to say about this actual product. It's sticky. It's that sort of packing tape that you can't rip apart with your fingers like duct tape, so in that sense, it's kind of annoying. You'll either need some scissors, a knife, or a tape dispenser. Basically, it's as good as any packing tape. I doubt that it's worth paying any extra for the "fragile" warning.
